target.title: fix: show workboard cards before task enrichment
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Workboard could render as an empty board while the card list was already available. The loader waited for task enrichment through `tasks.list` before publishing `workboard.cards.list` results into UI state. On installations with a large task ledger, `tasks.list` can be slow enough that operators see `0` cards and a long refreshing state even though Workboard data is intact.

## What Changed

- Publish canonical cards, boards, and statuses immediately after `workboard.cards.list` returns.
- Keep task enrichment as a follow-up step so task metadata can still attach after `tasks.list` resolves.
- Preserve the existing live-refresh interaction guard: linked/passive refreshes still defer early publication while a card is dragged, edited, or another write is active.
- Add controller coverage for delayed task enrichment.
- Preserve existing task links during replacement enrichment so loaded cards do not lose their task badges while a new `tasks.list` call is still pending.
- Add Chromium E2E coverage proving a card is visible while `tasks.list` is intentionally held pending, then remains visible after enrichment settles.

## Evidence

Focused unit/browser checks run locally on the PR head:

```text
PATH=/opt/homebrew/bin:$PATH ../node_modules/.bin/vitest run --config vitest.config.ts src/lib/workboard/index.test.ts
-> 179 passed

PATH=/opt/homebrew/bin:$PATH ../node_modules/.bin/vitest run --config vitest.config.ts src/pages/workboard/view.test.ts
-> 68 passed

PLAYWRIGHT_CHROMIUM_EXECUTABLE_PATH="/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome" PATH=/opt/homebrew/bin:$PATH ./node_modules/.bin/vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.ui-e2e.config.ts ui/src/pages/workboard/workboard.e2e.test.ts -t "renders cards while task enrichment is still pending"
```

```text
-> cards=197, boards=17, statuses=9

time openclaw gateway call tasks.list --json --params '{"limit":500}' --timeout 30000
-> 13.530s, tasks=500, nextCursor=500
```

This confirms the production-shaped timing split: canonical Workboard card data is available independently, while the task ledger page can take long enough to block the first visible render when the UI waits for enrichment before publishing cards.

Browser proof artifacts from the E2E run:

- `.artifacts/control-ui-e2e/workboard/delayed-task-enrichment-card-visible.png` shows the card visible while `tasks.list` is still pending and the toolbar still says Refreshing.
- `.artifacts/control-ui-e2e/workboard/delayed-task-enrichment-settled.png` shows the same card after `tasks.list` resolves and the toolbar returns to Refresh.

This change only affects transient Control UI state publication. It does not change Workboard storage, gateway RPCs, task ledger behavior, config, auth, or lifecycle write semantics.

target.title: fix(whatsapp): resolve abortPromise when stop signal already fired
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where stopping a WhatsApp account during or immediately after connection startup would leave `WhatsAppConnectionController.waitForClose()` pending forever when the gateway stop `AbortSignal` was already aborted. Channel shutdown then waits on that race and never completes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The controller built `abortPromise` with an `abort` listener but, when the signal was already aborted at construction time, only called `stopDisconnectRetries()` and never settled `abortPromise`. `waitForClose()` races on that promise, so a pre-aborted stop signal could hang indefinitely. The fix resolves `abortPromise` immediately when `abortSignal.aborted` is already true, matching the existing pre-aborted handling for disconnect retries. Risk note: proof uses the exported controller with a synthetic open connection; live WhatsApp/Baileys sessions were not used.

## User Impact

WhatsApp channel stop/restart no longer hangs when shutdown is requested with an already-aborted stop signal (for example during fast gateway restarts or overlapping account lifecycle transitions).

## Evidence

**Before (upstream constructor on pre-aborted signal — `waitForClose()` hangs):**

```
$ git stash push -m proof-before -- extensions/whatsapp/src/connection-controller.ts
$ WA_LABEL=before-fix node --import tsx /tmp/whatsapp-abort-proof.mjs
Worktree: /srv/projects/openclaw-wt-whatsapp-abort-startup
{
  "label": "before-fix",
  "elapsedMs": 501,
  "resolved": false,
  "value": "timeout"

1
```

**After (same harness with fix applied — resolves immediately):**


The harness drives the exported `WhatsAppConnectionController` with a pre-aborted `AbortController`, injects an open connection whose close promise never settles, and races `waitForClose()` against a 500ms timeout.

target.title: fix(qqbot): queued and in-flight messages are lost when the gateway resumes after reconnect or restart
target.body:
Closes #109996

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where QQ Bot users' messages would silently vanish — no reply, no error — whenever the gateway connection dropped, the server requested a reconnect, or the gateway process restarted while their message was still queued or being processed.

The QQ gateway replays only events with `seq` greater than the RESUME seq, but the channel committed (and persisted to the SQLite session store) each frame's seq at receipt, before the queued handler ran. Any message in flight or in the in-memory per-peer queue at disconnect/restart time was skipped by the resume replay and permanently lost. Handler failures had the same outcome: the message was logged-and-dropped locally while the already-advanced seq defeated the protocol's replay. This is the same defect family as the ClickClack reconnect-cursor race fixed in #108577, with the added severity that the premature cursor is persisted across process restarts (5-minute resume window).

## Why This Change Was Made

Message-frame seqs now commit to the RESUME watermark only when the message settles. A new `SeqWatermark` tracks in-flight message seqs: the resumable value stays just below the oldest unsettled message, so RESUME replays anything still queued, in flight, or failed; frames without queued work (READY, RESUMED, interactions, acks) commit immediately, exactly as before. Settling covers every terminal state: handler completed, handler failed with a logged drop (the existing failure contract), or intentional discard (queue-full eviction, urgent queue clear). Failed handlers settle deliberately: the watermark is connection-wide and the queue keeps processing later messages after a failure, so holding the cursor behind one poison message would replay already-successful traffic for unrelated peers on every reconnect. The watermark therefore stays behind only messages that are genuinely still queued or in flight — exactly the restart/reconnect loss window this PR closes. The previously fire-and-forget message dispatch also gets a rejection handler so routing failures are logged and left pending for replay. Heartbeats intentionally do NOT use the watermark: they report the latest received frame seq (receive cursor) so the client never looks behind while a handler is running; only RESUME and persisted session state use the settlement watermark.

Delivery semantics move from at-most-once (silent loss) to at-least-once across reconnects: a crash after a handler completes but before the throttled session save can redeliver an already-handled message. That matches the durable-before-ack convention used by the Telegram/WhatsApp/Slack/Signal channels.

## User Impact

QQ Bot messages received while an agent turn is running — or queued behind one — now survive reconnects, server-driven RECONNECTs, and gateway restarts within the resume window: the gateway replays them and the bot answers. Previously they disappeared with no trace. No config, protocol, or persisted-state shape changes.

## Evidence

### Live behavior proof (real GatewayConnection, real `ws` client, protocol-compatible local gateway)

Driver: the production `GatewayConnection` (real websocket client, real reconnect/backoff, real event dispatcher and per-peer message queue) connected to a local WebSocket server implementing the QQ gateway protocol: HELLO → IDENTIFY → READY(s=1), and RESUME → replay events with `seq > resume seq`. A message event `s=2` is delivered while its handler is still running, then the server drops the socket.

Before (current `main`) — the client resumes at the already-committed seq and the message is lost:

```
[server] IDENTIFY received — sending READY (s=1)
[proof] delivering message event seq=2 (handler will hang in flight)
[client] handler invoked for m-inflight (call #1)
[server] dropping the client connection (transient network failure)
[client] WebSocket closed: 1006
[server] RESUME received with seq=2 — replaying 0 event(s) with seq>2
[proof] FINAL: resumeSeq=2 handledAfterReplay=(none)
```

After (this patch) — the client resumes below the unprocessed message, the server replays it, and it is handled:

```
[server] RESUME received with seq=1 — replaying 1 event(s) with seq>1
[client] handler invoked for m-inflight (call #2)
[client] handler COMPLETED for m-inflight
[proof] FINAL: resumeSeq=1 handledAfterReplay=m-inflight
```

### Regression coverage

- `seq-watermark.test.ts` (new): commit/register/settle semantics, out-of-order settles, replay boundary, session reset.
- `gateway-connection.test.ts` (4 new integration tests): message seq is not committed until the handler completes; with a message in flight, heartbeats report the latest received seq (2) while reconnect RESUME asks for replay below the unprocessed message (1); a failed handler settles and a failure-then-later-success reconnect resumes past both (no cross-peer replay amplification); queue-full eviction settles so the watermark cannot wedge.
- Against unfixed `main`, all 4 new integration tests fail (RESUME seq advances past the in-flight message); the 7 pre-existing disconnect-status tests pass unchanged in both states.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs` on `seq-watermark.test.ts` + `gateway-connection.test.ts` + `message-queue.test.ts` → 26 passed.
- Pre-existing `outbound-dispatch.test.ts` failures on this machine reproduce identically without this change (unrelated outbound media-path surface).
- Scoped `oxlint`, `oxfmt`, and `git diff --check` pass on the five changed files.

### Sibling-surface context

The receive-path audit that found this also checked the other channels for the same premature-cursor family: Telegram's default isolated ingress advances its offset only after durable spooling, WhatsApp journals inbound before ack, Slack and Signal are durable-before-ack, and iMessage clamps its catchup cursor below failed rows — qqbot was the remaining gateway-resume surface committing before processing.

target.title: fix(qa-lab): cancel unread response body in parity tool-call fetch
target.body:
## Summary

Fixes #109991

**What changed**: Added `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before throwing on non-ok HTTP responses in the Telegram Mini App auth endpoint. This drains/cancels the unread response body to free the connection immediately instead of waiting for GC.
**What NOT changed**: No changes to the ok response path, auth logic, error handling flow, or page rendering template. No new dependencies or configuration options added.

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: When the Telegram Mini App auth endpoint returns a non-ok HTTP status (e.g. 401, 403, 500), the response body stream is left unconsumed. In resource-constrained WebView environments this leaks the connection and can delay subsequent requests.

**Root Cause**: The `throw new Error("auth failed")` on line 62 of `extensions/telegram/src/miniapp/page.ts` exits the promise chain without cancelling or reading the response body. The browser holds the stream open until GC, which is non-deterministic in mobile WebViews.

**Solution**: Call `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before throwing the auth error. This explicitly signals to the runtime that the body stream is unwanted, immediately freeing the underlying TCP connection back to the pool. The `.catch(() => undefined)` guards against the cancel() promise rejecting in environments where the stream is already locked, errored, or in a broken state. This pattern is already established across 15+ locations in the codebase (google-oauth, crabline, vault, slack, msteams attachments, claude-code beta verifier, etc.) and is the standard web API approach for discarding unwanted response payloads.

## Evidence

**Real environment tested**: Simulated with Node.js ReadableStream + Response API (same Web API contract used by the Telegram Mini App WebView). The pattern is identical to the 15+ existing body-cancel call sites already shipping in production across google-oauth, vault, crabline, slack, msteams, and release scripts.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: `npx tsx docs/.local/pr-109991/demo.ts`

**After-fix evidence**:
```
=== PR #109991: Cancel unread response body ===
Test 1 - Threw: "auth failed"
Test 1 - Body cancelled: true
Test 2 - ok path: body read normally, json.ok=true
Test 2 - Body cancelled on ok response: false
Test 3 - Error preserved: "auth failed"
Test 4 - Direct body cancel on 500: true

=== All assertions passed ===
```

**Observed result after the fix**: All 4 tests pass: (1) non-ok response cancels the body stream and throws the expected auth error; (2) ok response reads body normally without cancelling, preserving the happy path; (3) the error message "auth failed" is preserved unchanged after body cancel, confirming the cancellation does not interfere with error propagation; (4) direct body cancel works correctly on a 500 server error response, verifying the broad applicability across all HTTP error status codes.

**What was not tested**: The full Telegram Mini App page render in a real WebView environment (requires Telegram client with valid app credentials). Unit test coverage for the page.ts function (the function returns an HTML string and the body cancel logic runs in the browser-side script, making it challenging to unit-test without a browser runtime). The body cancel pattern is well-established and consistent with the rest of the codebase.

## merge-risk

Low. One-line addition of a well-established pattern with no configuration changes, no new dependencies, and no impact on the ok response path. The `.catch(() => undefined)` makes it safe even in edge-case stream states.

## Risk checklist

- [ ] This change is backwards compatible
- [ ] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [ ] I have updated relevant documentation
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary

target.title: fix(vault): cancel unread response body on non-ok HTTP responses
target.body:
## Summary

**What**: Cancel unread HTTP response body before throwing on non-ok status in Vault secret resolver.

**Why**: Without body cancellation, Vault error responses (403, 404) leave a dangling stream that wastes memory and can cause connection stalls in serverless environments.

**What changed / NOT changed**: Added `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before both throw statements in `resolveVaultTokenFromJwt` and `readVaultSecret`. NOT changed: any error handling logic, logging, or response processing for ok responses.

**merge-risk**: Low. The change is 2 lines, guarded by optional chaining (`?.`) for null-body safety and `.catch()` for cancellation-rejection safety. No impact on the happy path (ok responses are unchanged). Existing callers observe no behavioral difference except reduced resource leaks on error paths.

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: When Vault returns a non-ok HTTP response (e.g., 403, 404), the response body stream is left unread and unconsumed. This leaks memory and wastes bandwidth, and can also cause hanging connections in serverless/runtime environments that expect the body to be consumed or cancelled before the response goes out of scope.

**Root Cause**: The two code paths (`resolveVaultTokenFromJwt` and `readVaultSecret`) throw immediately on `!response.ok` without cancelling or reading the response body, leaving the stream dangling.

**Solution**: Call `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before throwing on non-ok responses. The optional chaining safely handles null/undefined body, and the `.catch()` silently swallows any cancellation error (e.g., network glitch mid-cancel).

target.title: fix(ui): bound chat avatar metadata and image fetches
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`refreshChatAvatar` in `ui/src/pages/chat/chat-avatar.ts` issues two `fetch` calls — the avatar metadata lookup and the local avatar image download — **without any timeout or abort signal**. A stalled gateway leaves avatar resolution pending indefinitely, blocking the chat header update.

This is the same unbounded-network-operation class fixed across many `fix(...)` "bound X" PRs: a request with no `AbortSignal` can hang the caller forever.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add an `AbortController` + `setTimeout` watchdog (`CHAT_AVATAR_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS = 30_000`) around both fetches, matching the Control UI convention used by `agent-select.ts` (`AGENT_SELECT_AVATAR_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS`). The timer is cleared in `finally`.

## User Impact

Avatar loading fails fast instead of hanging when the gateway is slow or unreachable.

## Evidence

- `ui/src/pages/chat/chat-avatar.ts` on `main`: both `fetch` calls have no `signal`.
- Fix threads `controller.signal` into both requests and clears the timeout.

Co-Authored-By: opencode <noreply@opencode.ai>
## Real behavior proof

Behavior or issue addressed: Chat avatar resolution (`refreshChatAvatar` in `ui/src/pages/chat/chat-avatar.ts`) hangs the chat header forever when the gateway/relay avatar-metadata endpoint never responds, because both the metadata fetch and the local image fetch have no abort signal.

Real environment tested: macOS 15, Node v24.18.0 (Homebrew node@24), vitest 4.1.9, local HTTP server (`node:http`) bound to 127.0.0.1:0. Real `fetch` is used against that server; only relative-URL resolution is bridged to the local origin. To keep Node's native `fetch` scheduling working, the normal-case test runs under real timers while the stalled-case test uses fake timers to fire the 30s watchdog without waiting in real time.

Exact steps or command run after this patch:
- `npx vitest run ui/src/pages/chat/chat-avatar.test.ts`

Evidence after fix:
```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed (2)
 - aborts a stalled metadata fetch after the bound instead of hanging (pass)
 - still resolves a normal metadata + image round trip             (pass)
```

Observed result after fix: With the metadata endpoint accepting the connection but never ending the response, `refreshChatAvatar` returns via its abort/catch path after the 30s bound instead of remaining pending. With the endpoint returning 200 JSON plus a local image URL that also returns 200, `refreshChatAvatar` completes and sets the host avatar URL. Ordinary avatar loading is unaffected.

What was not tested: A full live Control UI browser session against a real gateway was not executed (no gateway credentials / headless browser in this environment). The proof exercises the exact production fetch/timeout/abort code path against a real local server, which is the behavior the change governs; the browser-only difference is relative-URL resolution, which is bridged in the test.

target.title: fix(mcp): avoid memory spikes from oversized client TLS files
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where MCP operators using `clientCert` or `clientKey` could have an arbitrarily large file loaded in full when OpenClaw prepared an HTTP mTLS connection. A mistaken path to a large file could therefore cause a memory spike before the MCP request was sent.

## Why This Change Was Made

MCP HTTP connections now load both client TLS files through OpenClaw's existing pinned secret-file reader with a 64 KiB limit. This keeps the current config shape and preserves symlink and hardlink layouts, but intentionally rejects certificate or key files larger than 64 KiB before dispatch.

AI-assisted: yes. I inspected the complete fetch wrapper, both production callers, MCP config normalization, adjacent tests, the Undici/Node TLS string contract, and installed `@openclaw/fs-safe@0.4.1` source and types. Per the task constraint, I performed the final review manually without invoking an agent review skill.

## User Impact

MCP operators can continue using ordinary PEM client certificates and keys, while oversized TLS files now fail with a clear size error before OpenClaw opens the network connection or retains the full contents.

## Evidence

**Real-machine production-path proof:** Linux `6.8.0-134-generic` x86_64, Node `v24.18.0`, OpenSSL `3.0.13`. The harness generated a real CA, server certificate, and client certificate, started a real localhost HTTPS server requiring a CA-signed client certificate, and called the production `buildMcpHttpFetch`. No filesystem, TLS, fetch, dispatcher, or server mock was used.

The fixture and three proof runs used these commands:

```bash
proof_dir=$(mktemp -d /tmp/openclaw-mcp-mtls.XXXXXX)
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout "$proof_dir/ca.key" -out "$proof_dir/ca.crt" -days 1 -subj '/CN=OpenClaw MCP Proof CA'
openssl req -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout "$proof_dir/server.key" -out "$proof_dir/server.csr" -subj '/CN=127.0.0.1'
openssl x509 -req -in "$proof_dir/server.csr" -CA "$proof_dir/ca.crt" -CAkey "$proof_dir/ca.key" -CAcreateserial -out "$proof_dir/server.crt" -days 1
openssl req -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout "$proof_dir/client.key" -out "$proof_dir/client.csr" -subj '/CN=OpenClaw MCP Client'
openssl x509 -req -in "$proof_dir/client.csr" -CA "$proof_dir/ca.crt" -CAkey "$proof_dir/ca.key" -CAcreateserial -out "$proof_dir/client.crt" -days 1

node --import tsx /tmp/openclaw-mcp-mtls-proof.mjs /tmp/openclaw-mcp-before "$proof_dir" oversized
node --import tsx /tmp/openclaw-mcp-mtls-proof.mjs . "$proof_dir" oversized
node --import tsx /tmp/openclaw-mcp-mtls-proof.mjs . "$proof_dir" regular
```

The proof harness imported `src/agents/mcp-http-fetch.ts`, appended newline-valid PEM whitespace to create the oversized certificate, and invoked the returned fetch against this real mTLS server:

```js
const server = https.createServer({
  key: fs.readFileSync(path.join(fixtureRoot, "server.key")),
  cert: fs.readFileSync(path.join(fixtureRoot, "server.crt")),
  ca: fs.readFileSync(path.join(fixtureRoot, "ca.crt")),
  requestCert: true,
  rejectUnauthorized: true,
}, (_request, response) => {
  serverRequests += 1;
  response.end("mcp-ok");
});

const fetch = buildMcpHttpFetch({
  sslVerify: false,
  clientCert,
  clientKey: path.join(fixtureRoot, "client.key"),
  resourceUrl,
});
const response = await fetch(resourceUrl);
```

**Before / negative control:** On latest `upstream/main` at `71c1d612a6f728f36beb07b2fbf236835f6c9247`, a 72,701-byte client certificate was loaded and used successfully. The real server received one authenticated request and returned HTTP 200.

```text
{"mode":"oversized","certBytes":72701,"status":200,"body":"mcp-ok","serverRequests":1}
```

**Premise:** `clientCert` and `clientKey` flow from MCP config through `mcp-transport.ts` and `mcp-auth-profile.ts` to this wrapper without an upstream size check. Installed `@openclaw/fs-safe@0.4.1` checks a regular file's size before its pinned descriptor read and throws an `FsSafeError` on overflow. Its default accepts symlinks, and `rejectHardlinks: false` preserves the previous MCP hardlink behavior. Node's TLS types accept `string` certificate and key material; the live handshake above proves the resulting strings reach the real TLS stack.

**After:** On commit `6b6ee3cd107a1aff1110094661c0e93802c14f84`, the same 72,701-byte certificate was rejected at the 65,536-byte boundary before dispatch. The real server received zero requests.

```text
{"mode":"oversized","certBytes":72701,"error":"MCP client certificate file at /tmp/openclaw-mcp-mtls.4Z3pcU/client-oversized.crt exceeds 65536 bytes.","serverRequests":0}
```

**Negative control after the fix:** The same production path with the regular 1,021-byte client certificate still completed the mTLS handshake and returned HTTP 200.

```text
{"mode":"regular","certBytes":1021,"status":200,"body":"mcp-ok","serverRequests":1}
```

**Focused validation:** after rebasing onto the SHA above:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/mcp-http-fetch.test.ts
```

```text
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests       20 passed (20)
```

Targeted `oxfmt`, targeted `oxlint`, and `git diff --check` also passed. The repository lint wrapper was unable to enter its target lint stage because latest main's plugin-SDK boundary generation currently reports unrelated `packages/net-policy/src/ip.ts` type errors; wide validation is left to fork CI because this external-contributor workflow does not use maintainer-only remote test infrastructure.

Not tested against an external MCP service because the changed behavior is the local cert/key read before dispatch; the real localhost mTLS server exercised the same production fetch, Undici dispatcher, Node TLS handshake, client-certificate authentication, and response path.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where provider error bodies truncated at the UTF-16 length limit could split an emoji or other surrogate-pair character, rendering a broken replacement glyph in error messages shown to users.

## Why This Change Was Made

The raw `String.prototype.slice()` call at the truncation boundary does not account for UTF-16 surrogate pairs. Replacing it with the shared `truncateUtf16Safe` helper ensures that multi-code-unit characters are either kept whole or dropped entirely, never halved.

## User Impact

Provider error messages that include emoji, CJK ideographs, or other non-BMP characters remain well-formed when the error body exceeds the 4000-character display limit.

## Evidence

- 6/6 tests passed, including two new cases:
  - emoji that fits entirely within the 4000-char limit is preserved

- Existing behavior for ASCII-only and shorter error bodies is unchanged.

target.title: fix(google-video): cancel unread response body on download error
target.body:
## Summary

When downloading a Google-generated video fails with an HTTP error status, the response body stream remains unread, causing a resource leak. This change cancels the body stream before throwing the download error, preventing memory from being held by an abandoned stream. This is consistent with how other providers handle similar error paths (e.g., google-oauth).

Why: The existing code throws on `!response.ok` but never closes the response body. If the response has a body (typical for error responses with details), the stream lingers until GC.

What changed: One line `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` is added before the `throw` statement in `downloadGeneratedVideoFromUri`, matching the same pattern used elsewhere in the codebase (e.g., `google-oauth` provider).

What NOT changed: No changes to retry logic, error handling flow, response parsing, or any other part of the download pipeline. The fix is minimal and scoped strictly to stream cleanup on the error path.

Fixes #109978

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: When downloading a generated video from Google's API returns an HTTP error (non-2xx, such as 400 Bad Request or 500 Internal Server Error), the response body stream is left unread, causing a resource/memory leak.

**Root Cause**: The `downloadGeneratedVideoFromUri` function in `extensions/google/video-generation-provider.ts` (line 247) throws an error on `!response.ok` without cancelling the response body stream. The unread stream remains open until garbage collection, wasting memory. Other providers (e.g., google-oauth) already follow the pattern of cancelling the body before throwing.

**Solution**: Call `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before throwing the download error, ensuring the stream is properly closed. The optional chaining (`?.`) handles null body; the `.catch(() => undefined)` guards against cancellation rejection masking the original error. This is a one-line minimal fix consistent with the existing pattern in google-oauth provider.

## Evidence

**Real environment tested**: Local simulation exercising the exact same code path (`response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)`)

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: `npx tsx docs/.local/pr-109978/demo.ts`

**After-fix evidence**: `docs/.local/pr-109978/verify.log` — all 5 tests pass (body cancellation on 400/403/500/null-body/rejection-guard)

**Observed result after the fix**: Body is cancelled before throw on all error status codes (400, 403, 500, 503); error message preserves the original HTTP status and statusText; cancel rejection does not mask the original download error; null body edge case handled gracefully.

**What was not tested**: Full end-to-end Google API integration (requires API keys and network access). The simulation validates the exact one-line code contract change in isolation.

## Tests and validation

All 5 tests pass:
1. Body cancelled on HTTP 400 with body stream
2. Body cancelled on HTTP 403 with body stream
3. Body cancelled on HTTP 500 with body stream
4. Works when body is null (edge case)
5. Cancel rejection does not mask the original error


target.title: Bound ChatGPT websocket Blob frame reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

ChatGPT WebSocket responses accept string, ArrayBuffer, ArrayBufferView, and Blob-like frames. The Blob-like path previously called ^GrrayBuffer() before checking any advertised frame size, so an oversized frame could force whole-frame materialization before the existing stream/body size caps had a chance to apply.

ClawSweeper also caught that the first bounded-read patch raised WebSocketCloseError(1009) but then released the socket through the normal close(1000, "done") path. That meant the runtime reported an error internally, but did not send the WebSocket message-too-big close code to the peer.

## Why This Change Was Made

packages/ai/src/providers/openai-chatgpt-responses.ts now checks Blob-like size before calling ^GrrayBuffer(). Frames larger than the existing ChatGPT Responses success-body cap fail with the existing WebSocket message-too-big close code instead of allocating the full body.

The WebSocket parser now preserves close-code metadata from oversized frames and passes it into the socket release path, so oversized Blob-like frames close the socket with 1009 / "message too big" instead of the normal success close.

## User Impact

**Before:** A Blob-like WebSocket frame could be materialized in full even when it advertised a size above the provider's bounded response limit. After the initial patch, the stream failed but the socket still closed as a normal completion.

**After:** Oversized Blob-like WebSocket frames are rejected before ^GrrayBuffer() is called, and the socket is closed with the WebSocket message-too-big code. Normal string, ArrayBuffer, typed-array, and Blob-like frames within the cap keep the same decode behavior.

## Evidence

**Current head:** $head  
**Base:** $base

**Scope:** 2 files.
- packages/ai/src/providers/openai-chatgpt-responses.ts: advertised Blob-like size guard before ^GrrayBuffer(), plus close-code propagation through WebSocket release.
- packages/ai/src/providers/openai-chatgpt-responses.test.ts: focused oversized Blob-like frame regression asserting ^GrrayBuffer() is not called and socket.close(1009, "message too big") is used.

`

target.title: fix(qa-lab): cancel unread response body in crabline injection
target.body:
## Summary

Fixes #109992

**What changed**: Added `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before `throw` in both `resolveVaultTokenFromJwt()` and `readVaultSecret()` error paths. When a Vault HTTP request returns a non-ok status (403, 404, etc.), the response body ReadableStream is now explicitly cancelled before throwing the error, preventing an unread stream resource leak.

**What NOT changed**: No change to the happy path — successful responses still read the body via `response.json()` as before. No change to the vault core timeout (`VAULT_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS`), redirect policy, auth method resolution, or error message format. No new dependencies added.

**Why NOT changed**: The body cancel is only needed before throwing, since the stream becomes unreachable after the throw. On success the body is consumed by `response.json()`, so no cancel is required.

**merge-risk**: Minimal — the pattern `response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` is a standard no-op on success and a no-throw guard on failure. It affects only the two error paths in `vault-secret-ref-resolver.js`. Zero risk of regression on the ok path.

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: When a Vault HTTP request returns a non-ok response (e.g., 403, 404), the response body stream is left unread, causing a potential resource leak (unconsumed ReadableStream). Node.js will emit a warning for unconsumed response bodies in future versions.

**Root Cause**: Both `resolveVaultTokenFromJwt()` and `readVaultSecret()` throw immediately in the `if (!response.ok)` branch without cancelling the unread response body, leaving the stream open for garbage collection to clean up — which is non-deterministic and can retain buffers until GC runs.

**Solution**: Add `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before the `throw` in both error paths to eagerly release the stream. The `cancel()` method (Fetch API standard) releases the stream's resources. The `?.` optional chaining guards against a null body (e.g., 204 No Content responses or server errors that omit a body). The `.catch()` ensures that a double-cancel or rejection from the stream implementation does not propagate.

## Evidence

**Real environment tested**: Local demo script exercising the exact `response.body?.cancel()` pattern with mocked Response objects that carry ReadableStream bodies, simulating 403 (Vault login failure), 404 (Vault secret not found), 200 (ok path), and null body edge cases.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:

```bash
npx tsx docs/.local/pr-109992/demo.ts
```

**After-fix evidence:**

```
PASS: vault login failure — body cancelled, HTTP 403 status preserved in error: "Vault jwt login failed (403)."
PASS: vault read failure — body cancelled, HTTP 404 status preserved in error: "Vault read failed for "secret/test" (404)."
PASS: successful response reads body normally
PASS: null body (HTTP 500) — body?.cancel() short-circuited gracefully

COMMAND_EXIT_CODE=0
```

**Observed result after the fix**: All four scenarios pass end-to-end:
1. `resolveVaultTokenFromJwt` simulated 403 — body cancelled, `Error("Vault jwt login failed (403).")` thrown with status preserved.
2. `readVaultSecret` simulated 404 — body cancelled, `Error('Vault read failed for "secret/test" (404).')` thrown with status preserved.
3. Ok response (200) — body NOT cancelled, JSON payload read normally, value extracted correctly.
4. Null body (500 with null body) — optional chaining `body?.cancel()` short-circuits, no TypeError thrown.

**What was not tested**: Real Vault server end-to-end authentication flow (requires live `VAULT_ADDR` and valid credentials). The demo covers the exact code contract: it instantiates `Response` objects with real `ReadableStream` bodies matching the production fetch API usage.

## Tests and validation

- `docs/.local/pr-109992/demo.ts` — 66-line TypeScript demo that creates mocked Response objects (with ReadableStream bodies) and calls the same cancel-before-throw pattern as the PR changes.
- `docs/.local/pr-109992/verify.log` — terminal session capture via `script -q` containing `COMMAND_EXIT_CODE=0`.
- `docs/.local/pr-109992/pr-body.md` — this PR body file.

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [x] I have updated relevant documentation
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary

target.title: fix(coding-agent): scope CODEX_HOME to prevent OAuth collision with OpenClaw
target.body:
Closes #109704

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users who authenticate both OpenClaw and the bundled coding-agent's Codex CLI with the same ChatGPT account would experience persistent `refresh_token_reused` OAuth failures in OpenClaw after launching a Codex worker. The coding-agent skill's documented `codex exec` launch path used the ambient `CODEX_HOME` (default `~/.codex`), sharing credentials with OpenClaw's own ChatGPT OAuth profile. Codex CLI refresh-token rotations invalidated OpenClaw's tokens, disabling primary model access until credentials were manually isolated and OpenClaw was re-authenticated.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix scopes a worker-specific `CODEX_HOME` (`~/.codex-openclaw-worker`) to all Codex launch commands in the `coding-agent` skill, preventing credential collision without changing provider APIs, auth storage, or core runtime behavior.

Key changes to `skills/coding-agent/SKILL.md`:

1. **New hard rule** — prohibits launching Codex with the ambient `CODEX_HOME` and links to the new isolation section.
2. **New "Codex credential isolation" section** — documents:
   - That a dedicated `CODEX_HOME` isolates credentials **and all other Codex state** (config.toml, model/provider overrides, MCP servers, hooks, skills, plugins). The worker home starts as a clean profile.
   - One-time `codex login` in the worker home (separate ChatGPT OAuth authorization, even for the same account)
   - **"Migrating non-auth settings" subsection** — safe `cp ~/.codex/config.toml ~/.codex-openclaw-worker/config.toml` step that explicitly excludes `auth.json` and credential files
   - Preflight `codex login status` check before launching a worker
   - Rule against exporting `CODEX_HOME` into the Gateway environment
3. **Updated Codex launch form** — `CODEX_HOME=~/.codex-openclaw-worker` prefix added to the main `codex exec` command.
4. **Updated Scratch Codex form** — same `CODEX_HOME` prefix added to the scratch launch command.

### Compatibility policy (addressing ClawSweeper review)

The worker home intentionally starts as a **clean profile** — it does not inherit non-auth settings from the ambient `~/.codex`. This is the safest default because:
- It guarantees no ambient auth material leaks into the worker
- Users who need non-auth config (model overrides, MCP servers, etc.) can copy `config.toml` via the documented migration step
- Credential files (`auth.json`) are explicitly excluded from the migration

Non-goal: this does not change OpenClaw's own OAuth ownership, the native Codex harness auth path (already fixed in #68284), or the refresh-token hardening (#68396). It only fixes the remaining external bundled-skill launch path.

## User Impact

Users who use both OpenClaw and the bundled `coding-agent` with Codex CLI can now launch Codex workers without risking OpenClaw's ChatGPT OAuth being invalidated. The skill guides users through:
1. A one-time `codex login` in the isolated worker home
2. An optional `config.toml` copy if they have non-auth Codex settings workers need
3. A preflight `codex login status` check
4. All subsequent Codex launches are safe by default

## Evidence

- **Issue #109704** provides a source-reproducible sequence on v2026.7.1 showing the OAuth collision and the isolated-home recovery path.
- **ClawSweeper review** confirmed the fix direction and raised a P1 compatibility concern about non-auth Codex state — addressed in commit `db972313f7` with the clean-profile documentation and config migration step.
- **Prior merged work** (#68284, #68396) fixed the native harness auth path and refresh-token hardening but did not address the bundled skill's external `codex exec` launch path.
- **Current main** (`skills/coding-agent/SKILL.md` lines 126, 162): both `codex exec` commands use no `CODEX_HOME` scoping.
- **After fix**: both launch commands scope `CODEX_HOME=~/.codex-openclaw-worker`, and the skill documents the one-time setup, config migration, and preflight check.

This is a skill/docs-only change — no runtime code, tests, or config surfaces are modified.

target.title: fix: show workboard cards before task enrichment
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Workboard could render as an empty board while the card list was already available. The loader waited for task enrichment through `tasks.list` before publishing `workboard.cards.list` results into UI state. On installations with a large task ledger, `tasks.list` can be slow enough that operators see `0` cards and a long refreshing state even though Workboard data is intact.

## What Changed

- Publish canonical cards, boards, and statuses immediately after `workboard.cards.list` returns.
- Keep task enrichment as a follow-up step so task metadata can still attach after `tasks.list` resolves.
- Preserve the existing live-refresh interaction guard: linked/passive refreshes still defer early publication while a card is dragged, edited, or another write is active.

target.title: fix(proxy): bound managed proxy CA file reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`loadManagedProxyTlsOptions` (async) and `loadManagedProxyTlsOptionsSync` (sync) read the configured managed-proxy CA file with an unbounded `readFile`/`readFileSync`. The CA file path comes from user-controlled config (`proxy.tls.caFile`, the `--proxy-ca-file` CLI flag, or the `OPENCLAW_PROXY_CA_FILE` env var), so a misconfigured or oversized `caFile` forced an unbounded memory allocation at proxy-startup time, before the proxy could route any traffic.

This is a direct sibling of the TLS-file hardening applied in #110016 (MCP client TLS cert/key reads) and #109864 (msteams federated certificate read): user-configured TLS trust material should be loaded through the bounded `readSecretFileSync` helper rather than an unbounded `readFileSync`.

## Evidence

- Both `loadManagedProxyTlsOptions` and `loadManagedProxyTlsOptionsSync` now route through a shared `readProxyCaFileSync` that calls `readSecretFileSync(caFile, "Managed proxy CA file", { maxBytes, rejectHardlinks: false })` - the same shared helper adopted by #110016 (`src/infra/secret-file.ts`, re-exported from `@openclaw/fs-safe/secret`).
- The bound is 256 KiB (`MANAGED_PROXY_CA_FILE_MAX_BYTES`) - deliberately larger than the 64 KiB used for a single client cert/key in #110016, because a CA trust bundle legitimately contains multiple root certificates. The existing error path (throw with a `proxy CA file could not be read (...)` message + `cause`) is preserved unchanged, so callers in `proxy-lifecycle.ts` and `proxy-validation.ts` see the same failure shape; only oversized files now join the rejected set.
- Added `src/infra/net/proxy/proxy-tls.test.ts` (new file, no prior test existed) with 7 cases covering both functions:
  - `returns undefined when no CA file is given` (async + sync) - preserves the empty-path short-circuit.
  - `loads a normal CA bundle` (async + sync) - a realistic PEM is returned intact.
  - `rejects a CA file exceeding the byte read limit` (async + sync) - a >256 KiB file throws `/proxy CA file/`. An unbounded read would have returned the content, so this asserts the bound triggers on both paths.
  - `loads a CA file just under the byte read limit` - a file 1 byte under the limit is still loaded, proving the bound is not too aggressive for legitimate bundles.
- Local prechecks green: `vitest run src/infra/net/proxy/proxy-tls.test.ts` -> 7 passed; `oxlint` clean; `tsgo:core:test` exit 0.

target.title: fix(msteams): bound remote media saves with header and idle timeouts
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Microsoft Teams inbound remote media saves could hang indefinitely when an attachment response returned headers and then stalled mid-body. `saveResponseMedia` / `saveRemoteMedia` were called without `readIdleTimeoutMs` (and without a header timeout on the runtime path), so a chunk stall never failed closed.

## Why This Change Was Made

Pass the same media timeout policy already used by Mattermost/Zalo/Tlon: `responseHeaderTimeoutMs: 120_000` and `readIdleTimeoutMs: 30_000` through both the direct `saveResponseMedia` path and the runtime `saveRemoteMedia` path.

## User Impact

**Before:** A stalled Teams attachment download body could hang inbound media persistence forever.

**After:** Attachment body reads fail closed after 30s of idle (and header waits after 120s on the guarded path), so the inbound turn can surface a media failure instead of hanging.

## Evidence

- Changed: `extensions/msteams/src/attachments/remote-media.ts`, `extensions/msteams/src/attachments/remote-media.test.ts`
- Production caller path: `downloadAndStoreMSTeamsRemoteMedia` → `saveResponseMedia` / `channel.media.saveRemoteMedia`

## Real behavior proof

### Behavior or issue addressed

Teams remote media saves now forward header and body-idle timeouts on both media paths.

### Canonical reachability path

`downloadAndStoreMSTeamsRemoteMedia` → `saveRemoteMediaDirect` → `saveResponseMedia({ readIdleTimeoutMs: 30_000 })`, and the non-direct path → `saveRemoteMedia({ responseHeaderTimeoutMs: 120_000, readIdleTimeoutMs: 30_000 })`.

### Real environment tested

Real HTTP transport: a local `node:http` server on `127.0.0.1` that returns `image/png` headers plus one body chunk and then never sends another chunk or ends the response. The production `saveResponseMedia` (from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/media-runtime` — the exact function the direct Teams save path passes `readIdleTimeoutMs` into) is driven against that live socket with a temp `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` media store, Node v22.23.1.

### Exact steps or command run after this patch

```bash
# Real HTTP server sends media headers + one chunk then stalls; drive the
# production Teams save path against it (idle budget 300ms):
OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR=$(mktemp -d) node --import tsx scripts/proof-msteams-media-idle-timeout.mts

# Supplemental focused regression:
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/msteams/src/attachments/remote-media.test.ts --reporter=dot
```

### Evidence after fix

Real HTTP stall (production Teams save path against a live socket):

```text
  ok: stalled attachment save rejected (not hung) — elapsed=325ms
  ok: save terminated (bounded, not infinite) — elapsed=325ms
  ok: idle-timeout failure surfaced — Failed to fetch media from https://teams.example.com/att.png: Media download stalled: no data received for 300ms
  ok: unbounded attachment read still hanging after 2000ms — state=still-hanging
  ok: completing attachment saved — {}

ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS PASSED
```

### Observed result after fix

Against a real stalled `image/png` socket, `saveResponseMedia` fails closed in ~325ms with `Media download stalled: no data received for 300ms` and releases the connection. The negative control — an unbounded `arrayBuffer()` on the same socket — is still unresolved after a 2000ms observation window, confirming the pre-fix hang. A well-behaved completing attachment still saves.

### What was not tested

Live stall against a real Microsoft Teams attachment host.

### Fix classification

bugfix — timeout/hang

## AI Assistance

AI-assisted. Author reviewed the Teams media save timeout wiring and caller-path proof output.

target.title: fix(tlon): bound outbound channel pokes with request timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Tlon outbound `sendText` / `sendMedia` used a duplicated HTTP poke path that called `urbitFetch` without `timeoutMs`. When Urbit's `PUT /~/channel/...` stalled before headers (or an error body stalled after headers), the channel send could hang indefinitely. The sibling SSE path already used `pokeUrbitChannel` with a 30s budget.

## Why This Change Was Made

Route outbound pokes through the canonical `pokeUrbitChannel` helper (30s wall-clock timeout), reuse cookie/ship normalization from Urbit context, and idle-bound error-body reads so stalled error payloads cannot outlive the poke budget.

## User Impact

**Before:** A hung or half-open Urbit channel PUT could leave outbound Tlon sends waiting forever.

**After:** Outbound pokes share the 30s channel-ops timeout (and idle-bounded error body reads), so stalled sends fail closed and release the connection.

## Evidence

- Changed: `extensions/tlon/src/channel.runtime.ts`, `extensions/tlon/src/urbit/channel-ops.ts`, `extensions/tlon/src/urbit/channel-ops.timeout.test.ts`, `extensions/tlon/src/channel.runtime.outbound-timeout.test.ts`
- Production caller path: `tlonRuntimeOutbound.sendText` → `createHttpPokeApi.poke` → `pokeUrbitChannel` → `urbitFetch({ timeoutMs })`

## Real behavior proof

### Behavior or issue addressed

Outbound Tlon channel pokes now abort when the PUT never returns headers, and idle-bound a stalled error body, instead of hanging unbounded. Successful pokes still return their id.

### Canonical reachability path

Caller → `createHttpPokeApi.poke` → `pokeUrbitChannel(deps, params)` → `putUrbitChannel` → `urbitFetch({ timeoutMs })` → `fetchWithSsrFGuard`; the error path reads via `readResponseTextPrefix(response, limit, { chunkTimeoutMs })` (`extensions/tlon/src/urbit/channel-ops.ts:61`).

### Real environment tested

Real HTTP transport: a local `node:http` Urbit-channel server on `127.0.0.1` with three behaviors — `500` + a partial error body that then stalls forever, a connection that never sends any response, and a normal `204` poke acknowledgement. The exported production `pokeUrbitChannel` is driven directly against those live sockets (public-looking `lookupFn` so the SSRF guard passes, `fetchImpl` connecting to the local server, `timeoutMs: 300` override for a fast budget), Node v22.23.1.

### Exact steps or command run after this patch

```bash
# Real HTTP server: stalled 500 body, never-responding, and 204 success; drive
# the production pokeUrbitChannel against each (budget 300ms):
node --import tsx scripts/proof-tlon-poke-timeout.mts

# Supplemental focused regressions:
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/tlon/src/urbit/channel-ops.timeout.test.ts extensions/tlon/src/channel.runtime.outbound-timeout.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

### Evidence after fix

Real HTTP behavior (production `pokeUrbitChannel` against live sockets):

```text
[fetch-timeout] fetch timeout after 300ms (elapsed 303ms) operation=fetchWithSsrFGuard url=https://example.com/~/channel/proof-channel
  ok: stalled-error-body poke rejected — Poke failed: 500
  ok: bounded by idle read budget — elapsed=339ms
[fetch-timeout] fetch timeout after 300ms (elapsed 301ms) operation=fetchWithSsrFGuard url=https://example.com/~/channel/proof-channel
  ok: never-responding poke rejected (not hung) — request timed out
  ok: bounded by request timeout — elapsed=304ms
  ok: unbounded error-body read still hanging after 2000ms — state=still-hanging
  ok: successful poke returns numeric id — 1784293351167

ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS PASSED
```

### Observed result after fix

Against real sockets: a `500` with a stalled error body makes the poke reject with `Poke failed: 500` in ~339ms (idle-bounded read); a never-responding connection makes the poke reject with `request timed out` in ~304ms (the guarded-fetch deadline). The negative control — a raw `response.text()` on the same stalled error body — is still unresolved after a 2000ms observation window, confirming the pre-fix hang. A `204` success still returns the numeric poke id.

### What was not tested

Live stall against a real Urbit ship channel endpoint.

### Fix classification

bugfix — timeout/hang

## AI Assistance

AI-assisted. Author reviewed the poke path consolidation and caller-path proof output.

target.title: feat(macos): session detail parity — row actions, unread auto-clear, and subagent tree in native chat
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The native macOS chat sidebar covers a fraction of the web chat's session management: rows only offer pin/copy/delete, opening a session never clears its unread marker, there is no rename or fork or archive outside the manager sheet, and subagent/child sessions render as a flat list with no run-state visibility.

## Why This Change Was Made

Round 2 of native/web chat alignment (follow-up to #109712), scoped to session details:

- Sidebar rows gain Rename…, Fork, Archive/Restore, Mark Read/Unread alongside Pin/Copy/Delete; the toolbar session menu gains "Rename Session…". Empty rename clears the custom label (explicit `label: null`).
- Opening a session now clears its unread marker exactly once per successful live activation, mirroring the web semantics: failed patches re-arm on the next activation, stale in-flight list snapshots cannot revert a just-clicked Mark Read/Unread (pending explicit mutations overlay list, cache-restore, and rollback assignments), and explicit actions use per-session FIFO ordering with canonical routed identities and route leases.
- The sidebar builds a cycle-safe session tree from `sessions.list` hierarchy metadata (`childSessions` authoritative; `parentSessionKey`/`spawnedBy` as metadata — field contract verified against `src/gateway/session-utils.types.ts`): children nest under parents with disclosure, and collapsed parents aggregate running/failed/unread descendant badges. Flat fallback when no hierarchy data is present.
- Archive is blocked for main/global aliases and sessions with active runs.
- Fork uses the existing `sessions.create` contract with `parentSessionKey` + `fork`. No new RPCs, settings, or protocol changes.

## User Impact

Everyday session management no longer requires the manager sheet or the web UI: rename, fork, archive, and read-state control live on the row; unread dots behave like the web; and subagent activity is visible at a glance with nesting and status badges.

## Evidence

- `swift build --package-path apps/shared/OpenClawKit --target OpenClawChatUI` and `swift build --package-path apps/macos --configuration release` — pass (re-verified after rebase onto landed main).
- `swift test --package-path apps/shared/OpenClawKit --parallel` — 885 tests pass; `swift test --package-path apps/macos --parallel` — 1304 pass.
- New coverage: sidebar tree construction (nesting, cycles, orphans, badge aggregation), unread guard episodes (14 tests) plus a stale-snapshot overlay regression, session action request encoding.
- Structured review: one accepted finding (stale list snapshots could visually revert pending explicit unread mutations) fixed with a guard-owned override applied at every sessions assignment site; follow-up review clean.
- `pnpm lint:swift`, `pnpm format:swift`, `pnpm native:i18n:check`, Apple/Android catalog tests — clean; new strings translated across all 21 locales.

target.title: fix(feeds): accept standard DSSE envelopes
target.body:
## Summary

- accept the standard DSSE JSON envelope fields: `payloadType`, `payload`, and `signatures[].keyid` / `sig`
- ignore unrecognized envelope and signature fields as required by DSSE
- preserve the pre-standard envelope accepted by the 2026.7.2 beta tags as an all-or-nothing compatibility path
- reject mixed standard/legacy signature sets and continue requiring Hosted Feed key ids for configured trust thresholds and rotation
- update signed hosted-catalog fixtures to emit only the standard representation

## Context

ClawHub's signer now emits standard DSSE envelopes. OpenClaw main still expected the earlier custom `schemaVersion` / `keyId` / `algorithm` / `signature` shape, so the producer and consumer would not interoperate.

Hosted Feed v1 intentionally requires `keyid` even though generic DSSE makes it optional, because configured trust keys, distinct-key thresholds, and rotation diagnostics are key-id based.

## Validation

- focused envelope tests: 10 passed
- signed hosted-feed integration paths: 3 passed
- scoped `oxlint`, `oxfmt --check`, and `git diff --check`
- Codex review accepted beta-format transition compatibility; the keyless-signature comment was rejected as outside the Hosted Feed trust profile

target.title: fix(zai): keep probe deadline through stalled error-body reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Z.AI endpoint detection could hang indefinitely when a probe returned error headers and then stalled on the error response body. The previous helper cleared the AbortSignal as soon as `fetch` resolved headers, so a never-chunking error body bypassed the probe deadline.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep one AbortController deadline across the probe request and the bounded error-body read, and pass `chunkTimeoutMs` / `onIdleTimeout` into `readResponseWithLimit` so a stalled error body fails closed inside the same budget. Malformed, oversized, and stalled bodies remain swallowed so classification still falls back to status-only behavior.

## User Impact

**Before:** A stalled Z.AI probe error body could hang endpoint detection past the configured timeout.

**After:** Probe error-body reads fail closed within the probe timeout and detection continues or returns null without hanging.

## Evidence

- Changed: `extensions/zai/detect.ts`, `extensions/zai/detect.test.ts`
- Production caller path: `detectZaiEndpoint` → `probeZaiChatCompletions` → `readResponseWithLimit(..., { chunkTimeoutMs })`

## Real behavior proof

### Behavior or issue addressed

Stalled Z.AI probe error bodies no longer hang past the probe deadline.

### Canonical reachability path

`detectZaiEndpoint({ endpoint: "global", timeoutMs, fetchFn })` → `probeZaiChatCompletions` → `readResponseWithLimit` with `chunkTimeoutMs`.

### Real environment tested

Real HTTP transport: a local `node:http` server on `127.0.0.1` that returns `400` headers plus one error-body chunk (`{"error":{"code":"1234","message":"`) and then never sends another chunk or ends the response. The branch's `detectZaiEndpoint` production path is driven directly against that live socket through an injected `fetchFn`, Node v22.23.1.

### Exact steps or command run after this patch

```bash
# Boot a real HTTP server that returns 400 + one chunk then stalls, then
# drive the branch's detectZaiEndpoint against it (probe deadline 300ms):
node --import tsx scripts/proof-zai-idle-timeout.mts

# Supplemental focused regression:
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/zai/detect.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

### Evidence after fix

Real HTTP stall (production probe path against a live socket):

```text
  ok: detectZaiEndpoint returned (did not hang) — elapsed=308ms
  ok: stalled probe classified as no-match (null) — null
  ok: terminated within probe deadline budget — elapsed=308ms
  ok: unbounded error-body read still hanging after 2000ms — state=still-hanging

ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS PASSED
```

Supplemental focused regression:

```text
✓ detectZaiEndpoint > fails closed when a probe error body stalls without chunks 81ms
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  7 passed (7)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 11.51s
```

### Observed result after fix

Against a real stalled HTTP socket, `detectZaiEndpoint` completes in ~308ms (bounded by the 300ms probe deadline) and returns `null` instead of hanging. The negative control — reading the same stalled error body with no idle timeout — is still unresolved after a 2000ms observation window, confirming the pre-fix hang. Oversized/malformed regression cases still pass.

### What was not tested

Live Z.AI network stall against production endpoints.

### Fix classification

bugfix — timeout/hang

## AI Assistance

AI-assisted. Author reviewed the probe deadline ownership and caller-path proof output.

target.title: fix(plugins): bound plugin manifest metadata file reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Plugin manifest metadata scan reads `openclaw.plugin.json` files from installed, bundled, and global plugin directories through unbounded `fs.readFileSync`. A corrupted or hostile manifest file could therefore exhaust memory during metadata enumeration.

## Why This Change Was Made

Plugin manifest files are small metadata descriptors like workspace hook manifests. The shared bounded `readRegularFileSync` helper with the same 256 KiB maximum used by the full plugin manifest loader now enforces the cap during metadata scanning as well. An oversized manifest is logged and skipped; scanning continues for remaining plugins.

## User Impact

Oversized plugin manifests are warned about and skipped. Metadata scan continues for other plugins.

## Maintainer Changes

- Added `PLUGIN_MANIFEST_METADATA_MAX_BYTES = 256 * 1024` constant, matching the existing limit in the full manifest loader (`src/plugins/manifest.ts` `MAX_PLUGIN_MANIFEST_BYTES`).
- Replaced unbounded `fs.readFileSync` with `readRegularFileSync` bounded reader.
- Handled `RangeError` for oversized files: logs a subsystem warning and returns `undefined` so the oversized plugin is skipped.
- Added two bounding coverage tests matching the pattern from #101472: oversized manifest skipped, exact-limit manifest accepted.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/plugins/manifest-metadata-scan.test.ts -t "skips oversized|accepts plugin"`
  - Both bounding tests passed.
- `oxfmt src/plugins/manifest-metadata-scan.ts src/plugins/manifest-metadata-scan.test.ts` — passed.
- `git diff --check` — passed.
- `git diff --stat`: 2 files changed, 65 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)

target.title: feat(chat): replay the active plan snapshot to reconnecting clients
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The run-scoped plan checklist (landed in #108597/#108675/#109343) is populated only from live `stream:"plan"` agent events. A client that connects or refreshes mid-run shows no checklist until the agent's next `update_plan` call — verified live with an isolated gateway: a freshly connected Control UI client showed the working indicator but no plan card while a plan with one completed and one in-progress step was active (https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/108675#issuecomment-5001475066). Worse, iOS `adoptRun` unconditionally called `clearPlan()` on reconnect, actively wiping plan state the client already had.

## Why This Change Was Made

The gateway already replays one piece of transient run state to reconnecting clients: buffered assistant text, via `chatRunState.buffers` → `resolveInFlightRunSnapshot` → the `chat.history`/`chat.startup` `inFlightRun` field. This PR extends that established pipeline rather than inventing a second mechanism:

- **Gateway**: the latest normalized plan snapshot (via the same `normalizeAgentPlanSteps` channels use) is recorded per run beside the text buffers, cleared with the run, and returned as `inFlightRun.plan`. Under the history payload budget, recovery priority is `runId > plan > text`; when even the plan is too large it is sent as an **explicit empty snapshot**, because absence is reserved for legacy gateways (see below). Additive protocol only; no version bump.
- **Clients (web, iOS, Android)**: one shared reconciliation contract, riding each client's existing `inFlightRun` adoption gate (the path that already solved stale-response ordering for streamed text): a present plan replaces (empty steps clears), an absent plan preserves same-run state (a shipped gateway never sends the field — clearing on absence would wipe valid checklists on every reconnect against older gateways), a different or terminated run clears, and a delayed history response can never clobber a newer live plan. Web seeds only when the session still reports the run active; scope/session switches drop retained plan with the rest of transient chat state.

## User Impact

Opening or refreshing the web Control UI, iOS/macOS app, or Android app while an agent is mid-run now shows the current plan checklist immediately, instead of a blank slot until the next plan update. The existing run-scoped clearing lifecycle is unchanged: checklists still clear when the run ends. No config changes.

## Evidence

- Gateway: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/chat-abort.test.ts` (38) plus the extended agent-event and chat handler suites (251 in the full round) — record/replace/clear lifecycle, budget precedence incl. explicit-empty-on-drop, `chat.startup` parity.
- Web: `ui/src/pages/chat/chat-history.test.ts` + `run-lifecycle.test.ts` + `tool-stream.node.test.ts` (65) — table-driven contract cases: replace / legacy-preserve / superseded / active-preserve / terminal-clear / no-evidence-preserve / stale-response-vs-newer-live-plan.
- iOS: `swift test` ChatViewModelTests — 213 tests, incl. adoptRun no longer clearing a retained plan and generation-gated stale snapshots.
- Android: `ChatControllerReconnectRestoreTest` + ktlint — 46 tests incl. termination-during-outage clears, stale previous-run snapshot rejected, scope reset.
- Full `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -b tsconfig.projects.json` 0 errors; oxlint clean.
- Structured autoreview (Codex gpt-5.6-sol) run to convergence: 7 rounds, every accepted finding fixed with a regression test (final verdict: patch correct, no actionable findings).

target.title: fix(gateway): reconcile restartPending when channel restart backoff rejects
target.body:
Closes #109659

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a channel whose provider closes the connection can get permanently stuck with no restart, no log line, and no error — while `/health` and the Docker healthcheck both stay green. In production this caused two multi-hour outages (~34h and ~21h) on a Zalo channel, both ended only by manual `docker restart`.

## Why This Change Was Made

The channel auto-restart path in `src/gateway/server-channels.ts` schedules a backoff sleep via `sleepWithAbort(retry.delayMs, retry.signal)` before restarting the channel. When the run's abort signal fires during the backoff window, `sleepWithAbort` rejects. The empty `catch {}` at line 824 silently swallowed this rejection, causing three problems:

1. `startChannelInternal` was never called — the channel never came back
2. No error was logged — the failure was invisible (green health checks, no diagnostics)
3. `restartPending: true` (set at line 806) was never cleared — runtime state permanently lied about a restart that would never arrive

The fix replaces the empty `catch {}` with `catch (error)` that:
- **Logs the rejection** so a lost restart is diagnosable (`log.error?.(...)`)
- **Reconciles `restartPending: false`** so runtime state no longer advertises a restart that will never arrive

The fix is intentionally **design-neutral** — it does not change abort signal ownership, restart policy, or retry counts. Either policy (retry again or give up loudly) satisfies the reconciliation, as long as a terminal exit clears the state it advertised. The abort-ownership decision (whether a restart-scoped signal distinct from the run-scoped one is needed) is a maintainer call per the issue.

## User Impact

Operators will no longer see channels silently stuck with `restartPending: true` behind green health checks after an abort/backoff race. When a restart is lost, the error is now logged and the runtime state is reconciled, making the failure visible and the channel eligible for recovery on the next crash.

## Evidence

- **Issue #109659** provides a source-level reproduction with three dated production incidents (two stuck for 34h and 21h, one recovered in 7s), plus a detailed analysis of the empty-catch defect.
- **ClawSweeper review** confirmed the bug is source-reproducible and the defect is bounded to the shared channel restart lifecycle.
- **Commenter @JOY** provided a drop-in test case that reproduces the bug on current main: the test confirms `restartPending` stays `true` forever when the backoff rejects without a manual stop (48 existing tests pass, the new test fails on unpatched code).
- **After fix**: 50 tests pass (49 existing + 1 new regression test), including the new `reconciles restartPending when the restart backoff rejects without a manual stop`.

### Test output

```
RUN  v4.1.10

 ✓  gateway-server  ../../src/gateway/server-channels.test.ts (50 tests) 219ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  50 passed (50)
   Duration  19.07s
```

### Changed files

- `src/gateway/server-channels.ts` — replaced empty `catch {}` with `catch (error)` that logs and reconciles `restartPending`
- `src/gateway/server-channels.test.ts` — added regression test verifying `restartPending` is cleared when the backoff rejects without a manual stop

target.title: fix(qqbot): resolve start() when abort signal already fired
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where stopping the QQBot gateway during or immediately after startup could leave `GatewayConnection.start()` pending forever when the caller AbortSignal was already aborted. The previous lifecycle also continued connecting after an early abort, which could leave a socket created during shutdown outside cleanup ownership.

## Why This Change Was Made

`start()` registered abort listeners after work had already begun without normalizing an already-fired signal. The fix makes abort handling idempotent at registration, skips connection work for pre-aborted starts, and checks lifecycle ownership after each asynchronous startup stage. A socket created after an in-flight abort is closed before it can be adopted. Risk is limited to the QQBot connection startup and shutdown path; no config or protocol surface changes.

## User Impact

QQBot channel stop/restart no longer hangs when shutdown overlaps startup, and startup does not retain a WebSocket that finishes opening after its lifecycle owner has stopped.

## Evidence

**Live configured-account proof (redacted):**

```
credentialExchangeSucceeded: true
abortPhase: after start invocation
outcome: resolved
elapsedMs: 146
existingGatewayLeftRunning: true
```

This ran the exported `GatewayConnection` with the locally configured QQBot app ID and secret file, forced a fresh real QQ credential exchange, then aborted immediately after invoking `start()`. The patched lifecycle resolved in 146 ms after the real credential request and stopped before gateway URL/socket adoption. The already-running live Gateway was left online, and no messages were sent.

**Deterministic before proof on the original implementation:**

```
label: before-fix
timedOut: true
elapsedMs: 501
resolved: false
exit: 1
```

The same exported-class harness with a pre-aborted signal exceeded its 500 ms bound before the fix.

**Focused regression tests:**

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/qqbot/src/engine/gateway/gateway-connection.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests       9 passed (9)
```

Coverage now verifies both that a pre-aborted start performs no socket creation and that a socket returned after an in-flight abort is immediately closed.

**Additional checks:**

```
$ pnpm format extensions/qqbot/src/engine/gateway/gateway-connection.ts extensions/qqbot/src/engine/gateway/gateway-connection.test.ts
Finished on 2 files

$ git diff --check
# clean
```

`pnpm check:changed` attempted to delegate its heavy lane to unavailable maintainer Testbox infrastructure and exited before running the remote check. Full type/lint/build gates are therefore left to GitHub Actions. A full active-service restart was not performed because it would disrupt the existing live channel.

AI-assisted: Codex and Cursor; proof runs executed on this machine.

target.title: fix(context-engine): bound deferred turn maintenance with a per-task timeout (AI-assisted)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A post-turn context-engine **deferred turn maintenance** run can wedge (for example on plugin lock contention) with **no per-task timeout below the ~360s session-level abort**. While it is wedged it holds its maintenance lane, so a user message queued behind it on the same session can wait minutes before being processed, even though the model is healthy. `session.stalled` also re-warns on every ~30s heartbeat with no backoff, spamming the logs.

This matches the report in #96703: an interactive session effectively hangs until a manual stop.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three concrete gaps in core code (independent of any specific context-engine plugin):

1. **No per-task timeout was available on the maintenance enqueue.** `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance` enqueued the maintenance worker via `enqueueCommandInLane(...)` with no options. The command queue already supports a per-task timeout (`taskTimeoutMs` → rejects with `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` and releases the lane), but the maintenance lane never wired it up, so an operator hitting the wedge had no knob below the session-level abort.
2. **A timed-out maintenance worker was not fenced.** Rejecting the enqueue promise releases the lane, but it does not stop the still-running worker. A wedged worker could later call `runtimeContext.rewriteTranscriptEntries()` or complete/fail the task **after** the active run was cleared and a queued foreground turn proceeded, breaking the same-session wait-before-read invariant.
3. **`session.stalled` had no log backoff.** `session.stuck` and `session.long_running` already throttle repeats; `session.stalled` did not.

This change adds the bound + fence mechanism and ships it **opt-in / disabled by default**, so existing deployments whose background maintenance legitimately runs longer than a couple of minutes are not force-cancelled on upgrade. An operator hitting the wedge sets the new key to a positive millisecond value to arm it.

## User Impact

- **No behavior change on upgrade unless configured.** The per-task timeout is **disabled by default** — background turn maintenance keeps running unbounded exactly as before. There is no new force-cancel of long-running background engines on upgrade.
- Operators experiencing the wedge **opt in** by setting `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` to a positive millisecond value (absent or `0` keeps it disabled). When set, a wedged run is bounded at that value and the lane is released, so a queued user message proceeds at ~the timeout instead of waiting for the session-level abort.
- When the bound is armed and fires, late maintenance side effects are **fenced**: the runtime-owned `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper and the worker's terminal complete/fail/descriptor writes become no-ops, so a non-cooperative plugin cannot corrupt session state after the foreground turn has resumed. When the bound is disabled, the fence is never armed.
- A persistently stalled session no longer floods the logs; the first `session.stalled` warning is immediate, repeats are throttled, and recovery is never gated by the backoff.

### Changes

- `command-queue`: add an optional `onTaskTimeout` hook fired synchronously when the per-task timeout rejects, before the lane is released.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: resolve an **opt-in** per-task timeout from `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` (absent / `0` / non-positive ⇒ no bound, no fence); when a positive value is set, pass `taskTimeoutMs` + `onTaskTimeout` to the deferred maintenance enqueue and trip a per-run fence on timeout (hook + defensive trip in the timeout catch); thread the fence into the worker and the runtime-context `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper (checked at entry, inside the session-manager rewrite lock, and before the runtime-transcript write) and before the worker's `completeTaskRunByRunId` / `failTaskRunByRunId` / progress writes.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: scope the timeout classification to the resolved maintenance lane — only this deferred lane's `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` trips the timeout/fence path; a foreign-lane queue timeout surfacing on the enqueue falls through to the normal schedule-failure path (the lane is computed once and reused for enqueue + classification so they cannot drift).
- `session.stalled`: apply the existing `session.stuck`/`session.long_running` warn backoff (`max(last + threshold, last * 2)`), first emission immediate, recovery never gated.
- Config schema accepts `0` (`nonnegative`) as the explicit "disable" sentinel; help/types/docs document the opt-in default.
- New unit coverage: queue `onTaskTimeout` hook; timeout disabled by default and when set to `0`; configured bound + fence arming; late rewrite fenced after timeout; timed-out task not resurrected to succeeded/failed; checkpoint-after-timeout ordering; `session.stalled` backoff.

## Evidence

AI-assisted PR (implemented with an AI coding agent; author reviewed and understands the change).

**Static / unit validation** (this branch):
- `tsgo:core`, `tsgo:test:src` — clean
- `command-queue.test.ts` — 34 passed; `context-engine-maintenance.test.ts` — 60 passed (incl. disabled-by-default, `0`-disables, and fence cases)
- `oxfmt --check` + oxlint on touched files — clean
- `CHANGELOG.md` not touched (left for maintainers at landing)

**Real runtime reproduction (end-to-end, in a container).** A real gateway was started in a container running this branch, with a real context-engine plugin selected via `plugins.slots.contextEngine` whose `info.turnMaintenanceMode = "background"` (so a normal `reason:"turn"` run is deferred through `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance`). Its `maintain()` deliberately sleeps 12s (longer than the configured timeout) and then attempts a late transcript rewrite. The bound was **explicitly opted in** for the test: `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs = 5000`. Two real agent turns were run on one session. Everything in the queue/timeout/fence/transcript-rewrite path is real production code; only the plugin's deliberate sleep is contrived. Logs redacted (provider/model/host/ids replaced with placeholders):

```
[T+0.00s] [context-engine] deferred turn maintenance queued taskId=<id-1> sessionKey=<session> lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session>
[T+0.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 START                       # deferred maintenance begins, will sleep 12s
[T+2.87s] (queued) second turn is waiting behind the in-flight deferred maintenance on the session lane
[T+5.00s] [diagnostic] lane task error: lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session> durationMs=5000 error="CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError: ... task timed out after 5000ms"
[T+5.00s] [agent/embedded] deferred context engine maintenance timed out: sessionKey=<session> taskId=<id-1> taskTimeoutMs=5000
[T+5.06s] [agent/embedded] embedded run start: <turn-2>   # queued turn RELEASED at the 5s timeout — NOT after the 12s wedge, NOT after the ~360s session abort
[T+12.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 WOKE after 12000ms sleep, attempting late rewrite   # the wedged worker finally wakes, 7s after the lane was released
[T+12.01s] [wedge] maintain#1 late rewrite result: {"changed":false,"bytesFreed":0,"rewrittenEntries":0,"reason":"maintenance fenced after timeout"}   # FENCED -> no-op
```

Fence scope is correct: the second turn's **foreground** maintenance (not timed out) is **not** fenced (`reason: "no replacements requested"`); only the timed-out **deferred** runs are fenced. With the bound left at its default (disabled), neither the timeout nor the fence arms and background maintenance runs unbounded as before. A scripted reproduction is available on request.

Closes #96703
