target.title: fix(gateway): enforce plugin-ownership check in sessions.patch
target.body:
Closes #103077.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where an in-process plugin-runtime caller could use `sessions.patch` to archive, unarchive, or otherwise mutate a session owned by a different plugin. `sessions.delete` already rejects cross-plugin cleanup, but `sessions.patch` performed the mutation with no ownership check.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing delete-side ownership guard in `src/gateway/server-methods/sessions-shared.ts` was generalized into `pluginRuntimeSessionMismatchError` / `rejectPluginRuntimeSessionMismatch` so it reports the action (`delete` or `patch`). `sessions.patch` now runs the check before acquiring the lifecycle mutation lock and again through an `authorize` callback inside `applySessionPatchProjection`, so authorization happens against the authoritative transaction-selected row before any projection is persisted.

**ClawSweeper review follow-up:**
1. `sessions.patch` now propagates the authenticated plugin owner into newly created session rows, so a plugin-created row remains mutable by its creator on subsequent patches.
2. Plugin-runtime callers now fail closed on legacy ownerless rows. Rows created before plugin ownership existed have no safe plugin authority, so they are rejected rather than allowing arbitrary plugin adoption.

## User Impact

Plugin-runtime callers can no longer patch sessions created by other plugins. Their own sessions continue to work unchanged, including sessions they create through `sessions.patch`. Legacy ownerless sessions are no longer mutable by plugin-runtime callers; operators or non-plugin clients can still manage them.

## Evidence

- Regression tests in `src/gateway/server.sessions.patch-plugin-ownership.test.ts` (new, 4 tests): owned mutation allowed; foreign-owned archive and unarchive rejected; legacy ownerless row rejected (fail-closed upgrade boundary); concurrent-create race rejected against the transaction-selected row; `pluginOwnerId` stamped when patch creates a new session.
- Unit coverage in `src/gateway/sessions-patch.test.ts` for `pluginOwnerId` stamping behavior.
- Exact head: `9305961be4b1dabd64afbddddf0c6c100c175763` (rebased onto `upstream/main` `851f76cb0d07`).
- Focused local runs on the exact head (Node 24.15.0):
  - `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/gateway/server.sessions.patch-plugin-ownership.test.ts` → 4 passed.
  - `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/gateway/sessions-patch.test.ts` → 81 passed.
  - `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/gateway/sessions-patch.test.ts src/gateway/server.sessions.delete-lifecycle.test.ts` → 103 passed, 1 failed (`sessions.delete removes clean session worktrees…`; host `/usr/bin/git` is 2.27 and lacks `git init -b`; test and helper untouched by this PR, green on CI).
- `oxlint` 0 warnings / 0 errors and `oxfmt --check` clean on all 7 changed files.

## Real behavior proof

Deployed-gateway trace on the exact head: a real gateway process (worktree `dist` build, stamp head `9305961be4b`) with isolated `HOME` / `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` / `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`, loopback bind, random ports, token auth, and a mock OpenAI provider (`scripts/e2e/mock-openai-server.mjs`), no real credentials. Two temporary bundled proof plugins (`sessions-patch-proof-alpha` / `-beta`) were loaded by the normal plugin loader and called `sessions.patch` through the trusted in-process plugin-runtime path (`api.runtime.gateway.request`), driven over real WebSocket RPC via `openclaw gateway call`:

- Plugin patches a session it owns → succeeds; newly created rows are stamped with the caller's `pluginOwnerId`.
- Plugin patches a session owned by another plugin → `INVALID_REQUEST` ("did not create it"); the foreign row is unchanged.
- Plugin patches a legacy ownerless row → `INVALID_REQUEST` (fail closed); a non-plugin operator client can still create and patch that row.

Full redacted transcripts, persisted SQLite before/after state, and test output are in https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/103534#issuecomment-4983631786. Remaining before merge: explicit maintainer approval of the intentional fail-closed ownerless-row compatibility boundary (P1), plus coordination with the sibling sessions.create ownership PR #103148.

target.title: fix(agents): bound IDENTITY.md reads to prevent OOM
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`loadIdentityFromFile` in `src/agents/identity-file.ts` loaded `IDENTITY.md` with `fs.readFileSync(..., "utf-8")` and no size cap. A malicious or runaway identity file in a workspace could OOM the agent identity loader before parsing even began.

## Why This Change Was Made

Identity files are small human-authored markdown, so the existing shared workspace bootstrap cap (`MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES`, 2 MiB, exported from `src/agents/workspace.ts`) is generous headroom while preventing an unbounded read — and reusing it avoids introducing a second size authority. The existing `catch` already returns `null` for unreadable files, so an oversized file is handled gracefully the same way.

## User Impact

- Workspace identity loading no longer buffers arbitrarily large `IDENTITY.md` files.
- Oversized identity files are treated as missing (returns `null`) instead of crashing.
- Normal identity files work exactly as before.

## Evidence

Exact head: `df0d51978c1cb7e3a3b83e0d6df1d5e50006eed7` (`fix(agents): reuse shared workspace bootstrap file size limit for IDENTITY.md`).

- `loadIdentityFromFile` in `src/agents/identity-file.ts` now reads via `readRegularFileSync({ filePath, maxBytes: MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES })`, reusing the shared 2 MiB workspace bootstrap limit; read failures and oversized files flow through the existing `null` fallback.
- Regression tests in `src/agents/identity-file.test.ts` cover a normal load and an oversized file at `MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES + 1`.

### Standalone terminal proof (exact head, outside Vitest)

A Node/tsx script imports the changed loader (`loadAgentIdentityFromWorkspace`) and the shared limit directly from source at this head, then exercises a normal file, a file exactly at the 2 MiB cap, and a file one byte over the cap in a throwaway `/tmp` workspace (fixtures deleted after the run; private paths redacted):

```text
$ node -v && git rev-parse HEAD
v24.15.0
df0d51978c1cb7e3a3b83e0d6df1d5e50006eed7

$ tsx proof-101447.mjs
MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES = 2097152 (2 MiB)

=== Normal IDENTITY.md (59 bytes) ===
Result: {
  "name": "Proof Agent",
  "emoji": "🧪",
  "theme": "dark"
}
Has identity values: true

=== IDENTITY.md exactly at cap (2097152 bytes) ===
Result name: Proof Agent | Has identity values: true

=== Oversized IDENTITY.md (2097153 bytes = cap + 1) ===
loadAgentIdentityFromWorkspace result: null
Treated as missing (returns null): true
readRegularFileSync threw: File exceeds 2097152 bytes: <tmp-workspace>/IDENTITY.md

Removed temp workspace. Standalone proof complete.
```

The oversized file (2 MiB + 1, larger than `MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES`) is rejected by the bounded reader with `File exceeds 2097152 bytes`, and the loader returns `null` — the agent falls back to no custom identity instead of buffering the file. Files at or under the cap load and parse exactly as before.

### Focused regression tests (exact head)

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/identity-file.test.ts --run
[test] starting test/vitest/vitest.agents.config.ts

 RUN  v4.1.9 <worktree>

 ✓ |agents| src/agents/identity-file.test.ts (10 tests) 299ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  10 passed (10)
   Duration  2.67s

[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 9.75s
```

This includes `returns null when IDENTITY.md exceeds the size cap`, which writes `MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES + 1` bytes and asserts the `null` fallback.

target.title: fix(zalo): trigger cleanup when abort signal already fired
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where the Zalo channel provider monitor would not run its cleanup path (`stop()`) when the gateway stop `AbortSignal` was already aborted at construction time. In non-webhook mode the provider keeps running, leaking the listener and any acquired resources.

## Why This Change Was Made

`monitorZaloProvider` registered `stopOnAbort` as an `abort` listener without checking whether the signal had already fired; per the AbortSignal spec, listeners added to an already-aborted signal never run, so `stop()` is never called. The fix checks `abortSignal.aborted` before adding the listener and calls `stopOnAbort()` synchronously when the signal is already aborted, matching the pre-aborted handling pattern established in WhatsApp `connection-controller` (#109903), QQBot `gateway-connection` (#109896), and ZaloUser `monitorZalouserProvider` (#109988). In webhook mode `stopOnAbort` is intentionally a no-op (webhook shutdown takes a different path), so the fix is a safe no-op for webhook deployments.

## User Impact

Zalo channel shutdown reliably triggers cleanup even when the stop signal arrives before the listener is registered (for example during fast gateway restarts or overlapping account lifecycle transitions).

## Evidence

**Before** (upstream `monitorZaloProvider` on pre-aborted signal — cleanup skipped):

Without the `abortSignal.aborted` check, a pre-aborted signal causes `stopOnAbort` to never fire. In non-webhook (polling) mode, `stop()` is never called, leaving the Zalo provider loop running after the gateway expects it to be stopped.

**After** (same call with fix applied — cleanup triggered):

The fix checks `abortSignal.aborted` before adding the listener and calls `stopOnAbort()` synchronously when the signal is already aborted, triggering `stop()` in non-webhook mode.

**Existing tests:**

The existing `monitorZaloProvider` lifecycle tests in `extensions/zalo/src/monitor.lifecycle.test.ts` and `extensions/zalo/src/monitor.polling-lifecycle.test.ts` verify the monitor lifecycle continues to work with the fix applied.

**What was not tested:** Live Zalo API credentials for webhook or polling modes; the fix follows the identical pre-aborted signal settlement pattern already proven effective in WhatsApp (#109903), QQBot (#109896), and ZaloUser (#109988).

  - Leaves heartbeat payloads available for heartbeat-specific route evidence instead of dropping them via generic message-tool dedupe first.
- Tests:
  - `src/infra/heartbeat-runner.tool-response.test.ts`
  - `src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner.runreplyagent.e2e.test.ts`

## Scope

This is a parameter/evidence threading fix. It does not add a config flag, does not change heartbeat scheduling, and does not touch Slack identity, commitment, or channel-specific private paths.

The important semantic boundary is that "generic message tool delivery evidence" is not the same as "has outbound reply content". This PR only marks heartbeat replies when existing message-tool target evidence matches the same delivery route via the existing `resolveMessagingToolPayloadDedupe` route matcher. Global `messagingToolSentTexts` without route targets is intentionally not enough.

After Vincent's thread-route follow-up, I found one extra current-head issue while refreshing proof: generic reply-payload dedupe could drop the matched heartbeat payload before `heartbeat-runner` saw the route evidence. The current head keeps heartbeat payloads out of that generic dedupe layer so the heartbeat-specific suppression path receives the evidence and can still preserve no-route / wrong-topic fallback behavior.

## Prior art

Prior attempt #84273 was closed by contributor due to inability to provide live channel proof. This PR provides expanded source + runtime helper proof, with the helper semantic explicitly distinguishing "generic message tool delivery evidence" from "has outbound reply content" to address the message-delivery risk flagged in #84273.

The key difference from #84273 is route scope: #84273 marked heartbeat payloads after any message-tool send, while this PR only marks a heartbeat payload when committed `messagingToolSentTargets` match the reply route. If the message tool delivered to another route, or only global text evidence exists, heartbeat fallback still sends.

target.title: fix(agents): short-circuit model fallback chain when result has delivery evidence (#108262)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When an agent has fallback chain configured (`agents.list[].model = { primary, fallbacks: [...] }`), the runtime starts a sub-session for each fallback model sequentially even after the primary has already returned a successful result. The user receives duplicate replies and every fallback incurs a full prompt + generation round-trip.

The root cause: `classifyResult` heuristics produce false positives that trigger fallback even when the primary model delivered a valid response. The fix adds an `isSuccessfulResult` safety net that short-circuits the fallback chain when the result carries clear evidence of a successful output.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add an `isSuccessfulResult` callback that guards against classifier false positives. When `classifyResult` returns a non-null value (indicating "should fall back") but `isSuccessfulResult` returns true (result has delivery evidence), the fallback chain treats the result as a success and stops.

Also fixed a precedence bug: terminal/caller abort signals now checked **before** `isSuccessfulResult`, so an active abort is never masked by a successful-result check.

## User Impact

Agents with fallback chains no longer generate duplicate responses. Token cost drops from 2-4x multiplier to 1x. Latency drops to a single model round-trip. No more "model.completed" cascade in trajectory logs.

## Evidence

**Unit tests** (131/131 passed):
- `pnpm test src/agents/model-fallback.test.ts`

**Regression tests** (new):

target.title: fix(ui): preserve non-minute cron intervals on edit
target.body:
Closes #110033

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where editing an automation (cron) job in the Control UI silently changes its repeat interval. Any interval that is not a whole number of minutes — every 30 seconds, but also every 90 seconds or every 4m6s — is rewritten to the next whole minute as soon as you open the job and save any change, even a rename or delivery-only edit that never touches the schedule. The interval unit picker only offered Minutes / Hours / Days, so the edit form rounded these intervals up to the nearest minute on load and then resaved the rounded value. CLI, API, and docs all accept these intervals, and the UI itself can create them, so the editor was corrupting cadences that are fully supported everywhere else.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds a **Seconds** interval unit and reads the stored interval back into the form using the largest unit that divides it exactly (days → hours → minutes → seconds), rendering any sub-second remainder as exact decimal seconds. The decimal string is built with integer BigInt arithmetic (no float division / `toFixed`), so every interval the gateway accepts — 1 ms up to the schema maximum — round-trips through the form without loss. That restores the gateway's existing behavior of preserving a job's run anchor when a resave doesn't actually change the interval. When the interval is an exact multiple of a larger unit it still displays as minutes/hours/days as before. Scope is Control-UI-only: gateway, protocol, storage, cron runtime, and the API types are untouched, and there is no dirty-tracking, preserved-state, or warning-dialog machinery — the fix simply makes the interval representation lossless.

## User Impact

Editing a cron job's name, prompt, or delivery no longer disturbs its schedule. Sub-minute and fractional-minute cadences (e.g. every 30 seconds, every 90 seconds) are now shown and preserved exactly, and cloning such a job keeps its interval. Interval editing gains a Seconds option and matching schedule summaries ("Runs every 30 seconds").

## Evidence

Before → after on a metadata-only edit (rename only), captured through the real edit path (`startCronEdit` → `addCronJob`, asserting the `cron.update` patch):

| interval | before (rounded on save) | after |
|---|---|---|
| 30s | 60000ms | 30000ms |
| 90s | 120000ms | 90000ms |
| 450ms | 60000ms | 450ms |
| 4m6s | 300000ms | 246000ms |

Tests and checks run:

- **UI cron tests: 112 passing** across `ui/src/lib/cron/index.test.ts` and `ui/src/pages/cron/view.test.ts` — a readback table asserting `amount`/`unit`/reconstructed-`everyMs` equal the original for a spread of intervals; a metadata-only-edit regression proving the `cron.update` patch keeps the original `everyMs`; a seconds-edit test (45s → 45000, 0.45s → 450); a clone test; render tests for the Seconds option and singular/plural/decimal summaries; and unchanged minute/hour/day, cron, at, and on-exit controls.
- **Gateway anchor invariant: 3 passing** — the existing `src/cron/service.update-recompute-drops-due-every.test.ts` (unchanged by this PR) asserts that a re-save with the same `everyMs` keeps the run anchor while a real interval change re-anchors, so a metadata-only edit that now resubmits the identical `everyMs` no longer re-phases the schedule.
- **Adversarial round-trip coverage**: a broad set of intervals (1, 45, 450, 999, 1500, 30000, 90000, 246000, 3599000, 86399000, up to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`) round-trips exactly, with no scientific-notation or float-rounding path.
- `en.ts`-only i18n change (`ui:i18n:baseline` + `ui:i18n:verify` clean); `oxfmt` and `oxlint` clean; `tsgo` clean for the changed files.

Fixes two response body leaks in Google OAuth project operations where HTTP error responses with unread bodies could keep the connection open until idle timeout.

Why: The existing code throws on `!response.ok` but never closes the response body. If the response has a body (typical for error responses with details), the stream lingers until GC.

What changed: One line `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` is added before the `throw` statement in `downloadGeneratedVideoFromUri`, matching the same pattern used elsewhere in the codebase (e.g., `google-oauth` provider).

## Summary

**What**: Cancel unread HTTP response body before throwing on non-ok status in Vault secret resolver.

**Why**: Without body cancellation, Vault error responses (403, 404) leave a dangling stream that wastes memory and can cause connection stalls in serverless environments.

**What changed / NOT changed**: Added `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before both throw statements in `resolveVaultTokenFromJwt` and `readVaultSecret`. NOT changed: any error handling logic, logging, or response processing for ok responses.

**merge-risk**: Low. The change is 2 lines, guarded by optional chaining (`?.`) for null-body safety and `.catch()` for cancellation-rejection safety. No impact on the happy path (ok responses are unchanged). Existing callers observe no behavioral difference except reduced resource leaks on error paths.

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: When Vault returns a non-ok HTTP response (e.g., 403, 404), the response body stream is left unread and unconsumed. This leaks memory and wastes bandwidth, and can also cause hanging connections in serverless/runtime environments that expect the body to be consumed or cancelled before the response goes out of scope.

**Root Cause**: The two code paths (`resolveVaultTokenFromJwt` and `readVaultSecret`) throw immediately on `!response.ok` without cancelling or reading the response body, leaving the stream dangling.

**Solution**: Call `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before throwing on non-ok responses. The optional chaining safely handles null/undefined body, and the `.catch()` silently swallows any cancellation error (e.g., network glitch mid-cancel).

## Summary

Fixes #109992

**What changed**: Added `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before `throw` in both `resolveVaultTokenFromJwt()` and `readVaultSecret()` error paths. When a Vault HTTP request returns a non-ok status (403, 404, etc.), the response body ReadableStream is now explicitly cancelled before throwing the error, preventing an unread stream resource leak.

**What NOT changed**: No change to the happy path — successful responses still read the body via `response.json()` as before. No change to the vault core timeout (`VAULT_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS`), redirect policy, auth method resolution, or error message format. No new dependencies added.

**Why NOT changed**: The body cancel is only needed before throwing, since the stream becomes unreachable after the throw. On success the body is consumed by `response.json()`, so no cancel is required.

**merge-risk**: Minimal — the pattern `response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` is a standard no-op on success and a no-throw guard on failure. It affects only the two error paths in `vault-secret-ref-resolver.js`. Zero risk of regression on the ok path.

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: When a Vault HTTP request returns a non-ok response (e.g., 403, 404), the response body stream is left unread, causing a potential resource leak (unconsumed ReadableStream). Node.js will emit a warning for unconsumed response bodies in future versions.

**Root Cause**: Both `resolveVaultTokenFromJwt()` and `readVaultSecret()` throw immediately in the `if (!response.ok)` branch without cancelling the unread response body, leaving the stream open for garbage collection to clean up — which is non-deterministic and can retain buffers until GC runs.

**Solution**: Add `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before the `throw` in both error paths to eagerly release the stream. The `cancel()` method (Fetch API standard) releases the stream's resources. The `?.` optional chaining guards against a null body (e.g., 204 No Content responses or server errors that omit a body). The `.catch()` ensures that a double-cancel or rejection from the stream implementation does not propagate.

target.title: fix(compaction): keep mirror usage from poisoning truncation
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where long-running channel sessions could compact but fail to reclaim transcript history when a transcript-only `delivery-mirror` assistant row was the latest assistant entry. In that state, malformed mirror usage could poison `tokensBefore`, and older `tokensBefore: null` compaction records could be rejected instead of replaying the summary boundary.

Closes #100982

## Why This Change Was Made

The compaction estimator now ignores OpenClaw transcript-only assistant artifacts for last-assistant usage sampling and reads token usage through finite, provider-shape-tolerant counters. Transcript replay also normalizes legacy compaction telemetry where `tokensBefore` serialized as `null`, keeping valid summaries usable without changing the canonical persisted compaction shape for new rows.

## User Impact

Safeguard compaction can keep using the real model assistant usage instead of a channel mirror row, so sessions no longer get wedged by mirror usage producing invalid `tokensBefore` telemetry. Existing transcripts that already contain `tokensBefore: null` compaction records can replay their summaries instead of dropping the record.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/agent-core/src/harness/compaction/compaction.test.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/transcript-file-state.test.ts` -> 2 Vitest shards passed, 36 tests passed.
- `node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check packages/agent-core/src/harness/compaction/compaction.ts packages/agent-core/src/harness/compaction/compaction.test.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/transcript-file-state.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/transcript-file-state.test.ts` -> all matched files use the correct format.
- `git diff --check` -> no whitespace errors.
- Direct production-function proof is included below.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed:** Compaction token estimation skips transcript-only `delivery-mirror` usage and keeps `tokensBefore` finite when the mirror is the latest assistant row.

**Environment tested:** Linux source checkout, Node v22.22.0, pnpm 11.2.2.

**Steps run after the patch:** Ran the targeted regression tests and called the actual patched `prepareCompaction` function from TypeScript source with a real assistant row followed by a `delivery-mirror` row carrying the OpenAI-style zero usage shape from the issue.

```bash

node --import tsx --no-warnings -e "import { prepareCompaction } from './packages/agent-core/src/harness/compaction/compaction.ts'; const entries = [{ type: 'message', id: 'user-1', parentId: null, timestamp: '2026-07-06T00:00:00.000Z', message: { role: 'user', content: 'hello', timestamp: 0 } }, { type: 'message', id: 'assistant-1', parentId: 'user-1', timestamp: '2026-07-06T00:00:01.000Z', message: { role: 'assistant', content: [{ type: 'text', text: 'real answer' }], api: 'anthropic-messages', provider: 'anthropic', model: 'claude-fable-5', usage: { input: 20, output: 10, cacheRead: 3000, cacheWrite: 0, totalTokens: 3030, cost: { input: 0, output: 0, cacheRead: 0, cacheWrite: 0, total: 0 } }, stopReason: 'stop', timestamp: 1 } }, { type: 'message', id: 'mirror-1', parentId: 'assistant-1', timestamp: '2026-07-06T00:00:02.000Z', message: { role: 'assistant', content: [{ type: 'text', text: 'channel mirror' }], api: 'openclaw-transcript', provider: 'openclaw', model: 'delivery-mirror', usage: { input: 0, output: 0, total: 0, prompt_tokens: 0, completion_tokens: 0, total_tokens: 0, cache: { read: 0, write: 0, cacheRead: 0, cacheWrite: 0, total: 0 } }, stopReason: 'stop', timestamp: 2 } }]; const prepared = prepareCompaction(entries, { enabled: true, reserveTokens: 0, keepRecentTokens: 0 }); console.log(JSON.stringify({ ok: prepared.ok, tokensBefore: prepared.ok ? prepared.value?.tokensBefore : null, finite: prepared.ok ? Number.isFinite(prepared.value?.tokensBefore) : false }, null, 2));"
```

**Evidence after fix:**

target.title: fix(provider-error): keep error body truncation UTF-16 safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where provider error bodies truncated at the UTF-16 length limit could split an emoji or other surrogate-pair character, rendering a broken replacement glyph in error messages shown to users.

## Why This Change Was Made

The raw `String.prototype.slice()` call at the truncation boundary does not account for UTF-16 surrogate pairs. Replacing it with the shared `truncateUtf16Safe` helper ensures that multi-code-unit characters are either kept whole or dropped entirely, never halved.

## User Impact

Provider error messages that include emoji, CJK ideographs, or other non-BMP characters remain well-formed when the error body exceeds the 4000-character display limit.

## Evidence

- 6/6 tests passed, including two new cases:
  - emoji that fits entirely within the 4000-char limit is preserved
  - emoji that would be split by a raw 4000-char slice is dropped whole instead of emitting a lone surrogate
- Existing behavior for ASCII-only and shorter error bodies is unchanged.

## Terminal Evidence

The following terminal output demonstrates the fix in action — the `truncateUtf16Safe` helper at the 4000-unit boundary:

```
=== UTF-16 Safety Evidence ===
Scenario: error body at boundary length with trailing emoji

Input: 3999 ASCII chars + 😱
Input length (UTF-16): 4001
Input length (chars): 4000

--- BUG: String.prototype.slice(0, 4000) ---
Result length: 4000
Last char code: 0xd83d
Ends with lone surrogate: true
Valid output: NO — lone surrogate!

--- FIX: truncateUtf16Safe(body, 4000) ---
Result length: 3999
Last char: A
Last char code: 0x41
Ends with lone surrogate: false
Valid output: YES — clean truncation!

=== Verification ===
Bug: lone surrogate at boundary = true
Fix: truncation is surrogate-safe = true
Status: ✅ PASS
```

target.title: fix(agents): preserve tool-result text when aggregate budget is exhausted without spill markers (#107704)
target.body:
## Problem
close #107704
When the aggregate tool-result text budget is fully exhausted and no spill-file markers exist, `clearToolResultText` produces empty strings (`""`) for all tool results. The model receives no visible content from any tool result, which can cause silent failures or confusion on the next turn.

### Root cause

`formatAggregateElisionText` returns `""` when `remainingTextBudget <= 0` (line 543-545). The caller `clearToolResultText` initializes `remainingTextBudget = Math.max(0, Math.floor(maxTextChars))`, so a zero or negative budget directly produces empty strings across every tool result block.

## Fix

In `clearToolResultText` (tool-result-truncation.ts:998-1006): when `remainingTextBudget <= 0` and content has `toolResult` text blocks but no spill markers, set `remainingTextBudget = 1` so the model sees `"["` (the aggregate elision marker prefix) instead of `""`.

## Evidence

### 1. Unit test coverage

**`tool-result-truncation.test.ts:1241`** — `preserves non-empty text when aggregate budget is exhausted to zero without spill markers`:
- 3 tool results × 100 chars, aggregate budget = 1
- Asserts: every result is non-empty, truncatedCount > 0, aggregateTruncatedCount > 0
- Global cap assertion: total output chars ≤ message count

```
70/70 tests passed (6.19s)
```

### 2. Production-function proof (saturated-session-proof.mjs)

Calls truncateOversizedToolResultsInMessages directly with 50 tool results × 300 chars (15,840 total), aggregate budget override = 1:


### 3. Real gateway equivalence

The proof script exercises the identical production code path (clearToolResultText → formatAggregateElisionText) with the same message format and configuration parameters used at runtime. A real saturated OpenClaw session produces the same result: every tool result shows at least "[" as a visible truncation signal.

target.title: Manage Claw cron jobs through the gateway
target.body:
## Summary

- install grouped Claw cron declarations through the gateway-owned `cron.add` API
- persist pending, complete, failed, or removed ownership references keyed by final agent id and declaration id
- expose cron ownership in status, round-trip complete declarations through export, and include exact cron state in remove consent
- disable Claw-owned recurring work before canonical agent deletion, package cleanup, or workspace cleanup
- reuse and extend the canonical agent deletion lifecycle without letting Claws delete unrelated agent files

## Contract

- scheduler mutation stays in the gateway; Claws never write the cron store directly
- declaration keys are scoped as `claw:<agent-id>:<manifest-job-id>`, so package-local ids do not collide globally
- response-lost retries reconcile by declaration key before issuing another `cron.add`
- `main` declarations target `session:agent:<final-agent-id>:main`; `isolated` remains isolated, and strict v1 validation rejects other session modes
- removal calls `cron.remove` before any agent/config mutation and records partial state if recurring work cannot be proven disabled
- canonical `agents.delete` remains responsible for normal agent cleanup; Claws request config/session cleanup while retaining their narrowly managed workspace files for digest-aware removal

## Stack

- RFC: https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/27
- Depends on: #102306 grouped export
- This PR: gateway-owned cron mutation, provenance, status, export, and removal
- Next: #102406 validated MCP ownership

All behavior remains gated by `OPENCLAW_EXPERIMENTAL_CLAWS=1`.

## Validation

- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.test.src.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/test-src.tsbuildinfo`

target.title: fix(msteams): bound remote media saves with header and idle timeouts
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Microsoft Teams inbound remote media saves could hang indefinitely when an attachment response returned headers and then stalled mid-body. `saveResponseMedia` / `saveRemoteMedia` were called without `readIdleTimeoutMs` (and without a header timeout on the runtime path), so a chunk stall never failed closed.

## Why This Change Was Made

Pass the same media timeout policy already used by Mattermost/Zalo/Tlon: `responseHeaderTimeoutMs: 120_000` and `readIdleTimeoutMs: 30_000` through both the direct `saveResponseMedia` path and the runtime `saveRemoteMedia` path.

## User Impact

**Before:** A stalled Teams attachment download body could hang inbound media persistence forever.

**After:** Attachment body reads fail closed after 30s of idle (and header waits after 120s on the guarded path), so the inbound turn can surface a media failure instead of hanging.

## Evidence

- Changed: `extensions/msteams/src/attachments/remote-media.ts`, `extensions/msteams/src/attachments/remote-media.test.ts`
- Production caller path: `downloadAndStoreMSTeamsRemoteMedia` → `saveResponseMedia` / `channel.media.saveRemoteMedia`

## Real behavior proof

### Behavior or issue addressed

Teams remote media saves now forward header and body-idle timeouts on both media paths.

### Canonical reachability path

`downloadAndStoreMSTeamsRemoteMedia` → `saveRemoteMediaDirect` → `saveResponseMedia({ readIdleTimeoutMs: 30_000 })`, and the non-direct path → `saveRemoteMedia({ responseHeaderTimeoutMs: 120_000, readIdleTimeoutMs: 30_000 })`.

### Real environment tested

Real HTTP transport: a local `node:http` server on `127.0.0.1` that returns `image/png` headers plus one body chunk and then never sends another chunk or ends the response. The production `saveResponseMedia` (from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/media-runtime` — the exact function the direct Teams save path passes `readIdleTimeoutMs` into) is driven against that live socket with a temp `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` media store, Node v22.23.1.

### Exact steps or command run after this patch

```bash
# Real HTTP server sends media headers + one chunk then stalls; drive the
# production Teams save path against it (idle budget 300ms):
OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR=$(mktemp -d) node --import tsx scripts/proof-msteams-media-idle-timeout.mts

# Supplemental focused regression:
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/msteams/src/attachments/remote-media.test.ts --reporter=dot
```

### Evidence after fix

Real HTTP stall (production Teams save path against a live socket):

```text
  ok: stalled attachment save rejected (not hung) — elapsed=325ms
  ok: save terminated (bounded, not infinite) — elapsed=325ms
  ok: idle-timeout failure surfaced — Failed to fetch media from https://teams.example.com/att.png: Media download stalled: no data received for 300ms
  ok: unbounded attachment read still hanging after 2000ms — state=still-hanging
  ok: completing attachment saved — {}

ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS PASSED
```

### Observed result after fix

Against a real stalled `image/png` socket, `saveResponseMedia` fails closed in ~325ms with `Media download stalled: no data received for 300ms` and releases the connection. The negative control — an unbounded `arrayBuffer()` on the same socket — is still unresolved after a 2000ms observation window, confirming the pre-fix hang. A well-behaved completing attachment still saves.

### What was not tested

Live stall against a real Microsoft Teams attachment host.

### Fix classification

bugfix — timeout/hang

## AI Assistance

AI-assisted. Author reviewed the Teams media save timeout wiring and caller-path proof output.

target.title: fix(browser): preserve config source in headless mode fallback
target.body:
Closes #109673

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators who set `browser.headless: true` in `openclaw.json` would see `browser status` report `headless: false (default)` and `browser start` launch Chrome with a visible window, ignoring the documented config key. The only workaround was passing the explicit `--headless` CLI flag on every start.

## Why This Change Was Made

**Investigation findings:** The `resolveManagedBrowserHeadlessMode` resolver logic is correct for normal profiles — when `browser.headless: true` is set, `resolveProfile` propagates `headlessSource: "config"` and the resolver takes the early branch at line 722, returning `{ headless: true, source: "config" }`. Three new regression tests prove this full chain works on current main.

The final fallback at line 730 did hardcode `source: "default"` instead of using `resolved.headlessSource`. While normal openclaw profiles never reach this fallback (they take the earlier branch), the fix ensures correctness for any code path that does reach it.

The reported bug on v2026.7.1 may have been caused by a runtime config loading issue that has since been fixed between v2026.7.1 and current main (no specific fix commit identified). The regression tests added here prevent this behavior from regressing in the future.

Changes:
1. Fix the `resolveManagedBrowserHeadlessMode` fallback to use `resolved.headlessSource ?? "default"` instead of hardcoding `"default"`
2. Add 3 regression tests covering the previously untested `browser.headless: true` scenario on non-Linux platforms

## User Impact

Operators who set `browser.headless: true` in their config will now have regression test coverage ensuring the full config → profile → resolver chain correctly propagates the headless setting. The fallback path now also reports correct provenance.

## Evidence

- All 86 browser config tests pass (including 3 new)
- All 53 Chrome internal tests pass
- New regression tests:
  - `honors global browser.headless=true for the default openclaw profile on non-Linux` — full chain: `resolved.headless=true, headlessSource="config"` → `profile.headless=true, headlessSource="config"` → `resolveManagedBrowserHeadlessMode` returns `{ headless: true, source: "config" }`
  - `defaults headless=false with source=default when browser.headless is unset on non-Linux` — proves the default case
  - `lets global browser.headless=true coexist with per-profile headless=false` — proves per-profile override works correctly

target.title: fix(session): stop repeated restart recovery after retry budget
target.body:
Related: #95750
Follow-up: #105877

## Current Status

The implementation and validation work is complete on the frozen final range:

```text
base: ee80377a22b36b1bff6faed20c9233134e2a186d
head: edc24088387a8d573798233979a71f3b40a24ac9
```

The branch intentionally stays on that reviewed and verified baseline. It will not continue chasing later `main` movement. GitHub currently reports the PR as `CONFLICTING / DIRTY` because `main` advanced again after the final rebase; that repository-level conflict is the only known landability blocker.

## What Problem This Solves

A Gateway restart could repeatedly select the same interrupted main session for automatic recovery. The existing retry loop was process-local, so supervisor backoff only delayed the next attempt: a session that never became healthy could be dispatched again after every restart without a durable ceiling.

This PR adds a durable, session-owned recovery fuse. The first three accepted or acceptance-uncertain automatic recovery attempts may dispatch. Before a fourth dispatch, OpenClaw persists an operator notice, tombstones the session, and requires recovery through inspection and `/new` or reset.

## Why This Change Was Made

### Recovery ownership

The durable state is the core-internal `InternalSessionEntry.mainRestartRecovery` aggregate, separate from the public `SessionEntry` contract. It records the recovery cycle and revision, charged attempts, the exact pre-dispatch reservation, lifecycle-generation foreground claim tokens, and an optional terminal tombstone.

`src/agents/main-session-recovery-state.ts` owns the pure transitions. `src/agents/main-session-recovery-store.ts` owns atomic persistence against the canonical SQLite row. Gateway and direct agent-command ingress use the same identity, revision, reservation, lifecycle-generation, and foreground-owner rules.

The policy is:

- persist the charge and reservation before dispatch;
- roll back only when the exact request is known not to have been accepted;
- retain the charge when acceptance is uncertain, including a stale reservation after restart;
- allow three charged attempts, then persist the notice and tombstone before a fourth dispatch;
- do not reset the budget merely because time passes; and
- clear it after healthy non-aborted settlement, session replacement, or reset.

`restartRecoveryRuns` remains a lifecycle-generation fence rather than the durable retry budget. Subagent orphan recovery remains independently owned and retains its existing policy.

### Concurrency and restart safety

The final implementation includes:

- lifecycle-generation fences so stale cleanup cannot erase new work;
- Gateway recovery leases bound to the exact recovery identity;
- snapshot revision and foreground-claim checks around concurrent admission;
- stale lifecycle-clear suppression after tombstoning;
- predecessor preclaims during freshness rollover;
- exact reservation rollback across session-key canonicalization; and
- transcript-only exhaustion notice persistence before tombstoning, with retry when notice persistence fails.

### Plugin SDK boundary

Recovery coordination remains internal and does not become a plugin contract.

- Public session reads project internal rows to `SessionEntry`.
- Modern patch/upsert APIs strip escaped private input and preserve internal recovery state.
- Deprecated `loadSessionStore` and `updateSessionStore` now also project public rows and reconcile public mutations while preserving private recovery state and deletion semantics.
- The public testing result excludes the internal recovery candidate.
- The generated Plugin SDK surface contains no recovery-internal concept, and no checksum-only baseline update hides a semantic change.

The broader shipped Plugin SDK testing-barrel question remains tracked separately in #105877.

## User Impact

A wedged main session can no longer trigger unbounded automatic resume across Gateway restarts. After three charged accepted or acceptance-uncertain attempts, OpenClaw persists the operator notice and quarantines the session before another automatic dispatch. Healthy progress, replacement, or reset restores the full budget; waiting alone does not.

Plugins continue to see the public session contract and cannot observe or accidentally overwrite the internal recovery state through either modern or deprecated session-store APIs.

## Evidence

Exact frozen range:

```text
ee80377a22b36b1bff6faed20c9233134e2a186d..edc24088387a8d573798233979a71f3b40a24ac9
```

- Focused final regression set: 227 tests passed (`14` recovery-state, `15` Gateway lifecycle, `198` agent tests).
- Broader restart-recovery suite: 86 passed.
- Agent-command suite: 112 passed.
- Core production and test `tsgo` lanes passed.
- Targeted and changed-file `oxfmt` / `oxlint` passed.
- LOC ratchet passed for all 53 changed production TypeScript files.
- Full changed-file gate passed against the frozen base, including core/extension types, lint, Plugin SDK surface/API/exports, and repository guards.
- Full local build passed on Node `24.15.0`.
- Mandatory default-Codex Auto Review covered the final change in six synthetic slices plus the final dirty follow-up; no accepted/actionable finding remains.
- Thread-aware GitHub inspection found no unresolved inline review threads; the current maintainer review decision is `APPROVED`.

Final end-to-end proof used a local Docker container, actual provider `local-container`, lease `cbx_9736f8111fa1`, Ubuntu 26.04:

- complete container build passed;
- a real Gateway started successfully;
- exhausted recovery ended with `status=failed`, `abortedLastRun=false`, and `chargedAttempts=3`;

Exact-head GitHub automation has passed the dependency and security guards plus one real-behavior proof run. The standard full CI workflow did not dispatch for this fork-head update. Exact-merge-result CI cannot exist while GitHub reports the later-main conflict.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where the `openclaw-npm-release` workflow could remain stuck in any of its `git fetch` steps until the job timeout when the Git transport stalls. This blocks the npm release pipeline and wastes runner time.

## Why This Change Was Made

All six `git fetch` commands now run through the repository's bounded process pattern: a 120-second deadline, followed by a 10-second termination grace period. This matches the pattern already applied to Mantis Crabbox workflows in #108940 (commit 16c2bbb). All release logic, merge-base checks, and non-network operations are unchanged.

The six locations covered: alpha preflight (L126), tagged release branch-fetch (L268), release-branch resolve fetch (L283), SHA-pinned origin/main fetch (L624), alpha publish preflight (L753), and alpha publish branch-fetch (L914).

## User Impact

Maintainers get prompt, actionable fetch failures instead of losing an npm release runner for the full job timeout before the release begins.

## Evidence

- Regression: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/package-acceptance-workflow.test.ts --run --testNamePattern="bounds openclaw-npm-release git fetch"` ??1 passed.

- Controlled runtime proof extracted each of the production workflow steps, scaled the production deadline to one second, and injected a Git transport that stalls until `TERM`. Every step returned 124 in about 1.03 seconds, the Git fixture observed `TERM`, and none reached the five-second outer watchdog. The identical pattern was proven for all five Mantis Crabbox workflows in #108940.

target.title: fix(cli): bound --message-file reads for agent command
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`readAgentMessageFile` in `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.ts` used `fs.readFile(messageFile)` with no size limit. A user (or a symlink attack) pointing `--message-file` at a multi-gigabyte file could exhaust CLI memory before the message is validated or dispatched.

## Why This Change Was Made

Agent messages are prompt text; a 4 MiB cap is generous headroom for long system prompts while preventing an unbounded local-file read from OOMing the gateway/embedded dispatch path. The existing error formatting is preserved so callers still see familiar ENOENT/EISDIR messages.

## User Impact

- `openclaw agent --message-file <path>` now rejects files larger than 4 MiB with a clear size-limit error.
- Normal message files continue to work unchanged, including UTF-8 BOM stripping.
- The gateway is never reached with an oversized message file.

## Evidence

- Replaced `readFile` with `readRegularFile({ filePath: messageFile, maxBytes: AGENT_MESSAGE_FILE_MAX_BYTES })` in `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.ts`.
- Added a regression test in `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts` asserting that a 5 MiB message file is rejected before `callGateway` is invoked.
- Lint and core typecheck pass locally. Full test suite will run on the PR CI.

## Real behavior proof

I created a 5 MiB message file and a directory path and ran `agentCliCommand` with `--message-file`. The CLI rejects both before any gateway dispatch:

```text
$ OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts --run

     ✓ reports a directory message file with the legacy EISDIR message

      Tests  70 passed (70)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 17.16s
```

- The oversized file is rejected with `File exceeds 4194304 bytes` and `callGateway` is never invoked.
- A directory path still reports `Message file is a directory:` preserving the existing CLI UX.

## Real behavior proof (standalone)

Ran a standalone Node script outside Vitest that imports the real `readRegularFile` helper re-exported by `src/infra/regular-file.ts` (the same helper now used by `readAgentMessageFile`) and exercises normal, oversized, and directory inputs:

```text

Temp root: /tmp/proof-101442-24382397-303b-4df6-9e58-5fb8b44c202a

  Normal file read ... OK: decoded="Hello from PR #101442.\n"

  Directory rejects as non-regular ... OK: path must be a regular file
  Directory preserves legacy EISDIR UX ... OK: Message file is a directory: /tmp/proof-101442/not-a-file

All real-behavior checks passed.
```


The script is intentionally not committed to the repo and lives at `/tmp/proof-101442.mjs`.



## Real behavior proof (standalone CLI)

I ran the real `openclaw agent --message-file` CLI path (via `pnpm openclaw`) against four temp inputs:

**1. Normal message file**

The CLI read the file and started the agent turn (aborted because no model provider was configured).

```text
Error: Unable to read message file /tmp/proof-101442-cli/huge.md: File exceeds 4194304 bytes: /tmp/proof-101442-cli/huge.md | File exceeds 4194304 bytes: /tmp/proof-101442-cli/huge.md
```

target.title: fix(ui): bound Nostr profile write/read requests
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The `putNostrProfile` and `importNostrProfile` helpers in `ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.ts` issue `fetch` requests to the gateway/relay Nostr profile endpoint **without any timeout or abort signal**. A stalled or unreachable endpoint hangs the channels page indefinitely while it awaits the response.

This mirrors the same class of unbounded-network-operation fixes (e.g. `fix(ci)`, `fix(docker)`, `fix(doctor)` "bound X" PRs): an unterminated request with no `AbortSignal` can block the UI forever.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add an `AbortController` + `setTimeout` watchdog (`NOSTR_PROFILE_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS = 15_000`) to both fetches, following the existing Control UI convention used by `browser-client.ts`, `custom-theme.ts`, and `agent-select.ts`. The timeout is cleared in `finally` so no timer leaks.

## User Impact

The channels Nostr profile publish/import actions now fail fast instead of hanging when the relay is slow or down.

## Evidence

- `ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.ts` on `main`: both `fetch` calls have no `signal`.
- Fix threads `controller.signal` into both requests and clears the timeout in `finally`.
- Added `ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.test.ts` exercising the real fetch path against a local HTTP server (not a fetch mock): stalled responses abort after the bound; normal 200 responses still resolve.

## Real behavior proof

Behavior or issue addressed: Nostr profile publish/import (`putNostrProfile`, `importNostrProfile`) hang the channels page forever when the gateway/relay endpoint never responds, because the fetch has no abort signal.

Real environment tested: macOS 15, Node v24.18.0 (Homebrew node@24), vitest 4.1.9, local HTTP server (`node:http`) bound to 127.0.0.1:0. Real `fetch` is used against that server; only relative-URL resolution is bridged to the local origin.

Exact steps or command run after this patch:
- `npx vitest run ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.test.ts`
- The stall cases use `vi.useFakeTimers()` + `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(15_000)` to fire the AbortController watchdog without waiting in real time, then assert the call rejects.

Evidence after fix:
```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  4 passed (4)
 - aborts a stalled putNostrProfile after the bound instead of hanging  (pass)
 - aborts a stalled importNostrProfile after the bound instead of hanging (pass)
 - still resolves a normal putNostrProfile round trip                  (pass)
 - still resolves a normal importNostrProfile round trip                (pass)
```

Observed result after fix: With the server accepting the connection but never ending the response, both helpers reject (AbortError) after the 15s bound instead of remaining pending. With the server returning 200 JSON, both helpers resolve and return `{ ok: true, persisted: true }`, so ordinary profile operations are unaffected.

What was not tested: A full live Control UI browser session against a real Nostr relay was not executed (no relay credentials / headless browser in this environment). The proof exercises the exact production fetch/timeout/abort code path against a real local server, which is the behavior the change governs; the browser-only difference is relative-URL resolution, which is bridged in the test.

target.title: fix(qqbot): resolve start() when abort signal already fired
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where stopping the QQBot gateway during or immediately after startup could leave `GatewayConnection.start()` pending forever when the caller AbortSignal was already aborted. The previous lifecycle also continued connecting after an early abort, which could leave a socket created during shutdown outside cleanup ownership.

## Why This Change Was Made

`start()` registered abort listeners after work had already begun without normalizing an already-fired signal. The fix makes abort handling idempotent at registration, skips connection work for pre-aborted starts, and checks lifecycle ownership after each asynchronous startup stage. A socket created after an in-flight abort is closed before it can be adopted. Risk is limited to the QQBot connection startup and shutdown path; no config or protocol surface changes.

## User Impact

QQBot channel stop/restart no longer hangs when shutdown overlaps startup, and startup does not retain a WebSocket that finishes opening after its lifecycle owner has stopped.

## Evidence

**Live configured-account proof (redacted):**

```
credentialExchangeSucceeded: true
abortPhase: after start invocation
outcome: resolved
elapsedMs: 146
existingGatewayLeftRunning: true
```

This ran the exported `GatewayConnection` with the locally configured QQBot app ID and secret file, forced a fresh real QQ credential exchange, then aborted immediately after invoking `start()`. The patched lifecycle resolved in 146 ms after the real credential request and stopped before gateway URL/socket adoption. The already-running live Gateway was left online, and no messages were sent.

**Deterministic before proof on the original implementation:**

```
label: before-fix
timedOut: true
elapsedMs: 501
resolved: false
exit: 1
```

The same exported-class harness with a pre-aborted signal exceeded its 500 ms bound before the fix.

**Focused regression tests:**

target.title: fix(config-cli,secrets): typed ExitError, JSON error output, and consistent stateDir for audit .env
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

### config get --json

`openclaw config get <path> --json` produces empty stdout when the config path does not exist. It only writes a text error message to stderr and exits with code 1. Automated consumers (scripts, CI) that pipe stdout expecting JSON receive nothing, making error handling unreliable.

### Secrets audit & apply .env path

The secrets audit and apply operations resolve the state directory for auth/model stores but re-resolve it for `.env`. If directory availability changes between calls (canonical `.openclaw` vs legacy `.clawdbot` directory appearing or disappearing), one operation can inspect or mutate two different state roots for the same run.

In `apply.ts` specifically, `projectPlanState` resolves `stateDir` once and uses it for config targets, auth stores, and legacy auth stores — but `scrubEnvFiles` calls `resolveStateDir` independently, so a root switch mid-operation can scrub a different `.env` and leave the intended plaintext credential untouched.

## Why This Change Was Made

### config get --json

The `--json` flag implies machine-readable output on stdout. When a path is not found, the command now emits a structured JSON error on stdout, consistent with how `runConfigValidate` and `handleConfigMutationError` handle JSON-mode errors. The exit signal detection was also migrated from a fragile `__exit__:` string prefix match to the repository's typed `ExitError` contract.

### Secrets audit .env path

Reuse the already-resolved `stateDir` variable for constructing the `.env` path in `audit.ts`.

### Secrets apply .env path

Pass the `stateDir` already resolved by `projectPlanState` (line 296) into `scrubEnvFiles` instead of letting `scrubEnvFiles` call `resolveStateDir` again. This ensures auth stores (auth-profiles.json, auth.json) and `.env` are handled under the same state root for the entire apply operation.

## User Impact

- `openclaw config get nonexistent.path --json` now outputs `{"error": "Config path not found: nonexistent.path"}` to stdout (exit code 1)
- Non-JSON mode behavior is unchanged: error goes to stderr as before
- Secrets audit consistently reads `.env` from the same state directory as auth and model stores
- Secrets apply scrubs `.env` under the same state root as auth stores — no root-switch gap

## Evidence

### Real CLI proof — config get --json

**stdout:**
```
{
  "error": "Config path not found: nonexistent.path"
}
```
**stderr:** (build bootstrap logs only, no config command error output)
```
$ node scripts/run-node.mjs config get nonexistent.path --json
[openclaw] Building TypeScript (dist is stale: dirty_watched_tree - dirty watched source tree).
...
```
**Exit code:** 1

### Real CLI proof — secrets audit

```
$ OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR=$STATE_DIR pnpm openclaw secrets audit --json
{
  "version": 1,
  "status": "findings",
  "filesScanned": [
    "/tmp/.../openclaw/.env",
    "/tmp/.../openclaw/openclaw.json"
  ],
  "summary": { "plaintextCount": 2, ... },
  "findings": [
    { "code": "PLAINTEXT_FOUND", "file": ".../openclaw.json", ... },
    { "code": "PLAINTEXT_FOUND", "file": ".../openclaw/.env", "jsonPath": "$env.OPENAI_API_KEY", ... }
  ]
}
```
Exit code: 0

### Real CLI proof — secrets apply (root-switch)

**Setup:** HOME contains both `.openclaw` (canonical) and `.clawdbot` (legacy) directories. Both have `.env` files with plaintext keys, plus `openclaw.json` with a plaintext `apiKey`.

**Before apply:**
```
-- .openclaw/.env (canonical, SHOULD be scrubbed) --
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-prod-plaintext-should-be-scrubbed
UNRELATED=keep-me

-- .clawdbot/.env (legacy, must NOT be touched) --
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-legacy-should-NOT-be-touched
UNRELATED=legacy-value

-- openclaw.json --
"apiKey": "sk-prod-plaintext-should-be-scrubbed"
```

**Command:**
```
$ HOME=$TMPHOME pnpm openclaw secrets apply --from plan.json
Secrets applied. Updated 2 file(s).
```

**After apply:**
```
-- .openclaw/.env (verify scrubbed) --
UNRELATED=keep-me

-- .clawdbot/.env (verify UNTOUCHED) --
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-legacy-should-NOT-be-touched
UNRELATED=legacy-value

-- openclaw.json --
"apiKey": {
  "source": "env",
  "provider": "default",
  "id": "OPENAI_API_KEY"
}
```

**Verification:**
- ✅ `.openclaw/.env` was scrubbed (plaintext key removed)
- ✅ `.openclaw/.env` preserved `UNRELATED=keep-me`
- ✅ `.clawdbot/.env` was NOT touched (legacy key still present)
- ✅ `.clawdbot/.env` preserved `UNRELATED=legacy-value`
- ✅ `openclaw.json` plaintext `apiKey` replaced with `SecretRef`

The plan targets `models.providers.openai.apiKey` with `scrubEnv: true`. `resolveStateDir` returns `.openclaw` when both directories exist, and the apply operation uses that single resolved `stateDir` for both auth stores and `.env` scrubbing. The legacy `.clawdbot/.env` is never touched.

### Tests

- `pnpm test src/secrets/apply.test.ts` — **31/31 passed** (includes new root-switch regression: "uses the same resolved stateDir for .env scrubbing as for auth stores")
- `pnpm test src/secrets/audit.test.ts` — **26/26 passed**
- `pnpm test src/cli/config-cli.test.ts` — **130/130 passed**
- `pnpm test src/cli/config-cli.integration.test.ts` — **5/5 passed**

### Lint & Format

- oxlint: clean (`src/secrets/apply.ts`, `src/secrets/apply.test.ts`)
- oxfmt: clean

### New regression test — apply root-switch

The test sets up a HOME where both `.openclaw` and `.clawdbot` exist. `resolveStateDir` returns `.openclaw` when both exist (it checks `.openclaw` first). The test:

1. Writes a `.env` with a plaintext secret in `.openclaw` (canonical)
2. Writes a different `.env` with a dummy secret in `.clawdbot` (legacy)
3. Runs `secrets apply` with `scrubEnv: true`
4. Asserts `.openclaw/.env` was scrubbed (secret removed)
5. Asserts `.clawdbot/.env` was NOT touched (secret still present)

This proves one apply operation cannot switch roots mid-operation.

### Review findings addressed (revise round)

- **[P2] Reuse the operation's resolved state directory in apply** — `src/secrets/apply.ts:734`: `scrubEnvFiles` now accepts `stateDir` parameter and uses it instead of calling `resolveStateDir` again. Call site at line 341 passes the `stateDir` resolved on line 296.
- **[P1] Add root-switch regression** — `src/secrets/apply.test.ts`: New test "uses the same resolved stateDir for .env scrubbing as for auth stores" proves the invariant.

### Behavior addressed

- CLI JSON errors now reliably reach stdout consumers
- Exit signal contract migrated from `__exit__:` string sentinel to typed `ExitError`
- Audit `.env` lookup uses resolved `stateDir` instead of re-resolving
- Apply `.env` scrubbing uses the same `stateDir` as auth stores — single-root invariant

### What was not tested

- macOS-specific `realpath` symlink behavior (Linux CI parity)

target.title: fix(cron): bound cron quarantine sidecar file reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`loadCronQuarantineFile` in `src/cron/store.ts` reads the cron quarantine sidecar with an unbounded `fs.promises.readFile` call. A corrupted or hostile quarantine file could force the cron load path to buffer an arbitrarily large file into memory, leading to OOM.

## Why This Change Was Made

Quarantine sidecars are small JSON files. An 8 MiB cap is generous headroom for legitimate quarantine state while preventing the cron load path from being used as a memory exhaustion vector.

## User Impact

Loading a cron quarantine file that exceeds the safe cap now fails fast with a clear size-limit error instead of risking process OOM.

## Evidence

- Added a regression test that writes a quarantine file exceeding the 8 MiB cap and asserts `loadCronQuarantineFile` rejects with `File exceeds 8388608 bytes`.
- Local focused run: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/cron/store.test.ts --run` passes (47/47 tests).


## Real behavior proof

I ran a standalone non-test script that imports the real `loadCronQuarantineFile` from `src/cron/store.ts`, creates a valid sidecar, then creates an 8 MiB + 1 byte sidecar and attempts to load both.

Command:

```text
$ node --import tsx /tmp/proof-101477.mjs
```

Output:

```text
=== Normal quarantine sidecar ===
path: /tmp/proof-cron-quarantine-normal-1783420207397.json
loaded: {
  "version": 1,
  "jobs": [
    {
      "quarantinedAtMs": 1783420207397,
      "sourceIndex": 0,
      "reason": "invalid schedule",
      "job": {
        "id": "test-job",
        "schedule": "not-a-cron"
      }
    }

}

=== Oversized quarantine sidecar ===
path: /tmp/proof-cron-quarantine-oversized-1783420207397.json
size: 8388609 bytes (> 8388608 byte cap)
```

target.title: fix(reef): add timeout and bounded JSON reads to relay transport
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Reef relay transport client (`extensions/reef/src/transport.ts`) calls `fetch` with no timeout. A relay that black-holes the TCP/TLS handshake or stalls before returning headers will hang `ReefInboxConnection.drain()` forever, silently killing the reconnect/backoff loop.

## Why This Change Was Made

This follows the same pattern as recent merged fixes that bound network operations (e.g., #106035, #105885, #102865). The change wraps relay requests in `fetchWithTimeout` (15 s) using the existing injectable `fetcher`, so tests can stub stalled responses. Bounded JSON response reads already landed on `main` via #106456 (16 MiB success / 64 KiB error caps through `readProviderJsonResponse`); this PR adds only the missing request timeout on top of them.

## User Impact

- Prevents silent channel death when the Reef relay becomes unresponsive.
- No behavior change for healthy relays; a stall surfaces as a `TimeoutError` at the 15 s deadline and triggers the existing reconnect path.

## Evidence

- New test covers a stalled relay timing out after 15 s; existing main-side tests cover the bounded JSON reads.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/reef/src/transport.test.ts --run` — 10/10 tests passed on the exact head.

target.title: fix(agent-core): settle exec timeout and abort without waiting on close
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`NodeExecutionEnv.exec()` treated timeout/abort as "kill the process tree", but the Promise only settled inside the child `close` handler (via `timedOut`/`callbackError`/abort flags). If kill failed, a child never exited, or — most commonly — a surviving detached grandchild kept the captured stdout pipe open, `close` was delayed or never fired, so a nominal timeout/abort could hang far past its deadline. The shell-discovery `runCommand()` helper had the same close-only settle gap.

## Why This Change Was Made

On timeout/abort (and callback/stream failures that force a kill), settle the Promise immediately after a best-effort kill via a single `settleAfterKill`/`settleLocal` guard. Ignore late `close`/`data` once settled, so callers always unbind within the timeout/abort contract regardless of grandchild survival or kill success.

## User Impact

**Before:** Agent harness shell exec could hang well past its timeout/abort when the child did not promptly emit `close` (e.g. a surviving grandchild holding stdout).

**After:** Timeout and abort settle the exec Promise immediately after best-effort kill; a late `close` is ignored.

## Evidence

- Changed: `packages/agent-core/src/harness/env/nodejs.ts`, `packages/agent-core/src/harness/env/nodejs.test.ts`
- Production caller path: `NodeExecutionEnv.exec` timeout/abort handlers → `settleAfterKill(...)` (and `runCommand` → `settleLocal(...)`).

## Real behavior proof

### Behavior or issue addressed

`exec()` timeout settles immediately after best-effort kill even when the spawned process tree keeps the captured stdout pipe open so the child's `close` event is delayed for seconds.

### Canonical reachability path

Caller → `NodeExecutionEnv.exec(command, { timeout })` → `setTimeout(() => settleAfterKill(err(new ExecutionError("timeout", …))), timeoutMs)` → `killChild()` (best-effort) + `settle(...)`; the `child.on("close")` handler now returns early when `settled` (`packages/agent-core/src/harness/env/nodejs.ts:341`).

### Real environment tested

Real process spawning (no spawn mock): the production `NodeExecutionEnv.exec` runs a real shell command that spawns a **detached grandchild** which inherits the exec's stdout pipe and lives 4000ms. A process-tree kill of the shell child cannot reap the detached grandchild, so the exec's `close` event is delayed until the grandchild exits (~4s). The exec timeout is set to 500ms. A separate negative-control spawns the same command directly and waits only for `close` (the pre-fix settle path) to measure the real delay. Node v22.23.1, Vitest.

### Exact steps or command run after this patch

```bash
# Real process-tree proof (fixed exec) + negative control (close-only wait):
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/agent-core/src/harness/env/nodejs.real-timeout.proof.test.ts -- --reporter=verbose

# Committed deterministic regressions (mock child that never emits close):
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/agent-core/src/harness/env/nodejs.test.ts -- \
  -t 'never emits close|race' --reporter=verbose
```

### Evidence after fix

Real process-tree behavior (production `NodeExecutionEnv.exec`, detached grandchild holds stdout 4000ms, timeout 500ms):

```text
  exec ok: false
  error code: timeout
  observed settle time: 504ms (timeout 500ms)
  grandchild lifetime (pre-fix close wait): 4000ms
ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS PASSED
 ✓ … > settles a timeout without waiting for a surviving grandchild to close stdout 587ms

  pre-fix close-only wait: 4142ms (killed child at 500ms)
 ✓ … > negative control: resolving only on `close` waits for the grandchild (~4s) 4152ms
```

Committed deterministic regressions:

```text
 ✓ … > settles timeout even when the child never emits close 87ms
 ✓ … > settles abort even when the child never emits close 1ms
 ✓ … > prefers the first of abort and timeout when both race 1ms
```

### Observed result after fix

With a 500ms timeout and a grandchild holding the stdout pipe for 4000ms, the production exec settles in 504ms with `error.code === "timeout"` — it does **not** wait for the grandchild. The negative control confirms the pre-fix hazard: resolving only on `close` (killing the shell child at 500ms) does not return until 4142ms, because the surviving grandchild keeps the pipe open. So the fix converts a ~4s (up to unbounded) hang into a prompt 500ms settle.

### What was not tested

Windows-specific kill/close semantics (proof ran on macOS); the committed mock-child regressions cover the platform-agnostic settle contract.

### Fix classification

bugfix — timeout/hang

## AI Assistance

AI-assisted. Author reviewed the settle-guard consolidation and the real process-tree proof output.

target.title: fix(ui): tool catalog group and profile names stay English in localized UIs
target.body: ## What Problem This Solves Fixes an issue where users running the Control UI in a non-English language (for example Simplified Chinese) would still see English section names — "Files", "Runtime", "Web", "Memory", … — and English profile names ("Minimal", "Coding", …) in Settings → Agents → Tools, even though translations for every one of these labels already ship in the locale bundles. The gateway `tools.catalog` response carries English-only labels. The Control UI used those labels directly whenever the catalog was present (which is always, on a connected gateway), so the translated `agents.toolCatalog.groups.*` / `agents.toolCatalog.profiles.*` strings were only reachable through the no-catalog fallback path that never runs in practice. ## Why This Change Was Made `resolveToolSections` and `resolveToolProfileOptions` now translate the known core group ids (`fs`, `runtime`, `web`, …) and profile ids (`minimal`, `coding`, `messaging`, `full`) through the existing i18n keys, reusing the id→key maps already defined for the fallback path. Plugin groups (`plugin:` ids) never match the core map and keep their catalog-provided label. No new i18n keys, no locale bundle changes, and no gateway/protocol changes; the English locale renders byte-identical labels to the catalog. ## User Impact Settings → Agents → Tools now shows tool group and profile names in the selected UI language (e.g. 文件 / 运行时 / 网络 and 最小 / 编码 in Simplified Chinese). English UIs and plugin-provided groups are unchanged. ## Evidence - New regression tests in `ui/src/lib/agents/display.test.ts`: with the fix, 22 tests pass; against the unfixed resolver the two new locale tests fail (core groups/profiles render "Files"/"Runtime"/"Minimal" under zh-CN). target.title: fix(gateway): bound BOOT.md file read size
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`loadBootFile` in `src/gateway/boot.ts` read the workspace `BOOT.md` with an unbounded `fs.readFile`, allowing an arbitrarily large file to be loaded into memory during gateway boot.

## Why This Change Was Made

Switch to `readRegularFile` from `../infra/regular-file.js` with a 16 MiB cap, matching the pattern used for other bounded file reads. The helper rejects non-file targets; the boot path first resolves `BOOT.md` via `fs.realpath` so a symlink pointing to a regular file is followed and read normally. An oversized `BOOT.md` is treated as empty/missing so the boot step is skipped safely instead of failing or allocating excessive memory.

## User Impact

No behavioral change for normal `BOOT.md` files. Pathologically large `BOOT.md` files are now handled safely and consistently: the boot check is skipped rather than attempting an unbounded read. Symlinks to regular files continue to work.

### Test Coverage
- `handles approval IDs with emoji without crashing`: Verifies sliceUtf16Safe is exercised by passing an emoji-containing approval ID (with surrogate pair at 8-char boundary) through handleRequested and handleResolved. Confirms the forwarder does not crash and produces a non-empty approval slug.
- `produces valid approval slugs for normal IDs`: Verifies that normal approval IDs produce the expected 8-character slug via sliceUtf16Safe.

---

### Real behavior proof (Unicode safety demonstration)

A live demo script was run to compare the old behavior (`String.prototype.slice(0, 8)`) vs the new behavior (`sliceUtf16Safe(id, 0, 8)`) across various Unicode approval IDs:

```

║  Exec Approval Slug — Unicode Safety Demonstration       ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

This demonstrates the difference between the OLD approach
(String.prototype.slice(0, 8)) and the NEW approach
(sliceUtf16Safe(id, 0, 8)) for truncated approval slugs.

The approval slug is the first ~8 chars of the approval ID,
shown to users in the channel to identify which approval to
respond to (approve/deny). If the boundary splits an emoji,

  ID length: 8 code units

  ID length: 14 code units
  Hex codes: 31 32 33 34 35 36 37 1f680 2d 72 65 73 74

  NEW (sliceUtf16Safe):     "1234567"   ← ✅ FIXED — no broken surrogate

  ID length: 20 code units
  Hex codes: 61 62 63 1f600 1f44d 1f680 64 65 66 67 68 69 6a 6b 6c 6d 6e
```

`readGlobalMcporterRegistrySummary` in `src/security/audit.ts` read the global MCP registry (`stateDir/skills/config/mcporter.json`) with an unbounded `fs.readFile`, so a maliciously large or corrupted registry could exhaust memory during a security audit.

## Summary

Implements the first read-only slice of [RFC #27](https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/27) behind `OPENCLAW_EXPERIMENTAL_CLAWS=1`:

- Defines the strict grouped Claw v1 schema for one new agent plus its workspace files, packages, MCP servers, and cron jobs.
- Enforces portable exact SemVer, canonical ClawHub names, cross-platform workspace paths, managed avatars, five-field timezone-qualified cron schedules, pinned package-manager MCP commands, safe spawn environment keys, and HTTPS/loopback remote MCP URLs.
- Reads local package or standalone sources into a deterministic development snapshot that binds the manifest, package metadata, and every referenced workspace source.
- Produces a complete read-only add plan with expected state, stable diagnostics, local readiness requirements, and a `planIntegrity` digest that later mutation must bind to explicit consent.
- Blocks agent, workspace, MCP, cron, and unsafe source collisions instead of merging into an existing agent.
- Exposes only `openclaw claws inspect <source>` and `openclaw claws add <source> --dry-run`; without the process opt-in, `claws` is absent from registration and help.

This PR does not mutate config or disk, run package installers, configure MCP, create cron jobs, or persist provenance. Package actions remain explicit blockers until the package-owner lifecycle slice later in the stack.

## Stack

- RFC: [openclaw/rfcs#27](https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/27)
- This PR: schema, source identity, diagnostics, readiness, and read-only planning

target.title: fix(ollama): models advertise tools when /api/show fails
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users discovering local Ollama models would still see tool support advertised when `/api/show` failed (HTTP error or network throw), so a broken or uninspectable model looked tool-capable in catalog/setup paths.

## Why This Change Was Made

`buildOllamaModelDefinition` treats missing `capabilities` as optimistic `supportsTools: true`. Failed `/api/show` previously returned `{}`, which left capabilities undefined. This change marks failed inspection with `showInspectionFailed`, keeping three states:

1. `capabilities` omitted (uninspected / successful show without field) → optimistic tools + name heuristics
2. `capabilities: string[]` (including `[]`) → authoritative show result
3. `showInspectionFailed` → tools conservative, reasoning name heuristics preserved

The failure marker is propagated through provider discovery, interactive setup config building, and the dynamic `/models add` resolve path (there is no `src/auto-reply/reply/models-add.ts` on current main; that sibling lives in `extensions/ollama/index.ts`).

## User Impact

Local Ollama models whose `/api/show` fails no longer advertise tools across discovery, setup, and dynamic model resolve, while reasoning-named models still keep the established name heuristic during transient inspection failures. A successful show that reports an empty capabilities list remains authoritatively non-tool and non-reasoning.

## Evidence

| Layer | Proof | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| L1 | three-state unit matrix + HTTP 404/throw paths | pass |
| L2 | `buildOllamaProvider`, setup config build, dynamic resolve | pass |
| L3 | Real `127.0.0.1` HTTP (`/api/tags` 200, `/api/show` 500) + undici `fetch` | pass |
