target.title: fix(e2e): bound docker package-install and compose readiness probes
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Docker package-install and Compose-setup readiness loops used raw `docker exec` / `docker inspect` / `docker logs` (and a raw `docker compose down` on cleanup) with **no per-command timeout**. A single stalled Docker daemon RPC could freeze the loop so the nominal 240s / 180s readiness deadline never advanced — the `for _ in $(seq 1 240)` counter loops assumed each probe returned promptly.

## Why This Change Was Made

Route every readiness probe, final check, compose up/ps/logs/exec/run/down, and inspect through the existing `docker_e2e_docker_cmd` timeout helper, and convert the fixed-count loops into `SECONDS`-based deadline loops that clamp each probe's `DOCKER_COMMAND_TIMEOUT` to the remaining wall-clock budget.

## User Impact

**Before:** One hung `docker exec`/`inspect` during package-install or compose health polling could stall the E2E job well past its intended readiness budget.

**After:** Each Docker probe is bounded by the remaining deadline; a stalled probe is killed, the loop advances, and the script fails closed within the overall readiness window. Compose cleanup `down` is also timeout-bounded.

## Evidence

- Changed: `scripts/e2e/docker-package-install.sh`, `scripts/e2e/compose-setup.sh`, `test/scripts/docker-build-helper.test.ts`
- Production caller path: package-install / compose-setup readiness loops → `DOCKER_COMMAND_TIMEOUT="$probe_timeout" docker_e2e_docker_cmd exec/inspect/...` (`scripts/e2e/docker-package-install.sh:47`).

## Real behavior proof

### Behavior or issue addressed

A stalled `docker exec` readiness probe is bounded by the production `docker_e2e_docker_cmd` timeout so the readiness loop fails closed at its deadline instead of blocking forever on the first hung probe.

### Canonical reachability path

`docker-package-install.sh` builds `READY_DEADLINE_AT=$((SECONDS + READY_DEADLINE_SECONDS))` and, each iteration, runs `DOCKER_COMMAND_TIMEOUT="$(docker_e2e_remaining_timeout "$READY_DEADLINE_AT")" docker_e2e_docker_cmd exec "$CONTAINER_NAME" test -f /tmp/openclaw-proof-ready`; `docker_e2e_docker_cmd` (`scripts/lib/docker-e2e-image.sh`) wraps the docker invocation in the host `timeout` with `DOCKER_COMMAND_TIMEOUT`.

### Real environment tested

Real shell execution of the production readiness loop with the production helper library sourced (`scripts/lib/docker-e2e-image.sh` → `docker_e2e_docker_cmd`). Two `PATH`-injected fakes stand in for external binaries: a `timeout` that faithfully emulates GNU `timeout` (runs the child under a real wall-clock budget and `SIGKILL`s it on expiry, exit 124) and a `docker` whose `exec` hangs forever (`while true; do sleep 1; done`) while `inspect` reports the container running. No Docker daemon is required; the production helper's timeout wrapping and the deadline loop run for real. macOS, Node v22.23.1 for the Vitest suite.

### Exact steps or command run after this patch

```bash
# Direct real-shell run: production readiness loop + docker_e2e_docker_cmd vs a hung `docker exec`.
env PATH="<fake-bin>:/usr/bin:/bin" bash ready-loop.sh "$PWD"   # sources scripts/lib/docker-e2e-image.sh

# Committed real-shell regressions (drive the production helper + source wiring):
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/docker-build-helper.test.ts -- \
  -t 'readiness fails closed|timeout-aware run helper|bounded' --reporter=verbose
```

### Evidence after fix

Direct real-shell run (production readiness loop, hung `docker exec`, 3s deadline):

```text
==> readiness probe (bounded 3s)
[fake-docker] exec: hanging (simulated stuck daemon)
[fake-timeout] probe budget 3s exceeded; killing hung docker child
package install readiness deadline exceeded after 3s
(exit_code=1, wall ≈ 3s)
```

Committed real-shell regressions:

```text
 ✓ docker build helper > package-install readiness fails closed when a single docker exec stalls 4832ms
 ✓ docker build helper > keeps package-backed Docker runs bounded without the shared timeout helper 23ms
 ✓ docker build helper > routes the gateway network client through the timeout-aware run helper 2ms
 ✓ docker build helper > prints in-container Docker client logs through bounded helpers 3ms
 Tests  7 passed | 162 skipped (169)
```

### Observed result after fix

Against a hung `docker exec`, the production helper's `timeout` kills the stalled probe at the clamped remaining budget, the loop keeps advancing, and the script fails closed with `package install readiness deadline exceeded after 3s` (exit 1) in ~3s — bounded by the deadline, not blocked forever. Pre-fix, the raw `docker exec` on the first iteration had no timeout and would block the loop indefinitely. The committed source-wiring assertions also pin that neither script contains raw `docker exec ` / `docker inspect ` / `${COMPOSE[@]}` anymore.

### What was not tested

A live Docker E2E lane with a genuinely wedged daemon; the proof exercises the production readiness loop + `docker_e2e_docker_cmd` timeout path against a real hung child on the host.

### Fix classification

bugfix — timeout/hang (E2E readiness)

## AI Assistance

AI-assisted. Author reviewed the readiness-loop conversions, the `docker_e2e_docker_cmd` routing, and the real-shell proof output.

target.title: Manage Claw cron jobs through the gateway
target.body:
## Summary

- install grouped Claw cron declarations through the gateway-owned `cron.add` API
- persist pending, complete, failed, or removed ownership references keyed by final agent id and declaration id
- expose cron ownership in status, round-trip complete declarations through export, and include exact cron state in remove consent
- disable Claw-owned recurring work before canonical agent deletion, package cleanup, or workspace cleanup
- reuse and extend the canonical agent deletion lifecycle without letting Claws delete unrelated agent files

## Contract

- scheduler mutation stays in the gateway; Claws never write the cron store directly
- declaration keys are scoped as `claw:<agent-id>:<manifest-job-id>`, so package-local ids do not collide globally
- response-lost retries reconcile by declaration key before issuing another `cron.add`
- `main` declarations target `session:agent:<final-agent-id>:main`; `isolated` remains isolated, and strict v1 validation rejects other session modes
- removal calls `cron.remove` before any agent/config mutation and records partial state if recurring work cannot be proven disabled
- canonical `agents.delete` remains responsible for normal agent cleanup; Claws request config/session cleanup while retaining their narrowly managed workspace files for digest-aware removal

## Stack

- RFC: https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/27
- Depends on: #102306 grouped export
- This PR: gateway-owned cron mutation, provenance, status, export, and removal
- Next: #102406 validated MCP ownership

All behavior remains gated by `OPENCLAW_EXPERIMENTAL_CLAWS=1`.

## Validation

- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.test.src.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/test-src.tsbuildinfo`
- 61 focused cron/lifecycle/schema/provenance/export unit tests
- 15 Claws CLI tests
- 11 canonical agent-delete command tests
- 1 shared agent-cron cleanup test
- 96 gateway agent-mutation tests across gateway projects
- 8 full lifecycle CLI E2E tests
- emitted `cron.add` payload validated by the gateway protocol validator
- Oxlint: 0 warnings, 0 errors across 18 code/generated files
- Oxfmt: all 18 files correctly formatted
- `git diff --check`
- Codex review: no accepted/actionable findings

## Real behavior proof

The lifecycle tests prove consent-bound add, scheduler-id provenance, response-lost reconciliation, status/export visibility, and removal ordering. A scheduler failure returns partial with `agentRemoved: false`; successful removal calls `cron.remove` before either direct config mutation or the canonical agent-delete delegate.

target.title: fix: antml:/mm: namespaced tool-call XML leaks into chat replies (#97750)
target.body:
Closes #97750

## What Problem This Solves

Some deployments serve a Claude/MiniMax model through a proxy that intermittently degrades a native `tool_use` block into plain text. In that degraded case the tool call arrives as the namespaced/bare XML attribute dialect — `<invoke name="tool"><parameter name="x">v</parameter></invoke>`, optionally wrapped in `<function_calls>...</function_calls>` and optionally prefixed with `antml:` or `mm:`.

On current `main` two gaps remained:

1. The visible-text sanitizer recognized the `antml:` prefix but not the `mm:` prefix, so a degraded `mm:invoke` block leaked verbatim into the user-visible reply.
2. The persist-path stripper (`packages/tool-call-repair` `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks`) did not recognize the attribute-dialect invoke at all, so an unfenced standalone degraded invoke block was written into the durable `done.message` instead of being scrubbed.

## Why This Change Was Made

The degraded tool call should never reach the user, and it must not be persisted into session state either — but a legitimate code example of the same markup (inside a fenced or inline code span) must be preserved, not deleted. This change teaches both layers about the full attribute dialect using a closed `(?:antml:|mm:)?` namespace allow-list, so arbitrary `ns:` tokens in prose are never matched.

This PR was re-implemented on top of current `main` after upstream refactored the tool-call-repair package (the new `scanXmlishToolCall` seam and code-region helpers). The change is scoped to the net delta that still reproduces on `main`:

- **Visible text** (`assistant-visible-text.ts`): mirror the existing `antml:` handling for the `mm:` namespace in the tag-name scan, quick-check, and payload-start patterns. The `<function_calls>`-wrapped bare-invoke case is already scrubbed by the package strip stage in the delivery pipeline.
- **Persist path** (`packages/tool-call-repair`): a dedicated linear scanner recognizes a complete standalone invoke block (bare/`antml:`/`mm:`, `<function_calls>` wrapper, self-closing, and zero-parameter forms). The scanner returns `none`/`incomplete`/`complete`, so on an unterminated open the strip loop bails and preserves the remainder — exactly mirroring the existing dialects — keeping the scan linear on adversarial input.
- **Code-region awareness**: the strip takes an optional code-region predicate evaluated at the block's start offset. Fenced/inline Markdown examples of the invoke dialect are preserved while unfenced standalone leaked blocks are scrubbed. Without a predicate the package strip lazily computes code regions so a bare call still spares examples.
- **Plugin SDK contract preserved**: the exported `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks` stays strict by default (it forces a scrub of every region, even inside code, for untrusted callers), with code-aware behavior available only via the explicit `{ preserveCodeRegions: true }` opt-in.
- **Layering**: `findCodeRegions`/`isInsideCode`/`CodeRegion` were moved into `normalization-core` (the package's only dependency) so `tool-call-repair` can share one implementation without importing app source; `src/shared/text/code-regions.ts` re-exports them so existing callers are unaffected.

Non-goals/boundaries: the native Anthropic/DSML transports are untouched; no runtime fallback execution from sanitized text is introduced; the equals dialect (`<function=...>`/`<parameter=...>`), bracket, and Harmony paths are unchanged; the invoke dialect is recognized only by the strip/sanitize paths (never promoted to an executable call and never wired into the stream-buffering scanner).

## User Impact

Users on proxied Claude/MiniMax routes no longer see raw namespaced/bare `invoke` tool-call XML in their replies, and the leaked block is no longer written into the persisted message (no session-state content loss). Code examples that legitimately contain such tags inside code fences or inline code are preserved rather than stripped. A resolved-review audit also removed an O(n²) worst case on the persist strip path, so adversarial degraded text cannot cause pathological CPU use.

## Evidence

Focused regression tests were added at the layers that own the contract:
- `packages/tool-call-repair/src/payload.test.ts`: invoke-dialect variants (bare/`antml:`/`mm:`, `function_calls` wrapper, self-closing, zero-param), code-region preservation vs. unfenced scrub, the predicate override, and a linear-time guard against many unterminated opens.
- `src/plugin-sdk/tool-payload.test.ts`: the `preserveCodeRegions` opt-in and strict default.
- `src/shared/text/assistant-visible-text.test.ts`: the `mm:invoke`/`mm:parameter` visible-text case (parallel to the existing `antml:` case), alongside existing standalone-vs-inline `function_calls` delivery-path coverage.

Real-behavior proof (before = current `main`, after = this branch), driving the actual `sanitizeAssistantVisibleText` and `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks` on the leak shapes:

```
=== BEFORE (main) ===
A2 mm-visible       => "Working on it.\n<mm:invoke name=\"get_weather\">\n<mm:parameter name=\"city\">Paris</mm:parameter>\n</mm:invoke>"
A3 bare-fc-visible  => "Done.\n<function_calls>\n<invoke name=\"get_weather\">\n<parameter name=\"city\">Paris</parameter>\n</invoke>\n</function_calls>"
C1 persist-unfenced => "Here you go.\n<invoke name=\"get_weather\">\n<parameter name=\"city\">Paris</parameter>\n</invoke>"
B1 persist-fenced   => "...```xml\n<invoke ...>...\n```..."   (preserved)
B2 persist-inline   => "Use the `<invoke name=\"get_weather\">` opener to start."   (preserved)

=== AFTER (this branch) ===
A2 mm-visible       => "Working on it."
A3 bare-fc-visible  => "Done."
C1 persist-unfenced => "Here you go.\n"
B1 persist-fenced   => "...```xml\n<invoke ...>...\n```..."   (still preserved)
B2 persist-inline   => "Use the `<invoke name=\"get_weather\">` opener to start."   (still preserved)
```

The three real leak shapes (A2 visible `mm:`, A3 visible `function_calls`-wrapped bare invoke, C1 persisted unfenced standalone invoke) are now scrubbed, while the fenced (B1) and inline (B2) code examples remain untouched — the exact over-scrub concern is verified closed.

O(n²) audit fix: a resolved-review pass measured the persist strip degrading quadratically on adversarial input with many unterminated invoke opens (720 KB ≈ 977 ms, scaling to seconds for a few MB). Making the scanner bail on `incomplete` (mirroring the existing unterminated-candidate bail) brought the same 720 KB input to ≈ 0.8 ms and restored linear scaling; a regression test locks this.

Verification: `tool-call-repair` grammar/payload/stream-normalizer (157 passed), `provider-stream-shared` + `tool-payload` + `assistant-visible-text` + `sanitize-text` + `message-action-runner.send-validation` + `embedded-agent-utils` (all green), `tsgo:core` and `tsgo:core:test` exit 0, `plugin-sdk:api:check` and `plugin-sdk:surface:check` exit 0 (surface budget bumped by the one new `StripPlainTextToolCallOptions` type), oxfmt clean, `git diff --check` clean. Rebased onto current `main` (`9b823c61`).

Fixes an issue where users exporting a session to HTML could see a broken replacement glyph in compact tool-call previews when a bash command or serialized tool argument was truncated through an emoji.

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where the `openclaw-npm-release` workflow could remain stuck in any of its `git fetch` steps until the job timeout when the Git transport stalls. This blocks the npm release pipeline and wastes runner time.

## Why This Change Was Made

All six `git fetch` commands now run through the repository's bounded process pattern: a 120-second deadline, followed by a 10-second termination grace period. This matches the pattern already applied to Mantis Crabbox workflows in #108940 (commit 16c2bbb). All release logic, merge-base checks, and non-network operations are unchanged.

The six locations covered: alpha preflight (L126), tagged release branch-fetch (L268), release-branch resolve fetch (L283), SHA-pinned origin/main fetch (L624), alpha publish preflight (L753), and alpha publish branch-fetch (L914).

## User Impact

Maintainers get prompt, actionable fetch failures instead of losing an npm release runner for the full job timeout before the release begins.

## Evidence

- Regression: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/package-acceptance-workflow.test.ts --run --testNamePattern="bounds openclaw-npm-release git fetch"` ??1 passed.

- Controlled runtime proof extracted each of the production workflow steps, scaled the production deadline to one second, and injected a Git transport that stalls until `TERM`. Every step returned 124 in about 1.03 seconds, the Git fixture observed `TERM`, and none reached the five-second outer watchdog. The identical pattern was proven for all five Mantis Crabbox workflows in #108940.

- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check` passed for the changed file; `git diff --check` passed.

- The complete test suite was also attempted: 72 tests passed, while unrelated environment-dependent cases failed because the isolated host lacked GitHub CLI authentication/clean login-shell state. The affected focused regression is green.

target.title: fix(ci): bound Docker release BuildKit pre-pull with timeout retries
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Docker release "Pre-pull BuildKit image" step used a 4-attempt retry loop around a bare `docker pull` with **no per-attempt process timeout**. When the Docker daemon, DNS, or registry half-opens, the first `docker pull` never returns, so the loop blocks on attempt 1 forever and the remaining retries never run — the job stalls until the runner/job-level timeout.

## Why This Change Was Made

Route the BuildKit pre-pull through the existing bounded helper `scripts/ci-docker-pull-retry.sh`, which wraps each `docker pull` in the host `timeout`/`gtimeout` (with a `--kill-after` grace period) and retries. This matches the other CI Docker pull sites and makes a hung pull killable so retries can proceed.

## User Impact

**Before:** A hung `docker pull` during a Docker release could stall the job indefinitely (until the runner/job timeout), skipping all retries.

**After:** Each BuildKit pull attempt is bounded (default 180s, `--kill-after=30s`); a hung pull is killed and retried up to four times.

## Evidence

- Changed: `.github/workflows/docker-release.yml`, `test/scripts/ci-docker-pull-retry.test.ts`, `test/scripts/package-acceptance-workflow.test.ts`
- Production caller path: docker-release `Pre-pull BuildKit image` step → `bash scripts/ci-docker-pull-retry.sh "${BUILDKIT_IMAGE}"` → `openclaw_host_timeout_bin` → `timeout --kill-after=30s "${timeout_seconds}s" docker pull "$image"`.

## Real behavior proof

### Behavior or issue addressed

A permanently hung first `docker pull` is killed at its per-attempt timeout so a later retry can succeed, instead of blocking the retry loop indefinitely.

### Canonical reachability path

Workflow step → `bash scripts/ci-docker-pull-retry.sh "${BUILDKIT_IMAGE}"` (`.github/workflows/docker-release.yml:137`) → `run_docker_pull` → `"$timeout_bin" --kill-after=30s "${timeout_seconds}s" docker pull "$image"` (`scripts/ci-docker-pull-retry.sh`).

### Real environment tested

Real shell execution of the production `scripts/ci-docker-pull-retry.sh` via `/bin/bash`. Two `PATH`-injected fakes stand in for external binaries: a `timeout` that faithfully emulates GNU `timeout` (runs the child under a real wall-clock budget and `SIGTERM`/`SIGKILL`s it on expiry, exit 124) and a `docker` whose first `pull` hangs forever (`while true; do sleep 1; done`) and whose second `pull` succeeds. No Docker daemon is required; the script's own timeout-selection, kill-after, retry, and exit-status logic run for real. macOS, Node v22.23.1 for the Vitest suite.

### Exact steps or command run after this patch

```bash
# Direct real-shell run of the production script: hung attempt 1, OK attempt 2.
PATH="<fake-bin>:/usr/bin:/bin" \
  OPENCLAW_DOCKER_PULL_ATTEMPTS=3 OPENCLAW_DOCKER_PULL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=2 \
  OPENCLAW_DOCKER_PULL_RETRY_DELAY_SECONDS=0 \
  bash scripts/ci-docker-pull-retry.sh registry.example/openclaw:test

# Committed real-shell regressions (spawn the script against fake docker/timeout):
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/ci-docker-pull-retry.test.ts -- --reporter=verbose
```

### Evidence after fix

Direct real-shell run (production script, hung first pull bounded and retried):

```text
==> Pull Docker image attempt 1/3: registry.example/openclaw:test
[fake-docker] attempt 1: hanging (simulated stuck registry)
[fake-timeout] budget 2s exceeded (kill-after=30s); killing hung child
Docker pull failed or timed out after 2s: status=124
==> Pull Docker image attempt 2/3: registry.example/openclaw:test
[fake-docker] attempt 2: pull OK
----
script_exit_code=0  approx_wall_s=4  attempts_run=2
```

Committed real-shell regressions (production script via `/bin/bash`):

```text
 ✓ scripts/ci-docker-pull-retry.sh > uses a kill-after grace period when timeout supports it 1022ms
 ✓ scripts/ci-docker-pull-retry.sh > falls back to plain timeout when kill-after is unavailable 460ms
 ✓ scripts/ci-docker-pull-retry.sh > uses gtimeout when timeout is unavailable 491ms
 ✓ scripts/ci-docker-pull-retry.sh > fails fast when timeout and gtimeout are unavailable 6ms
 ✓ scripts/ci-docker-pull-retry.sh > returns the last pull failure status after retries are exhausted 491ms
 ✓ scripts/ci-docker-pull-retry.sh > kills a hung first pull so a later retry can succeed 2384ms
 Tests  6 passed (6)
```

### Observed result after fix

The hung first `docker pull` is killed at the 2s per-attempt budget (`status=124`), the loop advances, attempt 2 succeeds, and the script exits `0` after running exactly 2 attempts. Pre-fix, the bare `docker pull` on attempt 1 would never return, so the loop would block on the first attempt indefinitely and never retry. The `package-acceptance-workflow` test also pins that `docker-release.yml` now calls the bounded helper with `OPENCLAW_DOCKER_PULL_ATTEMPTS: "4"` and no longer contains the raw `if docker pull "${BUILDKIT_IMAGE}"` loop.

### What was not tested

A live GitHub Actions runner pulling `moby/buildkit` against a genuinely wedged registry; the proof exercises the production script's bounding/retry logic against a real hung child on the host.

### Fix classification

bugfix — CI timeout/hang

## AI Assistance

AI-assisted. Author reviewed the workflow step change and the real-shell proof output.

target.title: fix(ollama): models advertise tools when /api/show fails
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users discovering local Ollama models would still see tool support advertised when `/api/show` failed (HTTP error or network throw), so a broken or uninspectable model looked tool-capable in catalog/setup paths.

## Why This Change Was Made

`buildOllamaModelDefinition` treats missing `capabilities` as optimistic `supportsTools: true`. Failed `/api/show` previously returned `{}`, which left capabilities undefined. This change marks failed inspection with `showInspectionFailed`, keeping three states:

1. `capabilities` omitted (uninspected / successful show without field) → optimistic tools + name heuristics
2. `capabilities: string[]` (including `[]`) → authoritative show result
3. `showInspectionFailed` → tools conservative, reasoning name heuristics preserved

The failure marker is propagated through provider discovery, interactive setup config building, and the dynamic `/models add` resolve path (there is no `src/auto-reply/reply/models-add.ts` on current main; that sibling lives in `extensions/ollama/index.ts`).

## User Impact

Local Ollama models whose `/api/show` fails no longer advertise tools across discovery, setup, and dynamic model resolve, while reasoning-named models still keep the established name heuristic during transient inspection failures. A successful show that reports an empty capabilities list remains authoritatively non-tool and non-reasoning.

## Evidence

| --- | --- | --- |
| L1 | three-state unit matrix + HTTP 404/throw paths | pass |
| L2 | `buildOllamaProvider`, setup config build, dynamic resolve | pass |

target.title: fix(cross-os): clamp release-check loops to remaining deadline
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Cross-OS release-check loops declare a total deadline but still armed each iteration with a full fetch/CLI timeout and an unclamped sleep. Near the deadline edge, `runDashboardSmoke`/`verifyDashboardAssetUrls` dashboard asset probes (10s each) and the Discord host/guest readback polls (60s CLI, 2–3s sleeps) could overrun the advertised budget by tens of seconds — the final asset fetch could arm a fresh 10s `AbortSignal.timeout` when only milliseconds of the smoke deadline remained.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add shared `remainingMs` / `clampTimeoutMs` helpers and clamp every per-attempt fetch timeout, CLI timeout, and sleep to the remaining deadline. `verifyDashboardAssetUrls` now accepts an optional `deadline` (and passthrough `signal`) so nested asset fetches inherit the same budget and short-circuit once it is exhausted.

## User Impact

**Before:** The last dashboard-asset fetch / Discord poll could run a full fixed timeout past the smoke deadline, drifting lanes tens of seconds beyond budget.

**After:** Cross-OS dashboard and Discord smoke loops fail closed at (not well past) their configured deadlines; the final attempt is bounded by whatever budget remains.

## Evidence

- Changed: `scripts/lib/cross-os-release-checks/{shared,runtime,network-smokes}.ts`, `test/scripts/openclaw-cross-os-release-checks.test.ts`
- Production caller path: `runDashboardSmoke` → `verifyDashboardAssetUrls(assetUrls, fetch, { deadline })` → `AbortSignal.timeout(clampTimeoutMs(deadline, CROSS_OS_DASHBOARD_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS))` (`scripts/lib/cross-os-release-checks/network-smokes.ts:236`).

## Real behavior proof

### Behavior or issue addressed

A hung dashboard asset fetch on the final smoke iteration is aborted at the remaining deadline instead of arming a fresh 10s fetch timeout, so `verifyDashboardAssetUrls` cannot overrun the smoke budget. Reachable assets still verify OK; an already-exhausted deadline short-circuits before any fetch.

### Canonical reachability path

`runDashboardSmoke` (`scripts/lib/cross-os-release-checks/runtime.ts:340`) computes `deadline = Date.now() + CROSS_OS_DASHBOARD_SMOKE_TIMEOUT_MS` and calls `verifyDashboardAssetUrls(assetUrls, fetch, { deadline })`; each asset fetch uses `AbortSignal.timeout(clampTimeoutMs(deadline, CROSS_OS_DASHBOARD_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS))` and the loop bails when `remainingMs(deadline) <= 0`.

### Real environment tested

Real HTTP transport: a local `node:http` server on `127.0.0.1` with two behaviors — an asset endpoint that accepts the request but **never** sends a response (hang), and a normal `200 text/css` asset. The exported production `verifyDashboardAssetUrls` is driven directly against those live sockets with the real global `fetch` and a small `deadline`, so the abort is produced by the production clamp path, not a mock. `CROSS_OS_DASHBOARD_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS` = 10000ms. Node v22.23.1, Vitest.

### Exact steps or command run after this patch

```bash
# Real HTTP server: hung asset endpoint + a reachable asset; drive the production
# verifyDashboardAssetUrls with a small smoke deadline.
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/cross-os-dashboard-deadline.proof.test.ts -- --reporter=verbose

# Committed deterministic regressions (arithmetic + clamp + short-circuit):
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/openclaw-cross-os-release-checks.test.ts -- \
  -t 'clamp|deadline|dashboard asset' --reporter=verbose
```

### Evidence after fix

Real HTTP behavior (production `verifyDashboardAssetUrls` against live sockets):

```text
  hung-asset verify ok: false
  hung-asset elapsed: 306ms (deadline budget 300ms, fixed fetch timeout 10000ms)
  failure: http://127.0.0.1:58935/stall TimeoutError: The operation was aborted due to timeout
  reachable-asset verify ok: true

ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS PASSED
 ✓ test/scripts/cross-os-dashboard-deadline.proof.test.ts > aborts a hung asset fetch at the remaining deadline, not the 10s fetch timeout 318ms
```

Committed deterministic regressions:

```text
 ✓ … > clamps per-attempt timeouts to the remaining deadline budget 1ms
 ✓ … > clamps dashboard asset AbortSignal.timeout to remaining deadline on last iteration 2ms
 ✓ … > stops dashboard asset verification when the deadline is already exhausted 0ms
```

### Observed result after fix

Against a real hung socket with a 300ms remaining deadline, the asset fetch aborts with `TimeoutError: The operation was aborted due to timeout` in 306ms — bounded by the clamped remaining budget, far below the fixed 10000ms dashboard-fetch timeout that the pre-fix code would have armed. A reachable `200` asset still verifies OK, and an already-exhausted deadline short-circuits before any fetch (`fetchAsset` never called).

### What was not tested

A full live cross-OS release lane driving `runDashboardSmoke` end-to-end against a real gateway dashboard; the proof exercises the exported `verifyDashboardAssetUrls` clamp path directly against a real hung server.

### Fix classification

bugfix — timeout/deadline clamping

## AI Assistance

AI-assisted. Author reviewed the clamp helpers, the dashboard/Discord loop call sites, and the real-server proof output.

target.title: fix: avoid false stayed-stopped on launchd KeepAlive throttle
target.body:
Closes #109941

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators running `openclaw gateway restart` on macOS would see a definitive false failure (`service stayed stopped and health checks never came up`) while a LaunchAgent-supervised gateway with `KeepAlive` was still inside launchd's normal `ThrottleInterval` respawn window and would become healthy seconds later. Automation that trusted that verdict could escalate against a recovering service.

## Why This Change Was Made

Restart health now prepares launchd KeepAlive supervision facts once before the poll loop and extends the continuous stopped-and-port-free early-exit threshold past the product `ThrottleInterval` when a loaded LaunchAgent is present. Unloaded, unmanaged, non-macOS, and non-KeepAlive paths keep the baseline fast-fail threshold. No new config knobs; supervisor facts are not rediscovered on every poll.

Compatibility: no config/API change; optional prepared `supervisor` param only. Performance: one `isLoaded` prepare at wait start. Usability: false failure verdict avoided during normal KeepAlive recovery. Security: no auth/trust change.

## User Impact

On macOS managed LaunchAgent installs, `openclaw gateway restart` no longer reports a hard "stayed stopped" failure solely because launchd is throttling a KeepAlive respawn. Genuine permanent stop / unload still fails within the existing overall restart health budget.

## Evidence

Verification host: local macOS (Crabbox bypass)

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/cli/daemon-cli/restart-health-wait.test.ts
 ✓ |cli| src/cli/daemon-cli/restart-health-wait.test.ts (16 tests) 666ms
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  16 passed (16)

$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/cli/daemon-cli/restart-health.test.ts src/cli/daemon-cli/lifecycle.test.ts
 ✓ |cli| src/cli/daemon-cli/restart-health.test.ts (27 tests)
 ✓ |cli| src/cli/daemon-cli/lifecycle.test.ts (34 tests)
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  61 passed (61)

$ pnpm check:changed
[check:changed] lanes=core, coreTests
… typecheck core / core tests / lint on touched files …
check:changed exit=0
```

Key new cases:

- KeepAlive + ThrottleInterval=10s early-exits only after ~20s continuous stopped+free (not the previous ~12.5s baseline false window)
- KeepAlive recovery that binds after the old 12.5s window returns `healthy` instead of `stopped-free`
- Unloaded / non-KeepAlive still uses the baseline ~12.5s early exit

## Real behavior proof

Verification host: local macOS with an isolated real LaunchAgent. The active `ai.openclaw.gateway` service was not touched.

The proof used the production LaunchAgent installer, service adapter, port inspection, and `waitForGatewayHealthyRestart` path with a random temporary label, HOME, and port. The supervised child deliberately exited on launches 1 and 2, then bound its port on launch 3. Cleanup booted out the temporary job and removed its files.

```json
{
  "proof": "isolated-real-launchd-keepalive",
  "label": "<isolated-label>",
  "keepAlive": true,
  "throttleIntervalSeconds": 10,
  "attemptsObserved": 3,
  "respawnGapsMs": [10113, 10113],
  "waitOutcome": "healthy",
  "healthy": true,
  "runtimeStatus": "running",
  "portStatus": "busy",
  "elapsedMs": 20667.57,
  "exceededOldStoppedFreeWindow": true
}
```

This exercises real launchd KeepAlive/throttle cadence: recovery occurred after the old ~12.5s stopped-free verdict window, and the patched wait returned healthy. During proof hardening, the threshold was also corrected to sample one full poll after the throttle boundary (20.5s at 500ms), rather than exactly on it.

Focused validation after the proof hardening:

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/cli/daemon-cli/restart-health-wait.test.ts src/cli/daemon-cli/restart-health.test.ts src/cli/daemon-cli/lifecycle.test.ts
Test Files  3 passed (3)
Tests       77 passed (77)
```

target.title: fix(codex): guard state-dependent registration for lightweight CLI runtime
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where the Codex plugin crashes during `register()` in lightweight CLI runtimes (e.g. `openclaw nodes --help`) because `api.runtime.state` is absent and state-dependent registration code attempts to access `openSyncKeyedStore`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Main already has a lazy `lazyBindingStateStore` proxy (which defers state access until first use), but the code after `registerCodexCliMetadata(api)` unconditionally registers commands and event handlers that eventually dereference `api.runtime.state`. This PR adds a feature guard immediately after CLI metadata registration: if `api.runtime.state?.openSyncKeyedStore` is unavailable, the plugin returns early after registering only the CLI metadata, skipping all state-dependent registration (session catalog, commands, event listeners).

The lazy proxy and existing `bindingStore` initialization are preserved exactly as-is from main.

## User Impact

Lightweight CLI invocations no longer log `[plugins] codex failed during register ... TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`. Full gateway runtime behavior is unchanged.

## Evidence

- Regression: `pnpm test:extension codex` ??passed. Existing tests continue to pass; the guard short-circuits only when the state facade is absent, which does not affect integration/unit test environments.

- Controlled runtime proof: standalone Node.js proof confirmed that when `api.runtime.state` is `undefined`, the function exits early after `registerCodexCliMetadata(api)` without throwing. When `api.runtime.state` is present (normal gateway), all registration proceeds as before.

- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check` passed for the changed file; `git diff --check` passed.

- The complete codex extension test suite was also attempted: all tests passed. The affected focused regression is green.

Fixes an issue where QA Lab Crabline inbound injection and runtime-parity mock `/debug/requests` fetches could hang indefinitely. ## Why This Change Was Made

Copy the existing `suite-runtime-gateway` pattern: pass `timeoutMs: 15_000` into `fetchWithSsrFGuard` and read JSON through `readProviderJsonResponse` on both surfaces. Add a caller-path hang regression for runtime-parity capture and a focused Crabline inbound assertion that the production helper receives the timeout + bounded JSON reader.

## User Impact

target.title: fix(anthropic): complete transcript reverse-scan windows across short reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Opening a Claude session transcript in the session catalog can fail with a
`Claude transcript changed while it was being read` error even when the file was
not touched.

`readLocalClaudeTranscriptPage` in `extensions/anthropic/session-catalog.ts`
scans the transcript backwards in fixed windows. Each window was filled with a
single positional `handle.read(chunk, 0, size, position)` that then required
`bytesRead === size`, throwing otherwise. A positional read is allowed to return
fewer bytes than requested, so a benign short read tripped that check and failed
the transcript page with a message implying the file changed. The window is
in-bounds (`position` starts at `requestedEnd ≤ stat.size` and only decrements,
`size = min(chunk, position, …)`), so a short read there is not on its own a
reason to fail the page. The forward metadata scan in the same function already
completes short reads by looping; only this reverse scan threw.

## Why This Change Was Made

The reverse scan now fills each window across as many reads as it takes,
advancing both the buffer offset and the file position each read, so a benign
short read no longer surfaces a "transcript changed" error. A zero-byte read
before the window is filled is premature EOF, so that case still throws the same
error — only benign positive short reads stop failing the page. This is the same
loop the forward scan in this file already uses, and it follows the recently
merged short-read completion work (#108941, #108655, #108253) that had not
reached this plugin path; it is a different surface from #108242, which fills
bounded windows in the core gateway (`src/gateway/session-utils.fs.ts`).

## User Impact

Paging a Claude session transcript no longer fails with a spurious "Claude
transcript changed while it was being read" error when a benign positive short
read occurs in the reverse-window scan. A zero-byte read before the window is
filled (premature EOF, consistent with the file being truncated or replaced
mid-read) still surfaces the same error.

## Evidence

Changed files: `extensions/anthropic/session-catalog.ts` (reverse-scan fill
loop) and `extensions/anthropic/session-catalog.test.ts` (two regression tests).

The two colocated unit tests lock the regression behavior: one drives
`readLocalClaudeTranscriptPage` through capped short positional reads and asserts
the paged items/order/cursor match a normal read across two pages; the other
forces a zero-byte read mid-window and asserts the existing premature-EOF error
still raises.

Real-behavior proof came from driving the **exported** `readLocalClaudeTranscriptPage`
against a real on-disk, secretless Claude JSONL transcript of 204929 bytes (larger
than the 128 KiB reverse window) while capping the underlying `FileHandle.read` to
4096 bytes — the same real transcript and capping logic run against the
current-main module (before) and this branch (after). Raw run:

```text
real readLocalClaudeTranscriptPage · real FileHandle.read · transcript 204929 B · read cap 4096 B
baseline (before) SHA e0478e2d · after (this PR) SHA 223e79bca3

[1] NORMAL CONTROL   (after,  uncapped)  3 real reads · page-hash c573fe29… (2 pages)
[2] SHORT READ       (before, cap 4096)  throws "Claude transcript changed while it was being read" at read #1
[3] SHORT READ       (after,  cap 4096)  82 real reads · page-hash c573fe29… · identical to [1]: true
[4] ZERO-BYTE EOF    (after)             throws "Claude transcript changed while it was being read"
```

The `page-hash` is over both pages' items, ordering, and `nextCursor`; case [3]
matching case [1] means identical pagination. Of the 82 reads in [3], 79 are
within-window contiguous fills (buffer offset and file position each advance by
the previous read's length); the remaining reads are the first read of each new,
lower reverse window (position steps down), across the two requested pages.

Reproduce: on each SHA, call the exported `readLocalClaudeTranscriptPage` against
a >128 KiB Claude JSONL transcript while capping the underlying `FileHandle.read`
to 4 KiB; before the fix the first capped read throws, after the fix the windows
are completed and the two-page items/ordering/cursors are identical to an
uncapped read.

Focused suite: `vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-providers.config.ts
extensions/anthropic/session-catalog.test.ts` — 27 passed (25 existing + 2 new);
before the fix: 1 failed | 26 passed. oxfmt and oxlint clean; extensions
typecheck reports no errors in the changed files.

target.title: Export installed agents as grouped Claw packages
target.body:
## Summary

- add experimental `claws export <agent-id> --out <new-directory>`
- project one installed agent into the grouped portable Claw schema
- copy ledger-managed workspace files and safe workspace-relative avatars into package sidecars
- always assign regenerated exports a derivative package identity and content-derived version
- omit nonportable remote avatars, normalize empty optional arrays, and expand `~` in output paths

## Scope

Export reads the provenance established by the add/status lifecycle and writes a new self-contained package without mutating the installed Claw. It accepts an exact agent id, explicitly projects portable agent fields, copies only ledger-managed workspace files plus a validated local avatar, emits exact recorded package references, and refuses unavailable managed files or an existing output directory.

Image data avatars remain inline. A safe local avatar is read through the pinned workspace avatar boundary, copied under `workspace/`, and rewritten to a workspace-relative manifest path. Remote, missing, or unsafe local avatars are omitted because they are not portable package state.

Every regenerated package is emitted as `openclaw-claw-<agent-id>@0.0.0-export.<content-hash>`, including an unchanged installation. Export never reuses an authenticated publisher's package name/version unless it can return the byte-for-byte original artifact, which this command intentionally does not do.

This slice emits the schema's JSON-compatible representation. The later dedicated #106888 slice changes the canonical exported representation to `CLAW.md` while preserving this package and round-trip behavior.

## Stack

- RFC: https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/27
- Depends on: #102296 status/remove and ownership-aware lifecycle state
- This PR: portable creation/export experience
- Next: #102383 gateway-owned cron lifecycle
- Canonical `CLAW.md`: #106888

## Validation

- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.test.src.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/test-src.tsbuildinfo`
- Oxlint: 0 warnings, 0 errors across all 6 PR files
- Oxfmt: all 6 PR files correctly formatted
- 8 export unit tests
- 15 Claws CLI tests
- 8 full lifecycle E2E tests
- `git diff --check`
- Codex review: no accepted/actionable findings

## Real behavior proof

The real CLI E2E passes consent-bound add preview/apply -> export -> inspect -> consent-bound add preview/apply from the exported package in isolated state. Export writes `package.json`, `openclaw.claw.json`, managed workspace sidecars, and a portable agent manifest; the fresh add recreates the agent from the derivative package.

target.title: fix(acp): defer session snapshot update after newSession/resumeSession result
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`newSession()` and `resumeSession()` in the ACP bridge send the `session_info_update` notification via `sendSessionSnapshotUpdate` BEFORE returning the JSON-RPC result. Clients that key off `session_info_update` to learn the sessionId receive a notification referencing a sessionId they have not yet parsed from the result.

This causes Rabbit R1 sessions to hang indefinitely (rabbit-agent gates prompt delivery on receiving session_info_update after the result).

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix defers the notification and subsequent `sendAvailableCommands` to fire asynchronously after the result is returned, using `setTimeout(..., 0)` to cross the response-write boundary. Both `newSession()` (line 394) and `resumeSession()` (line 554) are fixed. The full promise chain has a terminal `.catch()` handler.

## User Impact

Clients that expect session_info_update after the session/new or resume result now receive correct ordering. No change to the API contract, response shape, or notification content.

## Evidence

### Ordering tests (transport-level)
```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  15 passed (15)
```
Two new tests verify that `session_info_update` is NOT called before the lifecycle handler resolves, and IS called after flushing timers — confirming result-before-notification ordering at the transport boundary.

### All ACP tests
```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  13 passed (13)
```

### Typecheck
```
pnpm tsgo:core — EXIT: 0
```

### Fix pattern
Before: `await sendSessionSnapshotUpdate(...)` → `return { sessionId, ... }`
After:  `return { sessionId, ... }` → `setTimeout(() => sendSessionSnapshotUpdate(...).then(...).catch(...), 0)`

target.title: Bound QA runtime parity mock request reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

QA runtime-parity reads `${mockBaseUrl}/debug/requests` from a local mock server and previously used `response.json()` directly. That endpoint should return a small request snapshot array, but a broken mock server could return a large successful body and make the QA process buffer it before any validation.

## Why This Change Was Made

This replaces the unbounded `response.json()` call with the shared `readResponseWithLimit` helper using a 256 KiB cap and a 30s idle timeout. The existing fail-closed behavior is preserved: non-OK, malformed, oversized, or stalled mock responses are caught by `loadRuntimeParityMockToolCalls` and treated as missing mock tool-call data.

## User Impact

QA runtime-parity remains tolerant of unavailable or malformed mock debug data, but successful mock responses are now bounded before JSON parsing. Valid mock request arrays still resolve tool-call order normally.

## Evidence

**Scope:** 2 files.
- `extensions/qa-lab/src/runtime-parity.ts` (+16/-1): bounded response read with 256 KiB cap and 30s idle timeout.
- `extensions/qa-lab/src/runtime-parity.test.ts` (+33/-1): regression tests for bounded reads.

### Regression Test

Added runtime-parity tests in `extensions/qa-lab/src/runtime-parity.test.ts` covering:

- non-OK `/debug/requests` returns no mock tool calls;
- oversized successful `/debug/requests` response returns no mock tool calls under the byte cap;
- malformed successful JSON returns no mock tool calls.

target.title: feat: trace Claude Code CLI model calls
target.body: ## What Problem This Solves Claude Code CLI turns did not emit trusted `model.call.started`, `model.call.completed`, and `model.call.error` diagnostics. Phoenix therefore could not show a useful model span with the OpenClaw-visible prompt, response, timing, and usage data for `claude-cli` runs. ## Why This Change Was Made Add synthetic turn-level model-call tracing at the honest Claude Code CLI boundary for one-shot, managed persistent stdio, and paired-node execution. Each admitted attempt now receives exactly one terminal lifecycle event, including retry attempts, aborts, timeouts, process/parse failures, deferred background completion, persistence failure, and cleanup failure. Content capture reuses the existing trusted capture policy and remains disabled by default. Granular capture includes only the effective OpenClaw prompt, OpenClaw-appended system prompt, and visible assistant blocks. It intentionally excludes Claude Code private prompts, hidden resume/compaction payloads, native tool schemas and arguments, raw Anthropic HTTP traffic, internal retries, upstream request IDs, and network TTFB. Terminal cumulative usage, including cache read/write tokens, is used for the model span while existing last-assistant-message reply accounting remains unchanged. ## User Impact Operators using OpenTelemetry/Phoenix can inspect a truthful Claude CLI model span with useful lifecycle, prompt/response, byte, timing, and aggregate usage data when content capture is explicitly enabled. Default installations remain metadata-only, and native OpenClaw/Codex tracing behavior is unchanged. AI-assisted: yes (Codex). I reviewed the implementation and validation results. ## Evidence - `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/cli-output.test.ts src/agents/cli-runner.spawn.test.ts src/agents/cli-runner/claude-live-session.background-tasks.test.ts`: 3 files, 170 tests passed. - Retry lifecycle regression filter: 6 tests passed; proves matched `started → error` and `started → completed` call IDs across fresh-session recovery. - Post-success cleanup regression filter: 2 tests passed; proves cleanup rejection emits error rather than completion. - `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/diagnostics-otel/src/service.test.ts`: 1 file, 108 tests passed, including `gen_ai.input.messages`, `gen_ai.output.messages`, and `gen_ai.system_instructions`. - Blacksmith Testbox: core production types, core test types, extension test types, and touched-file lint passed. Final correction proof: [run 29416165438](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29416165438). - `oxfmt --check` and `git diff --check`: passed. - Fresh structured autoreview after fixes: clean, no accepted/actionable findings; patch correct (0.86).

target.title: feat: let plugin tools yield turns
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Plugin tools can send work to an external interaction surface, but before this change they could only return a normal tool result. The agent loop could then continue in the same turn before the external callback arrived, which races native approval and form-card flows against the eventual user response.

## Why This Is Better Than The Current Behavior

This adds a narrow runtime control request on `AgentToolResult` and exposes `yieldToolResult(...)` from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/tool-results`. After a plugin tool returns that result, OpenClaw retains the successful tool result and routes through the existing `sessions_yield` turn-handoff path. A later inbound event can then resume the same session.

Control is applied only after the complete `afterToolCall` finalization lifecycle. Hook-added and hook-replaced controls therefore affect the actual runtime action, and runtimes without a control handler fail explicitly instead of silently continuing.

Tools that may yield must declare both `canYield: true` and `executionMode: "sequential"`. Agent-core validates both declarations; the scheduler sees the sequential identity before starting the batch, so a successful yield aborts the turn before later sibling tools run. Only `canYield` tools remain model-visible and are excluded from Tool Search, Code Mode, and headless catalogs because those outer bridges cannot preserve the target tool's pre-execution scheduling identity. Existing non-yielding sequential tools retain their prior catalog behavior.

The implementation remains channel-agnostic. Existing tools and plugins are unchanged when they return no `control` field.

## User Impact

Plugin authors can implement native interaction tools, such as approval or form-card prompts, without racing the model loop against the user callback. Existing plugin tools do not need migration; only tools that opt into yield declare the new capability and sequential execution.

## Implementation

- Add `AgentToolResult.control` and the public `yieldToolResult(...)` helper.
- Add a host-owned finalized-result control seam in agent-core.
- Add the explicit `canYield` tool capability and preserve it through tool-definition adapters.
- Wire embedded OpenClaw sessions to the existing `sessions_yield` lifecycle.
- Reject unsupported controls and controls from tools missing either required declaration.
- Stop a sequential batch after yield so later side-effectful sibling tools never start.
- Keep only `canYield` tools on the direct execution surface; ordinary sequential tools remain catalog-eligible.

## Evidence

### Real external plugin runtime proof

Environment: macOS arm64, Node 22.23.1.

A standalone external plugin was loaded from its real manifest through `loadOpenClawPlugins`, registered and resolved `proof_ask_user`, imported `yieldToolResult` from the public Plugin SDK entrypoint, and executed through a real `Agent`. The first run yielded; the finalized successful tool result remained in the transcript; a later inbound prompt on the same Agent completed normally.

Redacted observed output:

```json
{
  "plugin": {
    "id": "yield-proof",
    "loaded": true,
    "registeredTools": ["proof_ask_user"],
    "resolvedTool": "proof_ask_user"
  },
  "finalizedResult": {
    "content": [{ "type": "text", "text": "Question card sent." }],
    "details": {
      "status": "pending",
      "question": "Approve the deployment?",
      "cardId": "proof-card-1"
    },
    "control": {
      "type": "yield",
      "message": "Waiting for proof card answer"
    }
  },
  "runtime": {
    "sessionId": "proof-session-1",
    "yieldEvents": ["Waiting for proof card answer"],
    "yieldDetected": true,
    "modelCalls": 2,
    "retainedToolResult": {
      "toolName": "proof_ask_user",
      "details": { "status": "pending", "cardId": "proof-card-1" },
      "isError": false
    },
    "resumedAssistant": {
      "content": [{ "type": "text", "text": "Answer accepted." }],
      "stopReason": "stop"
    }
  }
}
```

### Finalization, scheduling, compatibility, and resume coverage

- Agent-core tests prove controls added or replaced by `afterToolCall` are applied only after finalization.
- Agent-core rejects yield from tools missing `canYield` or sequential execution before invoking the runtime handler.
- Agent-core proves a valid yielding tool prevents a later side-effectful sibling from starting.
- Adapter tests prove `canYield` survives AgentTool → ToolDefinition → AgentTool conversion.
- Catalog tests prove only `canYield` tools remain direct across Tool Search and Code Mode, while ordinary sequential tools stay cataloged; headless catalog behavior is covered too.
- Embedded orchestration proves a yielded run reports `paused` / `end_turn`, releases the active session, and accepts a later inbound turn on the same session.

### Verification

- Scheduler TDD RED: run `29575710823` failed before the sequential guard existed.
- Scheduler TDD GREEN: run `29576120720` passed after the guard landed.
- Catalog scheduling TDD RED: run `29577281682`, job `87874669293`, failed before yield tools were kept direct.
- Compatibility TDD RED: run `29578570258`, job `87878675234`, failed when generic sequential tools still bypassed catalogs.
- Exact-head GREEN: run `29578965700` passed on `1dd9cf88a4deaab45ad92a081b760789955c1c46`: 55 successful jobs, 11 conditional skips, 0 failures, 0 pending.
- `build-artifacts`, SDK declarations/surface checks, docs, lint/format, production types, test types, all selected Node shards, CodeQL, OpenGrep, and workflow sanity passed.
- GitHub reports the PR `MERGEABLE`; `git diff --check` passes and the worktree is clean.

## Notes

Prepared with AI assistance.

## Linked Issue

Closes #109761

target.title: Fix MSTeams card actions with durable receive before ACK
target.body:
## What problem this solves

Microsoft Teams adaptive-card actions were acknowledged before OpenClaw had durably recorded them. If the Gateway stopped after the invoke ACK but before asynchronous dispatch completed, the user saw a successful click while the action could be lost permanently.

## What changed

- Authenticate and normalize non-poll card actions before admitting them.
- Commit the action to the shared SQLite-backed channel ingress queue before returning the invoke ACK.
- Drain the queue asynchronously with bounded retry, dead-letter handling, claim fencing, and startup recovery.
- Derive stable event and conversation-lane identities so duplicate delivery cannot dispatch concurrently.
- Rebuild the Bot Framework conversation reference for proactive replay to the original conversation/thread.
- Keep queue-owned retry attempts silent: dispatch failures are rethrown to the queue without sending a generic failure reply on every attempt.

Normal messages and poll actions keep their existing paths; this change is limited to non-poll adaptive-card actions.

## Evidence

- Real SQLite lifecycle tests cover commit-before-return, restart recovery, bounded transient retry, post-adoption terminal handling, duplicate fencing, and correct conversation/thread replay.
- Focused Teams handler tests cover normal card completion, error propagation to the queue, and verify that retryable failures do not call `sendActivity`.
- The branch is refreshed onto current `main` at `907f5552f5f076f8ae2d50e16a707e4a7258f8c9`.
- [GitHub Actions CI run 29577503313](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29577503313) is green, including changed Node tests, production/test type checks, lint, dependency and package-boundary checks, build artifacts, and `openclaw/ci-gate`.
- The implementation was checked against the pinned `@microsoft/teams.apps` 2.0.13 invoke-response, proactive conversation, and activity-send contracts.

## Live Teams validation limitation

I cannot currently provide redacted live Microsoft Teams evidence because I do not have access to a Microsoft 365 tenant that permits custom Teams app upload.

I attempted to provision a Teams/Microsoft 365 trial, but the required payment-method verification was unsuccessful. The Microsoft 365 E5 developer sandbox is also eligibility-restricted and is not generally available to individual contributors.

After the branch refresh and review fixes above, complete reproduction steps and diagnostics are available, but a maintainer or contributor with an existing Teams development tenant is needed for the final live validation. I have requested maintainer-assisted validation in a PR comment.

Requested live scenarios:

1. Confirm the durable ingress record is committed before the invoke ACK.
2. Confirm a normal non-poll card action completes successfully.
3. Stop the Gateway after ACK and verify recovery after restart.
4. Inject a transient dispatch failure and verify bounded retry without duplicate user-visible failure replies.
5. Confirm duplicate delivery does not cause concurrent duplicate dispatch.
6. Confirm the proactive reply targets the correct conversation/thread.

All logs and recordings must redact tenant IDs, user IDs, service URLs, tokens, credentials, IP addresses, and message content.

target.title: [Bug]: OpenClaw v7.1 Dashboard Returns 400 Error with llamacpp due to Missing Regex Anchors in Auto-Generated GBNF Schema
target.body:
### Bug type

Regression (worked before, now fails)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

OpenClaw v7.1 Dashboard returns a 400 Bad Request error when interacting with a local llamacpp provider due to missing ^ and $ anchors in the auto-generated GBNF schema, while the exact same agent and model work perfectly through a standard Gateway message channel.

### Steps to reproduce

Configure OpenClaw v7.1 to use a local llamacpp provider (e.g., Qwen3.6-27B-UDiq3).
Open the native OpenClaw Web Dashboard and send a message that triggers a tool call or requires schema validation.
Observe that the request fails with a 400 error.
In the exact same session, send a message through a custom WebUI that uses the standard Gateway message routing (_send_to_gateway('main', text)).
Observe that the request succeeds with a 200 OK response.

### Expected behavior

In previous versions (and currently via the standard Gateway message channel), both the native Dashboard and external clients successfully communicate with the llamacpp provider without schema validation errors.

### Actual behavior

The native Dashboard fails with a 400 error. The attached gateway log shows the exact error at 18:21:55 UTC: 400 Unable to generate parser for this template. Automatic parser generation failed: JSON schema conversion failed: Pattern must start with '^' and end with '$'. The llamacpp provider strictly rejects the malformed pattern, while the custom WebUI processes the request successfully.

### OpenClaw version

2026.7.1

### Operating system

windows11

llamacpp/*

llamacpp with openai-completions

The Control UI mock has limited curated chat state for design QA, so reviewers have to rely on ad hoc sessions when checking empty chat, longer transcripts, markdown rendering, code blocks, tables, warnings, and recoverable error copy.

This PR adds stable dev/mock-only fixture sessions to the Control UI mock server. The proposed fixtures cover a New session empty state, a coding session, a response-shape showcase, and a markdown showcase without changing production gateway or session APIs.

## User Impact

There is no production user-facing behavior change. Developers and designers can load stable mock chat sessions for future Control UI visual review.

target.title: test(plugins): cover filtered bundle MCP servers
target.body:
## Summary

This PR tightens the existing compatible-bundle MCP path for bundles that need a narrower default tool surface.

- Adds regression coverage that a Codex-compatible bundle `.mcp.json` preserves `toolFilter.include`, `toolFilter.exclude`, and a relative bundle data root.
- Documents bundle MCP tool filters on the plugin-bundles page alongside the existing transport and tool-naming guidance.
- Keeps scope limited to bundle MCP loading/docs; runtime filtering behavior already exists and is covered separately.

Reviewers should focus on whether the bundle MCP docs accurately describe the existing runtime behavior and whether the new compatible-bundle regression is useful.

## Linked context

No issue filed.

Related precedent investigated: bundle MCP support and follow-up coverage in prior OpenClaw PRs such as #48611, #71287, #79686, and #88399. This PR follows that existing bundle MCP seam.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

Behavior addressed: Compatible bundles that contribute MCP servers can ship a narrow default tool surface through `toolFilter.include` and `toolFilter.exclude`; OpenClaw docs now describe that bundle path and a regression test proves the loader preserves the filter and relative app root.

Real environment tested: Local OpenClaw checkout on macOS, branch `test/filtered-bundle-mcp`, commit `d5bffb3dc0`, with an isolated temporary `HOME`, `OPENCLAW_HOME`, and `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`.

Exact steps or command run after this patch: Created a temporary Codex-compatible bundle containing `.codex-plugin/plugin.json`, `.mcp.json`, `skills/`, and `apps/`; ran `pnpm openclaw plugins install --link <temp>/vision-mcp`; ran `pnpm openclaw plugins inspect vision-mcp --json`; then loaded bundle MCP config with `node --import tsx` calling `loadEnabledBundleMcpConfig(...)` against the isolated home/config.

Evidence after fix: Terminal output from the temporary real OpenClaw setup:

```text
Proof root: /var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt
$ node scripts/run-node.mjs plugins install --link /var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt/vision-mcp
Linked plugin path: /var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt/vision-mcp
Restart the gateway to load plugins.
$ node scripts/run-node.mjs plugins inspect vision-mcp --json
{
  "diagnostics": [],
  "command": "npx",
  "args": [
    "-y",
    "@vision-mcp/cli@latest",
    "serve",
    "--apps-root",
    "/private/var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt/vision-mcp/apps"
  ],
  "cwdEndsWith": true,
  "toolFilter": {
    "include": [
      "capsule.*",
      "vision_map.snapshot",
      "vision_map.list_apps",
      "vision_map.list_workflows",
      "vision_map.describe_workflow",
      "vision_map.describe",
      "vision_map.detect_state",
      "vision_map.list_actions",
      "vision_map.describe_action",
      "vision_map.perform_action",
      "vision_map.run_workflow",
      "vision_map.verify",
      "vision_map.repair_minimal",
      "vision_map.export_trace"
    ],
    "exclude": [
      "vision_map.click_at",
      "vision_map.type_text",
      "vision_map.press_key",
      "vision_map.scroll",
      "vision_map.init",
      "vision_map.apply_patch",
      "vision_map.add_control",
      "vision_map.commit_*",
      "vision_map.harvest_session"
    ]
  }
}
```

Observed result after fix: OpenClaw linked the temporary compatible bundle, detected its bundle MCP server, preserved both include and exclude filter arrays, set `cwd` to the bundle root, and resolved `./apps` to an absolute path inside the installed bundle.

What was not tested: I did not launch the MCP server process, connect to a live desktop MCP server, or perform GUI automation. I also did not run a full Gateway agent turn against the temporary bundle.

Proof limitations or environment constraints: The proof uses a temporary local compatible bundle and the real OpenClaw plugin installer/loader, but the MCP server command itself is not started because this PR changes documentation and loader regression coverage, not MCP runtime execution behavior.

## Tests and validation

Commands run:

```text
node scripts/test-projects.mjs -- src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts --reporter=verbose
pnpm format:check src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts
git diff --check
pnpm check:docs
codex review --base origin/main
```

Regression coverage added: `src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts` now covers a Codex-compatible bundle MCP config with a filtered server and a relative `./apps` data root.

Validation results:

```text
src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts: 1 file passed, 8 tests passed
pnpm format:check src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts: All matched files use the correct format
git diff --check: passed
pnpm check:docs: Docs formatting clean; markdownlint 0 errors; MDX check passed; i18n glossary passed; checked_internal_links=4554; broken_links=0
codex review --base origin/main: No actionable correctness issues were found
```

## Risk checklist

Did user-visible behavior change? (`Yes/No`): No runtime behavior change; docs now describe existing bundle MCP filter behavior.

Did config, environment, or migration behavior change? (`Yes/No`): No.

Did security, auth, secrets, network, or tool execution behavior change? (`Yes/No`): No runtime change. The docs encourage narrow bundle MCP defaults for high-risk tool surfaces.

What is the highest-risk area? The docs could overstate which configured MCP fields bundle MCP entries support.

How is that risk mitigated? Existing runtime code already reads `toolFilter` from bundle-provided server config, existing runtime tests cover filtering behavior, and this PR adds loader coverage proving the bundle file path preserves the filter before runtime discovery.

## Current review state

AI-assisted: yes.

Next action: maintainer review.

target.title: docs(memory): align descriptors and docs with recursive memory/**/*.md
target.body:
## Summary
- The runtime already walks `memory/` recursively via `collectMemoryFilesFromDir` (`packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/internal.ts`), so nested files like `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md` are indexed and searched. But several agent-facing descriptors and public docs still said `memory/*.md`, which can mislead agents into thinking the index is flat.
- This PR updates the remaining stale references to `memory/**/*.md`. No runtime behavior change.

## Files touched
- `extensions/memory-core/index.ts` — lazy `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptors
- `extensions/memory-core/src/tools.ts` — concrete `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptions
- `extensions/memory-core/src/prompt-section.ts` — system-prompt recall guidance
- `src/config/schema.help.ts` — `agents.defaults.memorySearch` help text
- `docs/concepts/memory-builtin.md`, `memory.md`, `system-prompt.md`
- `docs/gateway/config-agents.md`, `docs/reference/token-use.md`
- `docs/.generated/config-baseline.sha256` regenerated via `pnpm config:docs:gen`

## Note
This supersedes #72748. That PR also carried QMD watcher changes that were independently resolved upstream by #81802 (`watch-settle.ts`), so the surviving value was just this wording alignment. Splitting it out as a small, behavior-neutral PR for easier review.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed**: Agent-facing descriptors and public docs said `memory/*.md` even though the runtime already walks `memory/` recursively and indexes nested files such as `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md`. This PR aligns the wording to `memory/**/*.md` so agents and readers see what is actually indexed. The change is wording-only; the proof below shows (a) the installed runtime already exhibits the recursive behavior the new wording describes, and (b) the after-patch descriptor and prompt strings on this branch actually carry the new `memory/**/*.md` wording when imported at runtime.

**Real environment tested**: Installed OpenClaw `2026.5.20` (npm global, current `latest` published build, ahead of the `acf265d` base this PR branches from), against the live workspace `~/.openclaw/workspace-moku` used by the gateway. Agent `main`, local embedding provider, per-agent SQLite memory store at `~/.openclaw/memory/main.sqlite`. After-patch text proof imports the modified TypeScript modules directly from this branch via `node --import tsx` against working tree at HEAD `30f15f4e22`.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:

Step 1 — drop a nested dated memory file under `memory/2026-05/` with a unique token:

```
cat > ~/.openclaw/workspace-moku/memory/2026-05/2026-05-24-recursive-proof.md <<'EOF'
Recursive memory search proof.
Unique token for PR 85899 smoke test: PROOFTOKEN_QXZ7K_NESTED_RECURSIVE_MEMORY
This file lives at memory/2026-05/2026-05-24-recursive-proof.md
EOF
```

Step 2 — reindex the live agent's memory store:

```
openclaw memory index
```

Step 3 — search for the unique token to prove the nested path was indexed and is retrievable:

```
openclaw memory search "PROOFTOKEN_QXZ7K_NESTED_RECURSIVE_MEMORY" --max-results 3
```

Step 4 — on the PR branch checkout (`30f15f4e22`), import the modified descriptor/help modules at runtime via `tsx` and print the after-patch strings to prove the new `memory/**/*.md` wording is observable from a real runtime call site (not just the diff):

```
node --import tsx _proof-c.mjs   # imports FIELD_HELP and buildPromptSection from this branch
```

**After-fix evidence**: Terminal output from the installed `openclaw 2026.5.20` runtime on the live workspace, plus runtime-imported after-patch strings from this branch (absolute paths redacted to `~`):

```
$ openclaw memory status
Memory Search (main)
Provider: local (requested: local)
Sources: memory
Extra paths: ~/.openclaw/shared-memory
Indexed: 105/105 files . 933 chunks
Workspace: ~/.openclaw/workspace-moku
By source:
  memory . 105/105 files . 933 chunks
```

```
$ openclaw memory index
[node-llama-cpp] ... falling back to using no GPU
Memory index updated (main).
```

```
$ openclaw memory search "PROOFTOKEN_QXZ7K_NESTED_RECURSIVE_MEMORY" --max-results 3
[node-llama-cpp] ... falling back to using no GPU
0.812 memory/2026-05/2026-05-24-recursive-proof.md:1-9
    Recursive memory search proof.
    Unique token for PR 85899 smoke test: PROOFTOKEN_QXZ7K_NESTED_RECURSIVE_MEMORY
    This file lives at memory/2026-05/2026-05-24-recursive-proof.md
    to verify that nested dated memory files are indexed and searchable
    by the runtime.

0.450 memory/fix-openclaw/memory-recursive-search/smoke/2026-04-27.md:1-6
0.432 memory/fix-openclaw/memory-recursive-search/pr-draft.md:1-32
```

After-patch text observed from this branch (HEAD `30f15f4e22`) by importing the modified modules at runtime:

```
$ node --import tsx _proof-c.mjs
=== schema.help.ts: FIELD_HELP['agents.defaults.memorySearch'] ===
Vector search over MEMORY.md and memory/**/*.md (per-agent overrides supported).

=== prompt-section.ts: buildPromptSection({ memory_search + memory_get }) ===
    [section header line: "## Memory Recall"]
    Before answering anything about prior work, decisions, dates, people, preferences, or todos: run memory_search on MEMORY.md + memory/**/*.md + indexed session transcripts; then use memory_get to pull only the needed lines. If low confidence after search, say you checked.
    Citations are disabled: do not mention file paths or line numbers in replies unless the user explicitly asks.

=== prompt-section.ts: buildPromptSection({ memory_search only }) ===
    [section header line: "## Memory Recall"]
    Before answering anything about prior work, decisions, dates, people, preferences, or todos: run memory_search on MEMORY.md + memory/**/*.md + indexed session transcripts and answer from the matching results. If low confidence after search, say you checked.
    Citations are disabled: do not mention file paths or line numbers in replies unless the user explicitly asks.

=== extensions/memory-core/index.ts (post-patch source lines) ===
 127      description:
 128        "Mandatory recall step: semantically search MEMORY.md + memory/**/*.md (and optional session transcripts) before answering questions about prior work, decisions, dates, people, preferences, or todos. ...",

 139      description:
 140        "Safe exact excerpt read from MEMORY.md or memory/**/*.md. Defaults to a bounded excerpt when lines are omitted, includes truncation/continuation info when more content exists, and `corpus=wiki` reads from registered compiled-wiki supplements.",

=== extensions/memory-core/src/tools.ts (post-patch source lines) ===
 240      description:
 241        "Mandatory recall step: semantically search MEMORY.md + memory/**/*.md (and optional session transcripts) before answering questions about prior work, decisions, dates, people, preferences, or todos. ...",

 410      description:
 411        "Safe exact excerpt read from MEMORY.md or memory/**/*.md. Defaults to a bounded excerpt when lines are omitted, includes truncation/continuation info when more content exists, and `corpus=wiki` reads from registered compiled-wiki supplements.",
```

**Observed result after fix**: (a) The freshly written nested file `memory/2026-05/2026-05-24-recursive-proof.md` (two levels deep under `memory/`) was indexed by `openclaw memory index` and returned as the top match (score `0.812`) for the unique token. A second nested hit from `memory/fix-openclaw/memory-recursive-search/smoke/2026-04-27.md` (three levels deep) confirms recursion is not limited to one level. (b) Importing the modified `FIELD_HELP` map and `buildPromptSection` from this branch at runtime shows the after-patch strings carry `memory/**/*.md` for both the config help text and the system-prompt memory recall guidance, matching the diff exactly. (c) The two `memory_search` / `memory_get` description strings in `extensions/memory-core/index.ts` and `extensions/memory-core/src/tools.ts` are inline string literals; the after-patch lines printed from this branch show the new wording in place. No runtime code paths are modified, only the descriptor and doc strings plus the regenerated `docs/.generated/config-baseline.sha256`.

**What was not tested**: This PR does not introduce or modify any runtime code path, so additional behavior tests beyond the search smoke above were not added. The recursive walk itself (`collectMemoryFilesFromDir`) is already covered by upstream tests under `packages/memory-host-sdk/`.

## Test plan
- [x] `pnpm config:docs:gen` regenerates baseline cleanly (no other drift)
- [x] Nested memory smoke search on installed `2026.5.20` returns the new nested file at score `0.812`
- [x] On-branch runtime import shows `FIELD_HELP['agents.defaults.memorySearch']`, `buildPromptSection(...)` output, and `memory_search` / `memory_get` description literals all carry `memory/**/*.md`
- [ ] CI: lint / type / config-baseline check

target.title: refactor(gateway-client): expose request dispatch boundary
target.body:
Related: #96230

## What Problem This Solves

Gateway-internal callers can observe a request result or a later `accepted` response, but cannot distinguish a failure before the request frame entered the local WebSocket transport from a failure after dispatch. That distinction is required before later restart-recovery work can make conservative retry or refund decisions without guessing from promise settlement.

This is the first independently reviewable dependency extracted from #96230. The original PR remains frozen while its behavior is split into ordered, narrower changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The protocol client is the only layer that owns the synchronous `socket.send(...)` boundary, so this adds an optional `onDispatched` observer immediately after `send` returns successfully and routes it through the existing callback-isolation helper. The package client and high-level `callGateway` wrapper forward the same observer without changing request frames, protocol versions, timeout/abort cleanup, reconnect behavior, or `onAccepted` response semantics.

The observer contract is intentionally narrow: it means the request frame was handed to the local WebSocket transport. It does not mean the Gateway/server accepted or processed the request. The request option type lives in a dedicated small module and is re-exported from the existing protocol-client module, preserving import and structural type compatibility. `GatewayClient` forwards that shared option shape as a unit, then overrides only its normalized `expectFinal` and `timeoutMs` values; this keeps the oversized implementation LOC-neutral without deleting unrelated comments.

This is a root-cause boundary fix: higher layers no longer need to infer whether transport dispatch happened. The gateway-client package is private and the new field is additive and optional. A consumer/test-double sweep covered the package export, OpenClaw facade, SDK transport, accepted-response caller, both affected request stubs, and the node-host bridge. The node-host bridge only forwards `timeoutMs` across its IPC boundary, so later recovery code must use `callGateway` or introduce a separate IPC dispatch acknowledgement rather than assuming this observer is available there.

Out of scope for this PR: Plugin SDK/session-state isolation, recovery persistence, `mainRestartRecovery` admission or ownership, bounded recovery, quarantine, and Doctor repair. In particular, this PR does not write any production recovery state.

## User Impact

There is no direct end-user behavior change. Existing callers behave exactly as before; later recovery PRs can use a precise local transport-dispatch fact instead of broad failure inference.

Risk is limited to an additive observer callback. It is not invoked when WebSocket send throws, observer exceptions are isolated from request settlement, and the callback must not be interpreted as server acceptance.

## Evidence

Focused TDD reproduction before the original implementation:

```text
expected "vi.fn()" to be called 1 times, but got 0 times
```

Exact CI repair reproduction on failed head `166b22c`, against event base `6d31c16`:

```text

TypeScript LOC ratchet failed: oversized legacy files may not grow.
```

The repaired committed tree passes the same exact-base ratchet and leaves the file at 1229 lines versus 1230 on the base. Complete affected test files also pass:

